📖 Worked example — a full challenge-style problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — bits, bytes, and cost together
Problem: An image is 2,000 × 1,000 pixels, 3 bytes per pixel. (a) Raw size? (b) After 4:1 compression? (c) How many compressed images fit in 3 GB?

(a) 2,000 × 1,000 = 2,000,000 pixels × 3 bytes = 6,000,000 bytes = 6 MB.
(b) 4:1 means one quarter the size: 6 MB ÷ 4 = 1.5 MB.
(c) 3 GB = 3,000 MB; 3,000 ÷ 1.5 = 2,000 images.

Every “cost” question is this pattern: count the units, multiply by size-per-unit, then divide into the budget.

Numbers, Bits, and Cost

Everything a computer does reduces to bit patterns and the operations over them, so fluency here is non-negotiable. To read an unsigned binary number, add the place values of the set bits: 10110110 is 128+32+16+4+2 = 182. Grouping bits by fours converts to hex instantly: 1011 0110 is B6.

Two's Complement

In n-bit two's complement the most significant bit has weight -2^(n-1). So 8-bit 11010110 is 214 - 256 = -42, and the representable range is -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1)-1, i.e. -128..127 for 8 bits. Signed overflow happens when two same-signed operands produce a result whose sign flips: 79 + 49 = 128 cannot fit in signed 8 bits, so the pattern 10000000 reads as -128.

Bitwise and Boolean

AND/OR/XOR act per bit; XOR flips where bits differ. A left shift by k multiplies by 2^k (dropping high bits); a right shift divides. Truth tables let you verify logical equivalences such as De Morgan's laws.

Algorithm Cost

Rank growth as O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n). Binary search does about ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons worst case; naive recursive Fibonacci makes an exponential number of calls because it recomputes subproblems. When a problem says compute or trace, walk the steps literally rather than guessing.

📖 Worked example — reasoning about a system end-to-end

WORKED EXAMPLE — one page load, every layer
Problem: You tap a link on Wi-Fi. List what happens, in order, naming each responsible part.

1. Browser (application) asks DNS to turn the name into an IP address.
2. TCP opens a reliable connection to that IP; the HTTP request is split into packets.
3. IP/routers forward each packet hop by hop (packets may take different routes).
4. On your local network, Wi-Fi (link layer) carries frames between your device and the router using MAC addresses.
5. The server’s OS schedules the web-server process; it reads files via the file system and replies.
6. TCP reassembles packets in order; the browser renders the page.

Exam skill: match each behavior to its layer/component — naming (DNS), reliability (TCP), routing (IP), local delivery (MAC/link), execution (OS/process).

How Systems Are Built and Connected

SDLC: Waterfall runs fixed phases (requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance) in sequence and suits stable, well-understood requirements; agile delivers in short iterations and adapts when requirements change often. Neither is universally 'better' — the trade-off is predictability versus flexibility.

Operating Systems

A process has its own memory space; threads within a process share that memory, which makes them lighter to create but prone to race conditions. The scheduler multiplexes the CPU among ready threads. The memory hierarchy trades speed for capacity: CPU registers < L1/L2 cache < RAM < SSD < hard disk, from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest.

Networking

Match functions to layers: HTTP and DNS are application-layer; TCP/UDP are transport; IP addressing and routing are the network layer. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (handshake, ordering, retransmission); UDP is connectionless and low-latency, good for streaming or DNS lookups. A subnet with h host bits supports 2^h - 2 usable hosts (subtracting the network and broadcast addresses).

Data Structures & Thinking

A stack is LIFO; a queue is FIFO. Arrays give O(1) indexed access but costly insertion; linked lists give O(1) insertion at a known node but O(n) access. Computational thinking combines decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design — and professionals apply it under ethical duties like honesty and protecting user data.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

A data type is not a label stuck on a value. It is a contract with the machine that answers three questions at once: how many bytes to reserve, how to interpret the bits in them, and which operations are legal. The same 32 bits in memory are the integer 1078530011 or the decimal 3.14159 depending on nothing but the declared type. Memory holds no meaning; the type supplies it.

Five core types cover almost everything the OA asks about, and the exam tests whether you can pick the right one for a described value rather than recite the list.

TypeHoldsExampleChoose it when
Integerwhole numbers, no fractional part42, −7, 0you are counting, indexing or storing an ID
Real / floatnumbers with a fractional part3.14, −0.5you are measuring — money is the exception
Characterexactly one symbol'A', '7', '$'a single letter, digit or punctuation mark
Stringtext of any length"hello"anything you will never do arithmetic on
Booleantrue or false, nothing elsetruea yes/no state — a checkbox, a flag

The line between these is sharper than it looks, and two distinctions carry most of the marks. The character '7' is a symbol; the integer 7 is a number you can do arithmetic on. And the two numeric types behave differently even when they hold the same value: as integers, 7 / 2 is 3, because integer division keeps only the whole part and throws the remainder away. As reals, 7.0 / 2.0 is 3.5. Same symbols, different type, different answer.

That is also why the difference between exact and approximate matters. Integers are exact but bounded — an unsigned 8-bit integer holds 0 to 255 and nothing more. Floating point buys an enormous range by storing a number as mantissa × baseexponent, which is scientific notation in binary, and pays for it with precision: any fraction whose denominator is not a power of two cannot be stored exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Counting uses integers. Measuring uses floats. Money uses neither — it uses whole cents in an integer, because a rounding error in a float is a rounding error in someone's balance.

Strong typing and type mismatch

A strongly typed language enforces the declared type and refuses to silently mix incompatible ones. Storing "abc" into an integer variable is a type mismatch — the language stops you rather than guessing. Python is strongly typed: "Hello" + 5 raises a TypeError, while "Hello" + str(5) works because you converted deliberately.

The version of this the OA loves is the concatenation trap. If finalScore holds the string '95' and you compute finalScore + 5, many languages join them as text and give '955', not 100. The + did text-joining because the operand was text. When you expected a number and got text, that is a type mismatch caused by mixing types.

Converting between types

An implicit conversion happens automatically when a value is promoted to a compatible type — an integer used inside a floating-point expression becomes a float. This is widening, and it is safe, because the target can hold everything the source could. An explicit conversion, or cast, is one you request: converting a float to an integer truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so int(3.9) is 3 and int(−3.9) is −3. That is narrowing, it loses information, and that is exactly why the language makes you ask for it.

How text, images and sound become numbers

Every type in the table above is ultimately bits, and the encodings that make that possible are examined by name. ASCII covers 128 characters in 7 bits, so 'A' is 65. Unicode extends that to every writing system, and UTF-8 is the encoding that stores it using 1 to 4 bytes per character — which is why in Unicode text the byte count and the character count are not the same number.

Images work the same way with a different table: each pixel stores an RGB triple, one value each for red, green and blue, so a colour is three numbers. Sound is analog — a continuous wave — and becomes digital through sampling: pulse-code modulation (PCM) measures the wave many times a second and stores each measurement as a number. Bandwidth is the maximum rate a path can carry those bits, in bits per second.

Compression

Storing every byte is often wasteful, and compression divides into two kinds with a hard difference between them.

KindKeeps every bit?Used for
LosslessYes — the original is perfectly recoverableZIP, PNG, all text encoding
LossyNo — some detail is discarded permanentlyJPEG, MP3

Three classic text techniques are all lossless and all named in questions. Run-length encoding replaces repeats with a count plus the symbol, so AAAABBBCC becomes 4A3B2C. Keyword encoding replaces common words with short codes, so "and" might become &. Huffman encoding gives the most frequent characters the shortest codes.

Compression ratio is asked in two conventions and you must read which the question uses. As compressed ÷ original, a 200KB file reduced to 50KB gives 0.25 and smaller is better. As original ÷ compressed — the wording in the WGU glossary — the same file gives 4, or 4:1, and larger is better. They describe identical compression with the direction flipped.

📘 DEFINITION

Data type: a contract fixing how many bytes a value takes, how the bits are interpreted, and what operations are legal

Strong typing: the language enforces types and refuses to mix them without an explicit conversion

Type mismatch: assigning a value of the wrong type to a variable, or an operator receiving a type it cannot handle

Implicit conversion: automatic promotion to a compatible type — safe, widening

Explicit conversion (cast): a conversion you request; may lose data, e.g. float to int truncates

Declaration: a statement that defines a variable and its type — float price = 19.99;

Boolean expression: a statement that is either true or false, such as 4 > 3

★ ON THE OA

Match the value to the type: a checkbox is boolean, a price is float, a name is string, a count is integer. Phone numbers, ZIP codes and student IDs are strings — you never add two of them, and a numeric type destroys the leading zero in 007. And remember that "strongly typed" means the language enforces types, not that it has a lot of them.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Integer division is the single most common arithmetic bug in this section. 9 / 4 with two integers is 2, not 2.25 — the remainder 1 is what 9 mod 4 would give you. If a calculation needs a decimal answer, at least one operand must be a real number.

Everything in the previous section assumed the computer can store a number at all. Underneath, it cannot — it has only switches that are on or off. Binary is how those switches become numbers, and every representation question on the OA comes back to it.

Any number system works by place value: each column is worth the base raised to a power, counting from zero on the right. Decimal columns are powers of ten. Binary columns are powers of two, doubling leftward — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Memorise those eight numbers and you can read any byte.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — binary → decimal

Add the columns that are switched on.

  1     1     0     1
128  64  32  16   8   4   2   1     <- place values
              1   1   0   1         <- the number 1101

8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — decimal → binary

Divide by 2 repeatedly, keep the remainders, then read them bottom to top.

27 ÷ 2 = 13  r1   <- last digit
13 ÷ 2 =  6  r1
 6 ÷ 2 =  3  r0
 3 ÷ 2 =  1  r1
 1 ÷ 2 =  0  r1   <- first digit

read upward: 11011      check: 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 27

The faster method for small numbers is subtraction: take the biggest place value that fits, mark a 1, and repeat with what is left. For 13 — 8 fits (mark 1, 5 left), 4 fits (mark 1, 1 left), 2 does not (mark 0), 1 fits (mark 1) — giving 1101.

Hexadecimal

Binary is correct and unreadable, so people write it in hexadecimal — base 16, using 0–9 then A–F for 10–15. Its usefulness is a coincidence of arithmetic: 16 is 24, so one hex digit is exactly four bits, and converting needs no division at all. Split the binary into groups of four from the right and translate each group.

1101 1010  ->  D    A    ->  0xDA   (13 and 10)
0xFF = 1111 1111 = 255 = the largest unsigned byte

Negative numbers: two's complement

Computers have no minus sign, only bits, so a negative number has to be encoded. The obvious scheme is signed magnitude: use the leftmost bit as the sign, 0 for positive and 1 for negative, and the rest for the value. It is easy to read and bad to compute with, because it needs separate circuitry for addition and subtraction and it produces two different zeros.

Two's complement is what real machines use, and the reason is elegant: it makes subtraction into addition, so one adder circuit handles both signs. To negate a number, flip every bit, then add 1.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — representing −5 in 8-bit two's complement
 5  = 0000 0101
flip  = 1111 1010
add 1 = 1111 1011   ->  −5

check: 5 + (−5)  ->  0000 0101 + 1111 1011 = 1 0000 0000
       the carry out of the top bit is dropped, leaving 0000 0000 = 0  ✓

Two facts follow that the OA asks for directly. −1 is always all ones (11111111 in 8 bits) and 0 is all zeros. And the range is asymmetric — 8 bits span −128 to +127, one more negative than positive — because there is only one zero, so the spare pattern goes to the negative side.

Overflow

Overflow is what happens when a result needs more bits than the type has. It is not an error the machine reports; the carry bit is simply dropped and the stored answer is wrong.

CalculationResultFits in unsigned 8-bit (max 255)?
200 + 70270No — overflow, carry dropped, stored value is wrong
100 + 50150Yes
254 + 1255Yes — exactly the maximum, still fine

The other signed representations

Two's complement is what machines use, and two earlier schemes are still examined because they show why it won. In all three the leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 means positive, 1 means negative.

SchemeTo negate−5 in 8 bitsProblem
Signed magnitudeflip the sign bit only1000 0101two zeros (+0 and −0); addition needs separate circuitry
One's complementflip every bit1111 1010still two zeros; needs an end-around carry
Two's complementflip every bit, then add 11111 1011none — one zero, one adder for both signs

Reading down the "to negate" column shows the progression, and it is the cleanest way to remember which is which: signed magnitude flips one bit, one's complement flips them all, two's complement flips them all and adds one. That final +1 is what removes the duplicate zero and makes a single adder circuit work for both positive and negative values.

📘 DEFINITION

Place value: each column is worth the base raised to a power, counting from 0 at the right

Binary (base 2): the two-symbol system a computer actually stores; columns double leftward

Hexadecimal (base 16): shorthand for binary; one hex digit is exactly four bits

Signed magnitude: leftmost bit is the sign, the rest is the value; produces two zeros

Two's complement: the standard encoding for negatives — flip all bits and add 1

Overflow: a result too large for the available bits; the carry is dropped and the value is wrong

Radix point: the "decimal point" in any base — binary 101.11 uses one

Bit / byte: a single 0 or 1; eight bits, enough for one character

★ ON THE OA

Storage units in order, each roughly a thousand of the last: bit → byte → KB → MB → GB → TB. Unsigned 8-bit range is 0–255; signed two's complement 8-bit is −128 to +127. To negate: flip every bit, add 1. One hex digit = four bits.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Check every conversion by converting back. It takes five seconds and it catches the reading-the-remainders-downward error, which is the one people actually make under time pressure.

A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while the program runs. It has five properties, and the two that exams probe are the last two: a name, a type, a value, an address in memory, a scope — where the name is visible — and a lifetime — how long the storage exists. Scope is about the source code; lifetime is about runtime. They are related and not the same thing.

Three separate events happen to a variable and keeping them apart explains most beginner confusion. Declaring reserves storage and fixes the type. Initializing gives it its first value. Assigning replaces that value later. Reading a variable that was declared but never initialized is a genuine hazard: some languages refuse to compile, and others hand you garbage — whatever bytes happened to already be at that address — producing bugs that appear on one machine and not another.

Constants

A constant is a value that cannot change during execution. An unnamed constant is a literal written straight into the code, like 3.14 — considered poor practice, and known as a magic number because nobody reading it can tell what it means. A named constant gives it a meaningful name: final double PI = 3.14159;. That buys three things — it documents intent, it centralises change so one edit updates all twelve uses, and it turns an accidental modification into a compile error.

Identifiers and naming

An identifier is the name of a variable, method or class. The rules are enforced by the language: it must start with a letter or underscore (never a digit), it must be a single word with no spaces, and it must not be a reserved keyword such as int, while or class. So total and _count are valid and 2nd is not.

Conventions, by contrast, are agreements between programmers that the compiler ignores entirely — and the OA tests whether you can name them.

ConventionLooks likeTypically used for
camelCasemyVariableNamevariables and methods in Java
PascalCaseMyVariableNameclass names
snake_casemy_variable_namePython variables, constants, config
kebab-casemy-variable-nameURLs and CSS — not valid in Java
Hungarian notationstrNamea type prefix on the name
Mixed case with underscoresMy_Variable_Namereadability in some house styles

Scope, and why global variables are discouraged

A local variable is declared inside a function and visible only there — created when the function starts, destroyed when it returns. A global variable is declared outside all functions, visible everywhere, and alive for the whole run. When a local shares a name with a global, the local shadows it: every assignment inside the function hits the local copy, and the global is untouched.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — shadowing
global total = 100

function f():
    total = 5           # a NEW local, not the global
    print(total)        # 5

f()
print(total)            # 100 — the global was never changed

Globals are readable from anywhere, which sounds convenient and is precisely the problem: any function may change one, so behaviour depends on execution order and bugs become impossible to trace. That is coupling, the thing modular design exists to reduce. The exam phrasing to recognise is that locals promote encapsulation and modularity while globals create hidden dependencies.

Lifetime explains the rest. Locals live in a stack frame created when a function is called and destroyed when it returns — which is why a local cannot be read after the function ends, why a value must be returned to survive, and why runaway recursion overflows the stack.

Literals, and naming conventions

A literal is a fixed value written directly in the code — 42, "dog", true. It is the value itself, not a name for one, which is exactly what makes an unexplained literal a magic number.

Identifiers follow conventions rather than rules, and the exam asks you to recognise them by name.

ConventionLooks likeConventionally used for
camelCasefinalScore, totalPricevariables and methods
PascalCaseMyClass, BankAccountclass and type names
snake_casefinal_scorevariables in Python and C
UPPER_SNAKELEGAL_AGE, TAX_RATEnamed constants

camelCase starts lower and capitalises each later word; PascalCase capitalises the first as well. That single difference is the whole question.

Mutability, and two names for one thing

Assigning one variable to another does not always copy. For a simple number it does. For a mutable object — a list, an array, a dictionary — the variable holds a reference to it, and assigning copies the reference, not the contents.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a            // b now refers to the SAME list
b.append(9)

a is [1, 2, 3, 9]    <- changed too; there is only one list

Both names point at one object, so a change through either is visible through both. To get an independent list you must copy it explicitly. Reading a variable before assigning it anything is the related trap: it holds either nothing or leftover memory, and the result is a crash or a silently wrong answer.

📘 DEFINITION

Variable: a named storage location whose value can change

Constant: a named value that cannot change during execution

Identifier: the name of a variable, method or class

Keyword: a reserved word with built-in meaning that cannot be used as an identifier

Scope: the region of the program where a name is visible

Lifetime: how long the storage for a variable exists at runtime

Garbage: the unpredictable leftover value in an uninitialized variable

Type safety: using a variable only in ways consistent with its type

Lvalue: something that can appear on the left of = — a memory location such as x

★ ON THE OA

A variable can change, a constant cannot, and a keyword is reserved by the language — an identifier is just a name, which both variables and constants have. Identifiers cannot start with a digit. Assignment is right-to-left associative, so a = b = c = 5 sets all three to 5.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Scope is the idea that makes everything later in this course possible: it is what encapsulation in object-oriented programming is built on, and the stack that holds local variables is the same stack the operating system allocates per thread in Section 4.

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, and pseudocode writes that logic in plain language without any real language's punctuation. What makes both tractable is a result worth stating outright: every algorithm ever written, however complex, can be expressed with exactly three control structures. This is the structured programming theorem, and it is a favourite exam idea because it means identifying which of the three a piece of logic uses answers most construct questions on its own.

ConstructWhat it doesLooks like
Sequencesteps run in order, top to bottom, once eachplain ordered statements
Selection (branch)chooses a path based on a conditionIF / IF-ELSE / SWITCH
Repetition (iteration)repeats a block while a condition holdsWHILE / FOR / DO-WHILE

Selection comes in two named forms the OA distinguishes: a single-alternative if does something only when a condition is true, while a dual-alternative if/else picks one of two paths. In a chain of conditions they are tested top to bottom and the first true branch wins — the rest are skipped even if they would also be true, which is the entire answer to grade-boundary trace questions.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — selection in pseudocode
START
  INPUT number
  IF number > 0 THEN
      PRINT "The number is positive."
  ELSE IF number < 0 THEN
      PRINT "The number is negative."
  ELSE
      PRINT "The number is zero."
  ENDIF
END

The four loops

Loops are where the distinctions get tested hardest, and the one that decides the most questions is when the condition is checked.

LoopTests the conditionRuns at least once?Use it when
Pretest (while)before each passNo — can run zero timesthe data might be empty
Posttest (do-while)after each passYes — always onceyou must prompt before you can judge the answer
Forbefore each pass, with a counternothe number of repetitions is known up front
Infinitea condition that never goes falseforevera background worker — otherwise a bug

Two more names for the same idea appear in WGU wording. A count-controlled loop repeats a known number of times: start a counter, test it against a limit, update it. An event-controlled loop keeps going until something happens, and the number of passes is not known in advance. The loop control variable is whichever variable the condition tests, and an infinite loop is almost always caused by forgetting to update it.

Nesting

A nested structure is simply one control structure placed inside another, and reading nested logic is what harder questions test.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading nested logic
WHILE (more students)
    IF (score >= 60)
        PRINT "Pass"
    ELSE
        PRINT "Fail"
    ENDIF
END WHILE

A loop around a decision: each pass makes one pass/fail judgement. If a question asks how many constructs are used, the answer is two — repetition and selection.

Nesting also has a cost you will meet again. Two nested loops each running n times execute the body n × n times, and that is precisely where O(n²) comes from in Section 3 — and why sorting algorithms built on nested loops collapse on large inputs.

Why the three-construct claim matters

It is tempting to treat "every program is sequence, selection and repetition" as a slogan. It is not — it is a statement about what you have to be able to read. When you meet unfamiliar code in an exam, you are never looking at something new; you are looking at those three shapes nested inside each other. The skill being tested is decomposing what you see back into them.

That is also why the goto statement disappeared from modern practice. Before structured programming, a program could jump anywhere, which made control flow impossible to follow — the famous "spaghetti code". The three constructs are sufficient, so the jump was unnecessary, and removing it made programs readable. If a question asks whether goto is needed for some piece of logic, the answer is always no.

One practical consequence for tracing: because a loop repeats and a branch chooses, the two nest in opposite ways with very different results. A branch inside a loop makes a decision on every pass. A loop inside a branch runs the whole loop, or does not run it at all. Reading which is on the outside is the first thing to establish before counting anything.

Input, processing and output

Before the three constructs there are the three stages every program has. Input is data coming in from outside — typed at a keyboard, read from a file, sampled from a sensor. Processing is the work done on it. Output is the result sent out — printed to the screen, written to a file, sent to a device.

The exam tests the direction: a keyboard, a mouse, a scanner and a sensor are input; a screen, a printer and a speaker are output. Printing a result to the screen is output even though it happens at the end of a calculation.

Choosing the loop from the description

The description saysUseBecause
exactly 50 items, 10 times, once per recorda count-controlled loop (FOR)the number of repeats is known before it starts
until the user types quit, until end of filean event-controlled loop (WHILE)the number of repeats depends on something that happens

Read for the phrase that fixes the count. "The 50 items in an array" fixes it; "until the correct password is entered" does not — you cannot know in advance how many attempts there will be.

Nested conditionals

When one of several ranges must be chosen, the constructs chain: IF … ELSE IF … ELSE IF … ELSE. Order matters, because the first true test wins and the rest are skipped.

IF   score >= 90 THEN grade = "A"
ELSE IF score >= 80 THEN grade = "B"
ELSE IF score >= 70 THEN grade = "C"
ELSE                      grade = "F"

Written descending as above, a score of 85 fails the first test and passes the second — correct. Written ascending, 85 would match >= 70 first and be graded C. The tests do not need an upper bound because everything higher was already caught.

Short-circuit evaluation

In most languages AND stops as soon as it meets a false operand, and OR stops as soon as it meets a true one — there is no point evaluating the rest. This is short-circuit evaluation, and it makes the order of the conditions part of the logic.

IF (x != 0 AND 10 / x > 2)     // SAFE
    x = 0 makes the first test false, so 10 / x is never evaluated

IF (10 / x > 2 AND x != 0)     // CRASHES
    the division runs first, and divides by zero

The guard must come first. Whenever a condition protects the one after it — a non-zero check before a division, a not-null check before a field access — reversing the two turns working code into a crash.

📘 DEFINITION

Algorithm: a step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem

Pseudocode: the logic written in plain language, without a real language's syntax

Sequence: statements executed in order, one after another

Selection / branch: the decision point where the path splits

Repetition / iteration: running instructions multiple times with a loop

Loop control variable: the variable the loop condition tests

Nested structure: one control structure placed inside another

Abstract step: a high-level "what to do" step that does not yet say how — e.g. "validate the username"

★ ON THE OA

Structured programming uses exactly three control structures and needs no goto. Map the keywords: IF/ELSE → selection, WHILE/FOR → repetition, plain ordered steps → sequence. If a question asks which loop is guaranteed to execute its body, the answer is the posttest do-while.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Off-by-one is the standard loop error: valid indexes run 0 to n−1, so the test is i < n. Writing i <= n reads one position past the end of the data.

When an expression mixes operators, two rules decide the answer before any arithmetic happens: precedence settles which operator goes first, and associativity settles which way to work when two operators tie.

The precedence ladder is short enough to memorise, and the OA expects you to have done so.

1.  ( )                      parentheses — always first
2.  exponents
3.  *  /  mod                multiplicative   (left to right)
4.  +  −                     additive         (left to right)
5.  <  <=  >  >=  ==  !=     comparison
6.  AND, OR, NOT             logic
7.  =                        assignment       (RIGHT to left)

The consequence that catches people is that arithmetic always finishes before comparison, and comparison always finishes before logic. So a + b > c means (a + b) > c, and no inner parentheses are needed in x > 0 AND y > 0.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 − 6 / 2

Multiplication and division first, left to right, then the additions.

2 + 3 * 4 − 6 / 2
2 +  12  −  3            <- * and / resolved first
        11               <- then + and −, left to right

with parentheses: (2 + 3) * 4 − 6 / 2  =  5 * 4 − 3  =  17

Associativity decides ties. Most arithmetic operators are left-to-right, so 10 − 3 − 2 is (10 − 3) − 2 = 5, not 10 − (3 − 2) = 9. Assignment is the exception and runs right-to-left, which is why a = b = c = 5 works and sets all three.

The modulo operator

mod returns the remainder of a division, not the quotient, and it is worth being fluent with because it powers a surprising number of exam questions. 10 mod 3 is 1; 10 mod 4 is 2, because 4 goes into 10 twice with 2 left over. Two idioms follow: n mod 2 == 0 tests whether n is even, and n mod 10 extracts the last digit of n.

Magic numbers

A magic number is a bare literal dropped into code with no explanation — if (age > 18) or a tax rate of 0.0825 repeated in four places. Nobody reading it can tell what it means, and nobody changing it can be sure they found all of them. The fix is the named constant from 1.2: final int LEGAL_AGE = 18; and then if (age > LEGAL_AGE).

Where precedence actually bites

Precedence questions rarely look like precedence questions. They look like a formula that produced the wrong number. The classic is an average: a + b + c / 3 divides only c by three, because division binds tighter than addition. The fix is parentheses — (a + b + c) / 3 — and the reason people miss it is that the written formula has a division bar, which is a parenthesis you cannot see.

The comparison and logic levels matter for the same reason one step later. Because arithmetic resolves before comparison, total + tax > limit compares the sum, which is what you meant. But because comparison resolves before logic, a > b AND c is not asking what an English reader thinks — it compares a with b, then combines that with c, which is only meaningful if c is itself a Boolean.

Unary operators and increment

A unary operator takes one operand rather than two: negation in −x, logical NOT in !flag. They sit near the top of the ladder, just under parentheses, so −2 ** 2 and (−2) ** 2 can differ depending on the language's convention. Increment and decrement, written ++ and −−, are unary shorthand for adding or subtracting one, and they are worth recognising in pseudocode even where the exam does not require you to write them.

= and == are different operators

One equals sign assigns; two equals signs compare. x = 5 stores 5 in x and is a statement; x == 5 asks whether x holds 5 and produces true or false.

x = 5        // assignment  — x now holds 5
x == 5       // comparison  — evaluates to true
x != 5       // comparison  — evaluates to false

IF (x = 5)   // a classic bug: assigns, then tests the result

They sit at opposite ends of the precedence ladder — comparison at level 5, assignment at level 7, last of all — which is why an assignment inside a condition binds after everything else and quietly succeeds instead of testing anything.

Division depends on the operand types

The division operator behaves differently depending on what it is dividing, and this produces more wrong answers than any other single rule.

ExpressionResultWhy
7 / 2 (both integers)3integer division truncates — the remainder is discarded
7 / 2.0 (one is real)3.5the integer is promoted, so real division happens
7 mod 21mod gives exactly the remainder integer division threw away

So total / count with total = 7 and count = 2 gives 2, not 3.5 — an average computed in integer arithmetic is silently wrong. The fix is to make one operand real. Together, / and mod recover the whole division: 7 / 2 is 3 remainder 1.

📘 DEFINITION

Precedence: which operator is applied first when several appear in one expression

Associativity: the direction operators of equal precedence group in — left-to-right for arithmetic, right-to-left for assignment

Operand: a value an operator acts on — 3 and 5 in 3 + 5

Binary operator: one that works on two operands

Modulo (mod): the remainder after division

Magic number: an unexplained hard-coded literal; replace it with a named constant

Overhead: extra time, memory or resources used beyond a program's core task

★ ON THE OA

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction: 5 + 2 × 3 is 11, not 21. When operators tie, go left to right. And mod gives the remainder — 10 mod 4 is 2, never 2.5.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When an expression looks ambiguous, add the parentheses even if precedence already gives the answer you want. It costs nothing at runtime and removes the reader's doubt — which includes yours, three weeks later.

Computational thinking is the structured thought process of framing a problem so that a computer — or anyone following instructions literally — could solve it. It is not programming, and that distinction is the point: you do it before any code exists, and it is what makes the code writeable.

Four pillars make it up, and the OA asks you to name the one a scenario describes, so learn them by what they do rather than as a list.

PillarWhat you actually doExample
Decompositionbreak a large problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved separately"build an online store" becomes catalogue, cart, checkout, accounts
Pattern recognitionspot similarities between problems or within datanoticing every report page needs the same header and filter logic
Abstractionignore the detail that does not matter to the problema route planner treats a city as points and distances, not buildings
Algorithm designwrite the ordered steps that solve itthe numbered procedure for checking out a cart

Abstraction is the pillar most often misread, because "ignoring detail" sounds like carelessness. It is the opposite: it is deciding deliberately which details are irrelevant to this problem. A map that showed every brick would be useless for navigation. In computing the same move appears at every level — a programmer uses a sort function without knowing which algorithm it runs, and that function uses memory without knowing about voltages.

The four are also not a strict sequence. In practice you decompose, notice a pattern between two of the pieces, abstract away what they do not share, and design one algorithm that handles both. But an exam question describing a single activity has one right label, and the labels are the ones above.

Why it comes before code

The practical version of all this is the habit from problem solving generally: understand the problem, work one example by hand, write the steps in plain language, and only then translate them into a language. Working an example by hand is the step people skip and the one that catches the most errors — if you cannot compute the answer for one specific input on paper, no amount of syntax will get you there.

Telling the four pillars apart under pressure

Because all four pillars sound reasonable for any problem, exam scenarios are written so that exactly one is being described. The reliable test is to ask what the person in the scenario is actually doing to the problem. Breaking it into parts is decomposition. Noticing that two parts are the same shape is pattern recognition. Deciding what can be ignored is abstraction. Writing the ordered steps is algorithm design.

A worked case makes it concrete. Planning a system to grade thousands of exams: splitting it into scanning, marking and reporting is decomposition. Noticing that every multiple-choice question is marked the same way is pattern recognition. Deciding the marker does not need the student's name, only the answers, is abstraction. Writing "for each answer, compare with the key, add one if it matches" is algorithm design.

One more distinction the OA relies on: computational thinking is a way of thinking about problems, not a programming skill. It applies to organising a wedding as much as to writing software, and questions sometimes deliberately use a non-computing scenario to check you understood that.

📘 DEFINITION

Computational thinking: framing a problem so that its solution can be carried out by a computer

Decomposition: breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems

Pattern recognition: identifying similarities between or within problems

Abstraction: deliberately ignoring detail that is irrelevant to the problem at hand

Algorithm design: specifying the ordered steps that solve the problem

Algorithm: a finite sequence of unambiguous steps producing a result

★ ON THE OA

A memory hook for the four pillars in order — All Programmers Practise Algorithms: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design. Splitting a big problem into sub-problems is decomposition; focusing only on the essentials is abstraction. Those two are the pair the OA most often asks you to tell apart.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Every later section is an application of this. The SDLC is decomposition applied to a whole project, subprograms are decomposition applied to code, and Big-O is what happens when you compare two algorithm designs for the same problem.

The Software Development Life Cycle is the organised, multi-phase process a team follows to build and maintain software. The analogy that makes it stick is building a house: you do not start nailing boards before you know what the owner wants, and you do not move people in before an inspection.

The classic ordering has seven phases, and the OA asks two things about them — the order, and what each one produces.

PhaseWhat happensWhat comes out
1. Planningdecide feasibility, scope, budget and schedulea project plan
2. Analysisgather requirements — what must it do?a requirements document
3. Designplan the logic and structureflowcharts, pseudocode, diagrams
4. Implementationwrite the code — "translate the design"working source code
5. Testingverify it does what the requirements saidtest results and defect reports
6. Deploymentrelease it to usersa live system
7. Maintenancefix, adapt and improve after releaseupdates and patches

Two of these carry more exam weight than the rest. Maintenance is where most of a system's total cost and time actually goes — it is the longest phase, not an afterthought, and questions about "the majority of a program's lifetime" point here. And design is the phase where flowcharts and pseudocode belong; if a question says "plan the logic", it is describing design, not implementation.

Models: waterfall and agile

The phases above describe what gets done. A model describes how they are sequenced. Waterfall runs them strictly once, in order, each phase finishing before the next begins — predictable and documented, but expensive to change once requirements are locked. Agile runs short iterations that each go through the whole cycle, delivering a working increment every few weeks — flexible and responsive to change, at the cost of less up-front certainty about the final scope.

The useful way to hold the difference: waterfall assumes you know the requirements at the start; agile assumes you will learn them as you go. Neither is the "right" one, and questions usually describe a situation and ask which fits.

Why the order is the question

Almost every SDLC question is really an ordering question in disguise. It describes an activity and asks which phase it belongs to, or asks what comes immediately before or after something. So it is worth being able to state not just the sequence but the reason for it: you cannot design what you have not specified, cannot code what you have not designed, cannot test what you have not built, and cannot deploy what has not passed testing. Each phase consumes the output of the one before.

The phase people place wrongly is design. Flowcharts, pseudocode and diagrams are design artefacts — planning the logic — not implementation. Implementation is writing the actual code, which WGU sometimes words as "translate the design into code". If a question mentions pseudocode, it is describing design.

Maintenance is the other one worth expecting. It is not a small tail on the end: most of a system's total cost and most of its calendar life happen after release, in fixing defects, adapting to new requirements and improving performance. A question about where the majority of effort goes over a program's lifetime is pointing at maintenance.

The other models, and what agile looks like in practice

Waterfall and agile are the two poles, and two more models appear in questions between them. The spiral model repeats the phases in cycles like agile, but adds an explicit risk analysis step to every cycle — so it suits large projects where the cost of getting it wrong is high. The iterative and incremental model builds the system in successive versions, each adding function to a working product.

Agile itself is a philosophy rather than a procedure, and Scrum is its most common concrete framework. Work happens in fixed-length sprints, usually two to four weeks, each ending in a potentially shippable increment. The vocabulary is examined: a product backlog is the prioritised list of everything wanted, a sprint backlog is what this sprint has committed to, the daily stand-up is a short synchronisation meeting, and the retrospective at the end asks how the team can work better next time.

📘 DEFINITION

SDLC: the multi-phase process for developing and maintaining software

Requirements: the statement of what the software must do, produced in analysis

Design: planning the logic and structure — flowcharts and pseudocode live here

Implementation: writing the code that realises the design

Testing: verifying the software meets its requirements

Deployment: releasing the software to its users

Maintenance: fixing and improving software after release — the longest phase

Waterfall: a sequential model completing each phase before the next

Agile: an iterative model delivering working increments in short cycles

★ ON THE OA

Know the phases in order and be able to name one from a scenario. "The team is writing test cases" is testing, which comes after implementation. "Gathering requirements" is analysis. "Writing code" is implementation. Order is what the question is testing.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a scenario mentions changing requirements mid-project, the expected answer is agile. When it mentions fixed requirements, regulatory sign-off or heavy documentation, it is waterfall.

A code of ethics is a set of professional guidelines governing how computing professionals should behave. It is not law and carries no criminal penalty — its force is professional: membership, reputation, and in some fields licensure. Two bodies publish the codes the OA cares about.

BodyFull nameCentre of gravity
ACMAssociation for Computing Machinerycomputing broadly — software, research, data
IEEEInstitute of Electrical and Electronics Engineershardware and electrical engineering

Both codes share the same themes, and the shared themes are what most questions test rather than the differences: protect the public — safety, health and welfare come first, ahead of employer or client interest; be honest and avoid conflicts of interest; respect privacy and confidentiality; credit others' work; and maintain and improve technical competence. That last phrase is WGU's own wording for what adopting the IEEE code commits a company to.

When a scenario violates both codes, it is typically one that puts people at risk while also concealing something — shipping a component known to be unsafe, or hiding a breach from the users it affects.

Intellectual property and licensing

Copyright protects a creative work automatically from the moment it is made. A licence is the creator saying what others may do with it — so a licence does not remove copyright, it grants permissions under it.

Licence typeWhat you may doExample
Proprietary (closed)use it under the terms you bought; you cannot see or change the sourcemost commercial software
Copyleft open sourceuse, modify and redistribute — but derivatives must stay open under the same licenceGPL
Permissive open sourceuse, modify and redistribute with few restrictions, including in closed productsMIT, Apache
Public domainanything — no rights reserved at allexpired copyright, or a deliberate release

The distinction that decides questions is copyleft versus permissive. Ship a commercial product built on GPL code and you must release your own source under the GPL; build the same product on MIT code and you need not. "Open source" alone does not tell you which — you have to read which family the licence is in.

Fair use is a separate idea and a narrow one: it is a legal doctrine permitting limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching and research. It is a defence judged case by case on factors including how much was used and whether the use harms the market for the original — not a blanket permission.

System versus application software

One more classification the OA asks for directly. System software manages the machine itself — the operating system, device drivers, utilities. Application software does a task for the user — a spreadsheet, a browser, a game. An OS is system software; a word processor is application software.

Software piracy

Piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software or media — downloading a paid application without paying, sharing a licence key, or distributing copyrighted films. It is a copyright violation rather than a licensing subtlety, and it is distinct from the open-source questions above: an open licence grants permissions, while piracy is use with no permission at all.

Cybercrime, and who investigates it

Ethics is what you should do; cybercrime is what the law forbids. A cybercrime is any crime committed using a computer or network — unauthorised access, identity theft, ransomware, phishing, denial-of-service, online fraud, and the distribution of copyrighted material. The exam asks you to recognise one from a scenario and to know where it is reported.

BodyWhat it isHandles
IC3Internet Crime Complaint Center, run by the FBIthe place U.S. victims file a cybercrime complaint
FBIFederal Bureau of Investigationcybercrime generally — intrusion, fraud, IP theft
U.S. Secret Servicea Treasury-founded agency, now Homeland Securityfinancial and payment-system crime — card fraud, counterfeiting

The distinction that gets tested: a victim reports to IC3; a payment-system or financial crime is investigated by the Secret Service. Complaints and reported losses to the FBI have risen year on year, not fallen. Penalties scale with harm and can include fines, restitution to victims, and imprisonment — a cybercrime is not a civil matter that ends with a payment.

The two professional bodies, and what each is for

BodyStands forIts focus
ACMAssociation for Computing Machinerythe Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct — how a computing professional must behave
IEEEInstitute of Electrical and Electronics Engineerstechnical standards for computing and electronics (Wi-Fi 802.11, Ethernet 802.3)

They also publish a joint Software Engineering Code of Ethics. The ACM code turns on one idea the OA tests repeatedly: the public good comes first. When a scenario pits your employer's reputation against user safety or honesty, the ethical answer is the one that protects the user — disclose the flaw, refuse to stay silent, report it up and then out if nothing is done.

The second recurring idea is that being able to is not being allowed to. Deploying employee surveillance simply because the technology makes it possible fails the code: capability is not justification.

Privacy principles

Privacy questions are scenario-shaped and resolve to a small number of named principles.

PrincipleMeansViolated by
Data minimisationcollect only what the stated purpose needsgathering extra personal data "just in case"
Purpose limitationuse data only for the purpose it was collected forselling analytics data collected for delivery tracking
Authorised accessonly people with a legitimate need may see itusing a coworker's login to read personnel records
Consentthe person knows and agreestracking location with no disclosure

Continuous monitoring of users' network activity and communications is surveillance, and it is a privacy concern whether or not it is legal where you are.

📘 DEFINITION

Code of ethics: professional guidelines for how computing professionals should behave

ACM: Association for Computing Machinery — its code covers computing broadly

IEEE: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers — hardware and electrical focus

Copyright: automatic legal protection for an original creative work

Licence: the permissions a creator grants others under copyright

Copyleft (GPL): open-source licensing requiring derivatives to stay open

Permissive (MIT, Apache): open-source licensing with few restrictions on reuse

Public domain: no rights reserved; free for any use

Fair use: limited use of copyrighted work without permission for purposes such as teaching or criticism

System software: software that manages the computer — OS, drivers, utilities

Application software: software that performs tasks for the user

★ ON THE OA

A question about a code focused on hardware or electronics points to IEEE; a general computing-professional code points to ACM. Both prioritise the public interest above employer or client. For licences: GPL forces your derivative open, MIT does not, public domain reserves nothing.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

"Open source" and "free" are not the same claim, and neither means "public domain". Open source describes access to the source under a licence with terms; public domain means no rights are reserved at all.

Ethics says what a professional should do. Security is the set of techniques for making the wrong thing hard to do, and forensics is what happens after someone does it anyway. All three appear on the OA as concepts rather than as anything you implement.

The frame everything else hangs on is the CIA triad — the three properties security is trying to preserve.

PropertyMeansBroken when
Confidentialityonly authorised parties can read the dataa database of customer records leaks
Integritythe data has not been altered without authorisationa transaction amount is silently changed
Availabilityauthorised users can reach it when neededa denial-of-service attack takes the site down

Encryption

Encryption scrambles readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption reverses it. The oldest form is a cipher such as the Caesar shift, which moves every letter a fixed number of places — trivially breakable, but it demonstrates the shape: an algorithm plus a key.

Modern encryption divides into two families, and the difference is which keys are involved.

TypeKeysTrade-offUsed for
Symmetricone shared key encrypts and decryptsfast, but both sides must already share the key secretlyencrypting stored files, bulk data
Asymmetrica public key encrypts, a private key decryptsslower, but no secret needs to be shared in advanceestablishing secure connections, digital signatures

Asymmetric encryption solves the problem symmetric encryption creates: how do two parties agree a shared secret over a channel someone may be listening to? You publish your public key freely, anyone can encrypt with it, and only your private key can undo it. In practice the two are combined — asymmetric to exchange a symmetric key, then symmetric for the actual traffic, because it is much faster.

Hashing is often grouped with these and is a different thing: a hash is one-way. It turns any input into a fixed-length value that cannot be reversed, which is why passwords are stored as hashes and why a matching hash proves a file has not been altered.

Digital forensics

Digital forensics is the disciplined recovery and analysis of digital evidence, and its governing idea is the chain of custody: a documented record of who handled the evidence, when, and what they did with it. Break the chain and the evidence may be inadmissible however incriminating it is.

That is why investigators never work on the original. They take a verified copy — verified by hashing the original and the copy and confirming the hashes match — and analyse that, leaving the original untouched. Altering the original breaks the chain of custody, and no result obtained afterwards can repair it.

Lawful surveillance and decryption follow the same logic in a different arena: they generally require a warrant or comparable legal authority. The technical ability to decrypt something is not the question the exam is asking — the authorisation is.

📘 DEFINITION

CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability — the three goals of information security

Plaintext / ciphertext: readable data before encryption; scrambled data after

Cipher: an algorithm for encrypting, such as the Caesar shift

Symmetric encryption: one shared key both encrypts and decrypts — fast, but the key must be shared securely

Asymmetric encryption: a public key encrypts and a private key decrypts; no shared secret needed

Hashing: a one-way function producing a fixed-length value, used for passwords and integrity checks

Digital forensics: the recovery and analysis of digital evidence for investigation

Chain of custody: the documented record of everyone who handled evidence and what they did

★ ON THE OA

Digital forensics preserves evidence through a documented chain of custody, and lawful decryption or surveillance normally requires a warrant. Symmetric = one shared key; asymmetric = public key encrypts, private key decrypts. Hashing is one-way and is not encryption.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Altering the original evidence breaks the chain of custody. Investigators work on a copy whose hash matches the original — that hash match is the proof nothing changed.

Before writing code, programmers plan the logic — and the two tools for that are a flowchart, which shows the flow as a diagram, and pseudocode, which writes it as plain steps that read like English but follow programming logic. Neither belongs to any language, which is the point: the logic can be checked before syntax gets in the way.

Flowchart shapes are standardised and the OA asks you to name them.

ShapeMeans
Ovalstart or end
Parallelograminput or output
Rectanglea process — a calculation or assignment
Diamonda decision — a condition with two exits
Arrowthe direction of flow

Reading WGU-style pseudocode

WGU uses a consistent style, and questions are usually "what does this output" rather than "write this". The keywords are INPUT, OUTPUT, IF/ELSE/ENDIF, WHILE/END WHILE and FOR, with assignment written as = or SET.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an average with validation
START
  SET total = 0
  SET count = 0
  INPUT n
  WHILE n != -1
      SET total = total + n
      SET count = count + 1
      INPUT n
  END WHILE
  IF count > 0 THEN
      OUTPUT total / count
  ELSE
      OUTPUT "no values entered"
  ENDIF
END

Notice the guard on the last decision. Dividing by count when no values were entered would divide by zero, so the IF exists to prevent it — the same defensive habit that shows up as parameter checking later.

Arithmetic in pseudocode

The arithmetic operators are where the OA plants its errors, and the three division operators must be kept apart.

OperatorDoesExample
/true (floating-point) division7 / 2 = 3.5
//floor or integer division — truncates7 // 2 = 3
%modulo — the remainder7 % 2 = 1
*multiplication7 * 2 = 14
**exponent7 ** 2 = 49

WGU also words type conversion in a specific way that is worth recognising verbatim: float(age) converts an integer to a floating-point number, and int(num) converts a float to an integer by truncating — not rounding. To add ten to a variable the expression is value + 10, and to store it back, value = value + 10.

How to be graded on pseudocode

Pseudocode has no compiler, so the standard it is held to is whether another person could follow it unambiguously. That means three habits. Name variables meaningfully — totalScore, not t. Indent the body of every branch and loop, because indentation is how a reader sees the structure. And close what you open: ENDIF for every IF, END WHILE for every WHILE, so where a block stops is never a guess.

The other half of the skill is reading it, which is what the OA mostly asks. Given a fragment and a set of inputs, the reliable method is a trace table: one column for each variable, one row for each pass, filled in line by line rather than held in your head. It feels slow and it is the difference between an answer you can check and an answer you guessed.

Watch the boundaries when you trace. A loop written WHILE count < 5 starting at 0 runs five times and leaves count at 5 — the value that failed the test. Questions frequently ask for the value after the loop, which is one more than the last value used inside it.

Connecting the symbols

The arrows joining flowchart shapes are called flowlines, and they carry the direction of flow. Two conventions matter for reading: flow runs top to bottom and left to right unless an arrowhead says otherwise, and every decision diamond has exactly two flowlines leaving it, labelled Yes/No or True/False. A shape with no outgoing flowline other than the terminal oval is a sign the diagram is incomplete.

Flowchart symbols

A flowchart shows the same algorithm as a picture, and each shape has a fixed meaning that is asked directly.

ShapeMeans
Oval (terminal)start or end
Parallelograminput or output — READ, DISPLAY
Rectanglea process — a calculation or an assignment
Diamonda decision — one way in, a labelled branch for each answer
Arrowthe flow of control from one step to the next

The rectangle is the one people lose marks on: "Multiply subtotal by taxRate" is a process step, not a decision and not output.

The accumulator pattern

Totalling and averaging appear constantly, and both use the same shape: a running total and a count, each initialised to zero before the loop and updated inside it.

SET total TO 0            // accumulator
SET count TO 0            // counter
FOR each number IN list
    SET total TO total + number
    SET count TO count + 1
END FOR
SET average TO total / count

Two things are tested. Initialising inside the loop resets the total every pass and the answer is always the last value. And an average needs both running values — a total alone cannot produce one.

Off-by-one

An array of length n has indices 0 to n − 1. A loop written FOR i = 0 TO length inclusive runs one time too many and reads index n, which does not exist — an off-by-one error, and the crash is an index-out-of-bounds. The correct bound is length − 1, or a loop that stops before length.

📘 DEFINITION

Flowchart: a diagram of program flow using standard shapes

Pseudocode: algorithm steps in plain, language-neutral terms

INPUT / OUTPUT: the pseudocode keywords for reading data in and producing results

True division (/): produces a fractional result

Floor division (//): produces the whole part only, discarding the remainder

Modulo (%): produces the remainder of a division

float() / int(): conversion operations; int() truncates rather than rounds

★ ON THE OA

Keep the three division operators apart: 7 / 2 = 3.5, 7 // 2 = 3, 7 % 2 = 1. In a language where / on two integers is itself integer division — Java, for instance — 7 / 2 is 3. Read which convention the question is using.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a "what does this pseudocode print" question, make a small table with one column per variable and one row per pass through the loop. It is slower than reading and it is right far more often.

An operating system is the software that manages a computer's hardware and provides services to every other program — Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS. The single sentence to hold on to is that the OS is the resource manager: it decides who gets the CPU, who gets memory, and who may touch a device, so that applications never have to negotiate with each other.

Four responsibilities cover almost every question, and they map onto four resources.

ResponsibilityWhat the OS doesWithout it
Process managementcreates processes, schedules the CPU between themone program would monopolise the machine
Memory managementallocates and reclaims RAM, provides virtual memoryprograms would overwrite each other
File managementorganises files and enforces permissionsno structure, no access control
Device managementtalks to hardware through driversevery program would need code for every device

Processes, threads and CPU scheduling

A process is a program in execution, with its own memory. A thread is a lighter unit inside a process: threads of one process share its memory, which makes switching between them cheap and makes it possible for them to corrupt each other's data — the trade that defines concurrent programming.

When many processes want the one CPU, the OS plays traffic cop. Each strategy has a name, and the OA asks you to match the name to its one-line behaviour.

AlgorithmPicksStrengthWeakness
FCFS (first-come, first-served)whoever arrived firstsimple and fair by arrivalone long job blocks everyone behind it
SJN / SJF (shortest job next / first)the shortest execution timeminimises average waiting timelong jobs can starve indefinitely
Round robineach in turn for a fixed time sliceresponsive and faircontext switching costs overhead
Prioritythe highest-priority jobimportant work goes firstlow-priority jobs can starve

WGU's phrasings are worth memorising as phrases: "selects the process with the smallest execution time remaining" is shortest job next; "each process gets a fixed time slice in rotation" is round robin.

Memory management

Memory techniques evolved to solve one problem — fitting several programs into one physical memory.

TechniqueHow it worksWeakness
Single contiguousone program plus the OS occupy all of memoryonly one program at a time
Fixed partitioningmemory split into fixed-size blocks set in advancewasted space inside each block
Dynamic partitioningblocks sized to each program as it loadsgaps build up between them — fragmentation
Paging / virtual memorymemory divided into fixed pages; unused pages held on diskdisk access is slow — thrashing if overused

Virtual memory is the one to understand rather than memorise. It gives every process its own large address space and keeps only the pages currently in use in real RAM, holding the rest on disk. That is why a machine can run programs whose combined size exceeds its physical memory, and why it slows dramatically when it runs out — it starts swapping pages to disk.

Deadlock

A deadlock is two or more processes each holding a resource the other needs, so neither can ever proceed — process A holds the printer and wants the scanner, process B holds the scanner and wants the printer. Nothing resolves it on its own; the OS must prevent, avoid or detect and break it.

What "resource manager" really means

The phrase is easy to repeat and worth unpacking, because it is what makes the OS necessary rather than merely convenient. Without one, every program would have to know which region of memory was free, take turns with the CPU voluntarily, and contain a driver for every model of printer. Programs would have to cooperate, and a single badly written one could take down the machine.

The OS solves that by standing between applications and hardware and refusing to let them talk directly. An application asks for memory and gets an address; it asks to write a file and the OS decides whether it is allowed. That indirection is also the security boundary — the reason one program cannot read another's memory, and the reason permissions can be enforced at all.

Multitasking is an illusion, mostly

A single-core CPU runs exactly one instruction stream at a time. What looks like several programs running at once is the scheduler switching between them thousands of times a second — concurrency, achieved by a context switch that saves one process's state and restores another's. Genuine simultaneity needs multiple cores, and that is parallelism. Questions that ask whether a single-core machine can truly run two programs at the same instant are testing exactly this distinction, and the answer is no.

How memory protection actually works

Saying the OS "manages memory" leaves out the mechanism the exam asks about. Each process is given a base register holding the starting address of its partition and a bounds (limit) register holding its length. Every address the process generates is checked against that pair, and an address outside the range is refused — which is precisely what stops one program reading another's memory.

That also explains logical versus physical addresses. A process works in logical (relative) addresses starting at 0, as though it owned the machine; the hardware adds the base register to produce the real physical address. The translation is invisible to the program and is what makes relocation possible.

Two kinds of fragmentation

KindWhere the waste isCaused by
Internal fragmentationinside an allocated blockfixed-size blocks larger than the program needs
External fragmentationbetween allocated blocksvariable-size blocks leaving gaps as processes come and go

The distinction is worth holding by where the unusable space sits. Fixed partitioning wastes space within each block, because a 10KB program in a 16KB partition leaves 6KB unusable inside it. Dynamic partitioning fits each program exactly and instead leaves scattered gaps between them, none individually large enough to be useful. Paging reduces external fragmentation by dividing memory into fixed frames and programs into equal-sized pages, so any page fits any free frame — leaving only a little internal fragmentation in the final page.

Pushing paging too far causes thrashing: so little real memory is available that the system spends more time swapping pages to disk than executing instructions, and throughput collapses.

Multiprogramming, multitasking and preemption

Three related terms describe how an OS keeps several programs going, and questions ask you to tell them apart.

TermMeans
Multiprogrammingseveral programs are loaded in memory at once, so the CPU switches to another when one waits for I/O
Multitaskingthe same idea with rapid switching, so the user perceives simultaneous execution
Multiprocessinggenuinely simultaneous execution on more than one processor or core
Multithreadingseveral threads of execution within one process

Scheduling is also either preemptive or non-preemptive. A preemptive scheduler can preempt a running process — take the CPU away when its time slice (quantum) expires — which is what round robin does. A non-preemptive scheduler waits for the process to yield, which is why one long job under FCFS blocks everything behind it.

The life of a process

When you launch a program the OS creates a process — an instance of that program actually running, with its own memory and its own place in the schedule. The program on disk is passive; the process is the live thing.

A process moves through a fixed set of states, and the order is asked directly:

NEW  ->  READY  ->  RUNNING  ->  TERMINATED
            ^         |
            |         v
          WAITING (blocked, e.g. on input)

New — being created. Ready — able to run, waiting for a CPU. Running — on the CPU now. Waiting (or blocked) — cannot continue until something outside finishes, typically I/O; it returns to ready, never straight to running. Terminated — finished.

Where a job is placed in memory

With dynamic partitions, free memory is a set of holes of different sizes, and the OS must choose one for an arriving job. Three named strategies, and the OA gives you the numbers.

StrategyChoosesTrade-off
First fitthe first hole big enough, scanning from the startfastest — no full scan needed
Best fitthe smallest hole that still fitsleast waste in that hole; leaves slivers, and must scan all
Worst fitthe largest hole of allleaves a big usable remainder; must scan all
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — holes of 400 KB, 250 KB and 600 KB; a 200 KB job arrives
first fit -> 400 KB   (the first one large enough)
best  fit -> 250 KB   (the smallest that still fits)
worst fit -> 600 KB   (the largest, whatever else is free)

Read the hole list in the order printed — "first fit" depends on that order, the other two do not.

How the machine is used, and how you talk to it

TermMeans
Batch processingjobs are collected and run as a group with no user interaction — the earliest style, still used for payroll and billing
Time sharingmany users interact at once, the CPU switching between them fast enough to feel simultaneous
CLIcommand-line interface — you type commands; scriptable and precise
GUIgraphical user interface — windows, icons and a pointer; easier to learn, harder to automate

When the power comes on, the CPU runs firmware from ROM which finds and loads the operating system into RAM — booting. The OS is not running before this; it is loaded from storage like anything else, which is why a corrupt boot sector stops the machine before any program can start.

📘 DEFINITION

Operating system: system software that manages hardware and provides services to applications

Process: a program in execution, with its own memory space

Thread: a unit of execution inside a process, sharing that process's memory

Scheduler: the OS component deciding which process runs next

Context switch: saving one process's state and restoring another's

Virtual memory: giving each process a large address space by paging unused parts to disk

Fragmentation: unusable gaps left in memory by repeated allocation and release

Deadlock: processes permanently blocked, each holding what another needs

Kernel: the core of the OS, with direct hardware access

Device driver: software letting the OS communicate with a particular piece of hardware

★ ON THE OA

The OS is the resource manager — it schedules the CPU, manages memory, controls files and devices. You never allocate RAM directly; the OS does. Learn the scheduling algorithms by their one-line behaviour: round robin = fixed time slice in rotation, SJF = shortest job first, FCFS = arrival order.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Round robin optimises responsiveness and fairness; SJF optimises average waiting time but can starve long jobs. If a question mentions starvation, the answer is SJF or priority — never round robin.
