A file is a named collection of data on storage. A file system is the method an operating system uses to organise, name, store and retrieve those files — it is the part of file management from the previous lesson, in detail.

Files are organised into directories (folders), which contain files and further directories, forming a tree that starts at the root. A path is the route through that tree to a particular file, and the two kinds of path are asked about directly.

Path typeStarts fromExample
Absolutethe root — unambiguous from anywhere/home/user/notes/file.txt
Relativethe current working directorynotes/file.txt

A relative path is shorter and breaks the moment the working directory changes, which is the single most common cause of "it worked in my editor and failed from the terminal".

Metadata and permissions

Alongside the contents, the file system stores metadata — data about the data: name, size, type, creation and modification dates, owner, and permissions. Metadata is why a file listing can show sizes and dates without opening anything.

Permissions control who may do what, conventionally read, write and execute, granted separately to the owner, a group and everyone else. That three-by-three grid is the whole of the classic Unix permission model, and it is the file-level end of the access control that security depends on.

How data is actually stored

Files are stored in fixed-size blocks, and a file larger than one block occupies several. When those blocks end up scattered across the disk rather than adjacent, the file is fragmented — reading it means more seeking, so it is slower. Defragmentation rearranges blocks to make files contiguous again, which matters on spinning hard disks and much less on solid-state drives, where there is no physical seek.

Two more distinctions the OA uses. A text file stores characters in an encoding you can read; a binary file stores raw bytes meaningful only to the program that wrote it. And access can be sequential — read from the start through to what you want — or direct/random, jumping straight to a position.

The file system as an abstraction

A disk has no notion of files. It has numbered blocks, and that is all. "File", "folder" and "path" are inventions of the file system, which keeps its own index recording which blocks belong to which file and what each file is called. This is abstraction in the sense of the earlier section: you work with a name and the system deals in block numbers.

Recognising that explains behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary. Deleting a large file is instant because normally only the index entry is removed and the blocks are marked free — the data is still physically there, which is precisely why deleted files can often be recovered forensically. Renaming is instant for the same reason. And copying is slow, because that genuinely moves every block.

It also explains why the file system is where permissions live. The index is the one place that knows who owns each file, so it is the natural place to record who may read or change it.

Names, extensions and what they really do

A file name usually ends in a file extension — the part after the final dot, as in report.pdf. The extension is a convention: it tells the operating system which application to open the file with, and it tells you what to expect. It does not create or change the contents.

That is why renaming report.docx to report.txt changes nothing but the name. The bytes are identical; the OS now offers the wrong program to open them, and the file appears broken. Format is decided by how the data was written, never by the label on the end.

Paths

A path is the route to a file through the directory tree, and it comes in two kinds.

KindStarts fromExample
Absolutethe root of the file system — same meaning from anywhere/home/nat/notes/d684.txt
Relativethe current working directorynotes/d684.txt
.     the current directory
..    the PARENT directory — one level up
../..  two levels up

from /home/nat/notes :
    ../photos/cat.png   ->  /home/nat/photos/cat.png

A relative path is shorter but only means what it says from where you are standing; an absolute path always resolves the same way.

Copying, moving, and surviving a crash

A copy creates a second independent file — two copies exist afterwards, and changing one leaves the other alone. A move relocates the single file — one copy exists afterwards. Within the same drive a move usually rewrites only the directory entry, which is why it is instant on a large file while a copy is not.

A journaling file system keeps a log of what it is about to do before it does it. If the power fails mid-write, the OS replays or discards the journal on restart and the file system is left consistent instead of half-updated. It exists to solve corruption from interrupted writes — not to save space and not to make writes faster.

📘 DEFINITION

File: a named collection of data held on storage

File system: the structure and method an OS uses to organise and retrieve files

Directory / folder: a container organising files and other directories

Root: the top of the directory tree

Absolute path: a path from the root — valid from anywhere

Relative path: a path from the current working directory

Metadata: data about a file: size, dates, owner, permissions

Permissions: the read, write and execute rights granted to owner, group and others

Fragmentation: a file stored in non-adjacent blocks, slowing reads

Sequential vs direct access: reading from the start versus jumping straight to a position

★ ON THE OA

A file is named data on disk; a directory organises files hierarchically; a path locates one. An absolute path starts from the root, a relative path from the current directory. Metadata records size, dates and permissions — not the contents.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

File systems are the reason anything survives a reboot. RAM is volatile and loses everything when power goes; a file is how a program's results outlive the process that produced them.

Everything so far assumed one operating system running on one machine. Virtualization breaks that assumption: it lets one physical computer run several complete operating systems at once, each believing it has the machine to itself.

The component that makes it work is the hypervisor, a layer that sits between the hardware and the virtual machines and hands each one a slice of the real CPU, memory and storage. A virtual machine is one of those guests — a full operating system with its own kernel, isolated from its neighbours.

TypeRuns onUsed for
Type 1 (bare metal)directly on the hardwaredata centres and servers — faster, no host OS in the way
Type 2 (hosted)as an application on a normal OSa desktop running Linux inside Windows for testing

The payoff is consolidation. A physical server running one application typically wastes most of its capacity; running ten virtual machines on it uses hardware that was already paid for, and each one can be snapshotted, copied or moved to another host. That efficiency is exactly what makes cloud computing economically possible — a cloud provider is running virtualization at enormous scale.

Containers are the lighter relative worth knowing about. A container packages an application with its dependencies but shares the host's kernel rather than running a whole operating system, so it starts in seconds instead of minutes and uses far less memory. A VM virtualises the machine; a container virtualises the application's environment.

Cloud computing

Cloud computing means renting computing over the internet instead of owning hardware. Rather than buying servers, you use someone else's and pay for what you consume. The three service models are asked about constantly, and the way to keep them straight is to ask how much of the stack you still manage.

ModelYou getYou manageExample
IaaS — Infrastructure as a Serviceraw compute, storage and networkthe OS, runtime and your applicationrenting virtual machines
PaaS — Platform as a Servicea platform to build and deploy ononly your application and dataa managed app hosting platform
SaaS — Software as a Servicefinished software, ready to usenothing but your own data and settingsGmail, Office 365

Read the table downward and the pattern is a trade: the further down, the less you manage and the less control you have. IaaS gives you the most control and the most responsibility; SaaS gives you the least of both.

Beyond the service models, the OA also asks about deployment models — public cloud (shared infrastructure from a provider), private cloud (dedicated to one organisation), and hybrid (a mix, often keeping sensitive data private while using public capacity for the rest). And edge computing is the counter-move: processing data on or near the device that generated it rather than shipping it to a distant data centre, which cuts latency and bandwidth — the reason a self-driving car does not ask the cloud whether to brake.

📘 DEFINITION

Virtualization: running several complete operating systems on one physical machine

Hypervisor: the layer allocating real hardware to virtual machines

Virtual machine: a complete guest operating system running on virtualised hardware

Container: an application packaged with its dependencies, sharing the host kernel

Cloud computing: renting computing resources over the internet instead of owning them

IaaS: raw infrastructure — you manage the OS and everything above it

PaaS: a platform to deploy onto — you manage only your application

SaaS: finished software delivered over the internet

Edge computing: processing data near where it is generated instead of in a distant data centre

Scalability / elasticity: adding or removing capacity as demand changes

★ ON THE OA

Learn the three service models by an example each: Gmail = SaaS, a managed app platform = PaaS, renting virtual machines = IaaS. More control means further up the stack toward IaaS. A hypervisor is what makes virtual machines possible.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

A virtual machine and a container are not the same thing. A VM includes a whole guest operating system; a container shares the host kernel and packages only the application and its dependencies.

The CPU — the central processing unit — executes instructions, and everything else on the motherboard exists to feed it. The model the OA tests is von Neumann architecture, and its defining claim is that program instructions and data share the same memory. That is why a computer is general-purpose: change the contents of memory and you change what the machine does.

Von Neumann architecture has five parts, and the grouping matters as much as the list.

PartJob
Control unitdirects the fetch-decode-execute cycle and tells everything else what to do
ALU (arithmetic logic unit)performs the arithmetic and the logical comparisons
Memoryholds both the instructions and the data
Inputbrings data in — keyboard, sensor, network
Outputsends results out — screen, file, network

The control unit and the ALU together are the CPU; memory, input and output sit outside it. Getting that grouping right answers a surprising share of architecture questions.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle

Every instruction goes through the same three steps, billions of times per second.

FETCH    the control unit gets the next instruction from memory
DECODE   it works out what the instruction means
EXECUTE  the ALU (or another unit) carries it out
         ...store the result, then repeat

Registers are tiny storage locations inside the CPU itself, used to hold the values an instruction is working on right now. They are the fastest storage in the machine because they are physically closest — which is the whole idea behind the memory hierarchy.

The memory hierarchy

Speed and capacity trade against each other, and the machine resolves that by having several layers rather than one.

LevelSpeedSizeVolatile?
Registersfastesta few dozen valuesyes
Cache (L1, L2, L3)very fastkilobytes to megabytesyes
RAM (main memory)fastgigabytesyes — lost on power off
SSD / hard diskslowhundreds of gigabytes upno — survives power off

Cache exists because RAM is slower than the CPU. It holds recently and frequently used data close to the processor, so most requests never have to travel to main memory. And the volatility column is the reason files exist at all: everything in RAM disappears when the power goes, so anything that must survive has to be written to storage.

The rest of the board

The motherboard is the board connecting everything, and a bus is the set of wires carrying data between components — a data bus for the values, an address bus for locations, a control bus for signals. Clock speed, measured in gigahertz, is how many cycles the CPU performs per second, and cores are independent processing units on one chip, so a quad-core processor can genuinely execute four instruction streams at once.

Why the von Neumann design matters

The claim that instructions and data share one memory sounds like a technicality and is the reason computers are general-purpose machines rather than appliances. Because a program is just data in memory, a computer can load a different program and become a different tool — and it is also why a computer can compile, generate or modify programs at all. Earlier machines were wired for a specific calculation and had to be physically rewired to do something else.

The same design has a cost the exam sometimes names: the von Neumann bottleneck. Because instructions and data travel over the same path between the CPU and memory, that path limits how fast the processor can be fed, no matter how fast the processor is. Cache exists largely to soften that bottleneck, and it is why adding cache can speed up a machine more than raising its clock speed.

One clarification on clock speed: it counts cycles, not instructions, so a 3 GHz processor does not perform three billion instructions a second. Comparing chips by gigahertz alone is unreliable, which is why cores, cache and architecture appear alongside it in any real specification.

The registers that drive the cycle

The fetch-decode-execute cycle needs somewhere to keep track of where it is, and that is what the special-purpose registers do. Two are named directly in exam questions.

RegisterHolds
Program counter (PC)the address of the next instruction to fetch
Instruction register (IR)the instruction currently being executed
Accumulatorthe working value the ALU is operating on
Memory address register (MAR)the address currently being read from or written to
Memory data register (MDR)the data travelling to or from that address

The two that matter most are easy to confuse and easy to separate once stated side by side: the PC points at what comes next, the IR holds what is happening now. Each pass of the cycle fetches the instruction at the PC, copies it into the IR, advances the PC, then decodes and executes.

FETCH     read the instruction at the address in the PC
          copy it into the IR,  then ADVANCE the PC
DECODE    the control unit works out what the instruction means
EXECUTE   the ALU (or another unit) carries it out, result to a register
          ...repeat

Watching a tiny program run makes the division of labour concrete. For LOAD A, ADD B, STORE C with A = 4 and B = 3: the control unit fetches each instruction (the PC says where), decodes it, and the ALU does the addition, leaving 7 in a register until STORE C writes it back to memory.

Bus width and clock speed

Bus width is the number of bits the bus carries at once — the number of lanes on the highway. A wider bus moves more data per transfer, which is why 64-bit systems can move twice as much per cycle as 32-bit ones. Clock speed, in gigahertz, is how many cycles happen per second, and it counts cycles rather than instructions, so it is not on its own a measure of how fast a processor gets work done.

📘 DEFINITION

CPU: the processor — control unit plus ALU — which executes instructions

Von Neumann architecture: a design in which instructions and data share the same memory

Control unit: directs the fetch-decode-execute cycle

ALU: performs arithmetic and logic operations

Register: a very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU

Cache: fast memory close to the CPU holding recently used data

RAM: volatile main memory — erased when power is lost

Motherboard: the board connecting CPU, memory and peripherals

Bus: the wires carrying data, addresses and control signals between components

Clock speed: cycles per second, measured in GHz

Core: an independent processing unit within a CPU

★ ON THE OA

Von Neumann has five parts — control unit, ALU, memory, input, output — and CU + ALU = the CPU. Program and data share the same memory. The ALU does arithmetic and logic; the control unit directs the fetch-decode-execute flow. Do not swap those two.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

The memory hierarchy explains costs you meet everywhere else: why a variable is fast and a file is slow, why virtual memory hurts performance when it starts swapping, and why an algorithm that touches memory in order beats one that jumps around, even at the same Big-O.

A network is a group of devices linked to communicate and share resources. The internet is the largest one — an enormous number of computers passing messages — and it works because every device follows the same agreed rules, called protocols.

Networks are classified first by how far they reach. A LAN (local area network) covers one building or site; a WAN (wide area network) spans cities or countries, and the internet is the largest WAN. A MAN covers a metropolitan area, and a PAN is personal-scale, like a phone and its headphones.

Topologies

Topology is the shape of the connections, and the OA asks what happens to each shape when something fails.

TopologyArrangementIf one part fails
Busall devices share one backbone cablea break in the backbone takes down the whole network
Ringeach device connects to two neighbours in a loopone break can split the ring unless it is dual-ring
Starevery device connects to a central hub or switchone device failing is fine; the hub failing drops everything
Meshmany devices interconnected with redundant pathstraffic routes around the failure — the most fault-tolerant

Packets, addresses and names

Data does not travel as a whole file. It is broken into packets, each carrying a piece of the data plus the source and destination addresses. Packets travel independently, may take different routes, and are reassembled in order at the far end — which is what makes the network resilient, since losing one packet means resending one packet.

Every device has two addresses and the difference is examined. A MAC address is burned into the network hardware and does not change — it identifies the device physically. An IP address is assigned by the network and identifies the device logically; it changes when the device joins a different network.

DNS, the domain name system, is the internet's phone book: it translates a human-readable name into an IP address. Typing a URL triggers a DNS lookup first, then packets route to the returned address.

ProtocolDoes
TCP/IPthe core suite — IP routes packets, TCP guarantees they arrive in order
HTTP / HTTPStransfers web pages; HTTPS adds encryption
DNStranslates domain names into IP addresses
DHCPautomatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network
FTPtransfers files
SMTPsends email

The layered models

A network model is a layered blueprint in which each layer does one job and hands the data to the next. Two are examined: the OSI model with seven layers — physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application — and the TCP/IP model with four: link, internet, transport, application. OSI is the teaching model; TCP/IP is what the internet actually runs on.

Finally, the devices: a switch connects devices within one network and forwards frames to the right port; a router connects different networks and decides which path a packet takes; a firewall filters traffic against rules, allowing or blocking it at the boundary.

TCP, UDP and ports

IP routes packets to the right machine; a transport protocol decides what guarantees come with them, and the two choices are a genuine trade.

TCPUDP
Connectionestablishes one firstnone — just sends
Guaranteesdelivery, order, error checkingnone
Speedslower — acknowledgements and retriesfaster — no overhead
Used forweb pages, email, file transferlive video, voice, gaming

The rule of thumb is that TCP is right when a missing piece ruins the result, and UDP is right when a late piece is worse than a missing one — a dropped frame in a video call is better than a call that stalls to re-send it.

A port number identifies which application on the machine a packet is for, so the IP address finds the computer and the port finds the program. The ones asked about are 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 25 for SMTP, 53 for DNS and 22 for SSH.

The client-server model and status codes

Most of the internet follows the client-server model: a client requests, a server responds. Your browser is the client, the machine holding the site is the server, and each request gets an HTTP status code saying what happened — 200 OK, 301 moved permanently, 404 not found, 500 server error. The first digit gives the category: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client's fault, 5xx the server's.

The alternative arrangement is peer-to-peer, where every machine is both client and server — used for file sharing and some messaging, with no central server to fail or to control.

Connection types

Broadband means a high-capacity, always-on connection, as opposed to the dial-up it replaced. The common kinds are DSL over telephone lines, cable over the television network, fibre optic, and cellular. Bandwidth is measured in bits per second — Mbps, Gbps — and is the maximum rate rather than a guaranteed one, which is why latency, the delay before data starts arriving, is a separate measure that matters just as much for interactive use.

TypeBuilt forExample

The pair most often confused is supercomputer and mainframe, and the distinction is what "big" means. A supercomputer is optimised for speed on a single enormous computation; a mainframe is optimised for throughput and uptime across millions of small transactions. A weather model wants a supercomputer; a bank wants a mainframe.

Embedded systems and the Internet of Things

An embedded system is a computer built into a larger device to do one dedicated job. It usually has limited memory and processing power, often runs a real-time operating system, and typically has no general-purpose interface — you never install software on your microwave.

The Internet of Things is what happens when those embedded devices get network connectivity: everyday objects that sense, report and can be controlled remotely. A smart thermostat, a fitness tracker, a connected doorbell and an industrial sensor are all IoT devices, and the pattern is always the same — sense, transmit, analyse, act.

Two consequences follow, and the exam asks about both. IoT generates enormous volumes of data from the edge of the network, which is why edge computing exists — process it near the device rather than shipping it all to a data centre. And these devices are a security problem out of proportion to their size: they are numerous, rarely updated, often shipped with default passwords, and physically accessible. A compromised sensor is a foothold on the network it sits in.

Why the categories exist

It would be reasonable to ask why the scale categories matter when every one of these devices has the same von Neumann parts inside. The answer is that each is optimised for a different constraint, and the constraint is what the question is really describing. A supercomputer optimises raw floating-point throughput and accepts enormous power and cooling costs. A mainframe optimises reliability and transaction volume — it is built to run for years without stopping. An embedded system optimises cost, size and power, because it may run on a battery for a decade.

So when a scenario mentions a requirement rather than a machine — "must never go down", "must fit on a battery-powered sensor", "must model the atmosphere overnight" — it is naming the constraint, and the constraint identifies the category.

Embedded systems bring one more idea worth holding: many are real-time systems, meaning a correct answer delivered too late counts as a failure. An airbag controller that computes the right response fifty milliseconds after the crash has not partly succeeded. That is a different standard from ordinary software, where slow is merely slow.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• Distinguish data from information and explain why the difference matters in computing.

• Explain why computers store everything in binary, and why binary is more reliable than analog.

• Contrast analog and digital data, and describe how reclocking and PCM protect digital signals from degradation.

• Calculate how many bits are needed to represent N distinct things using the rule 2ⁿ.

• Define data compression, compute a compression ratio, and tell lossless from lossy.

• 🔎 Convert whole numbers between decimal, binary, and hexadecimal (the number-systems skill this unit is built on).

Plain-English First

Imagine a shoebox full of loose receipts. That pile is data — raw facts with no order. Now imagine you sort those receipts by month and add up each month's spending. The tidy summary that answers "how much did I spend in March?" is information. Same raw material; one is organized so it informs a decision. That single idea — that a computer's whole job is turning data into information — is the theme of this entire unit.

Here's the second big idea. The real world is continuous: a dimmer switch can be at any brightness, a thermometer can read 74.568°, and there are infinitely many numbers between 1 and 2. Computers are finite machines — they only have so many switches. So a computer has to digitize: chop the smooth, infinite world into separate, countable pieces and store each piece as a string of 1s and 0s. Everything — a photo, a song, this sentence — ultimately becomes binary digits (bits).

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

Data is basic values or facts that can lack context. Information is data that has been organized or processed to be useful in solving a problem. The distinction is relative to the user's needs, but it captures the essence of what computers do for us.

Analog data is a continuous representation, analogous to the actual thing it represents — like mercury rising smoothly in a thermometer. Digital data is a discrete representation that breaks information into separate elements. Computers digitize continuous entities and then represent each discrete element in binary.

Why binary and not decimal? Computers could use other number systems (some early machines did), but the hardware that stores and moves data is far cheaper and far more reliable when each device only has to be one of two states. An analog signal fluctuates continuously in voltage; a digital signal holds only a high or low state — the two binary digits.

Every electronic signal degrades as it travels down a line because voltage fluctuates from environmental effects. This is where digital wins decisively:

When an analog signal degrades, information is lost immediately — because any voltage in the range is "valid," you can't tell what the original was.

A digital signal jumps sharply between two extremes — a behavior called pulse-code modulation (PCM). It can degrade quite a lot before any information is lost, because any voltage above a threshold reads as "high" and any below reads as "low." Periodically the signal is reclocked — refreshed to its original crisp shape. Reclock before too much degradation and no information is lost.

Bits and how many things they can represent

One bit is either 0 or 1 — so one bit represents exactly two things (e.g., sweet=0, sour=1). To represent more, use more bits. Two bits give four combinations (00, 01, 10, 11); three bits give eight; and so on. The master rule:

📌 MUST-KNOW FORMULA

n bits can represent 2ⁿ things. Each extra bit doubles what you can represent. Turned around: to represent N distinct things you need the smallest n where 2ⁿ ≥ N.

Example of the "turned-around" version: to represent 25 unique things, 4 bits (16) is too few, so you need 5 bits (32) — and 32 − 25 = 7 bit combinations simply go unused. Note also that even when you only need a few bits, hardware allocates storage in fixed chunks (a power of 2 such as 8, 16, or 32 bits), so real storage is given in multiples of that.

Data compression and the compression ratio

Data compression reduces the amount of space needed to store data. We care today less because of storage cost and more because of bandwidth — the maximum number of bits that can travel across a network in a fixed time (think streaming video). The compression ratio measures how much shrinking happened:

📌 MUST-KNOW FORMULA

Compression ratio = (size of compressed data) ÷ (size of original data). Both values must measure the same thing (bits, or characters). The result falls between 0 and 1 — the closer to 0, the tighter the compression.

A technique is lossless if the original data can be perfectly reconstructed (nothing lost), or lossy if some information is permanently discarded to save space. We never want to lose information, but sometimes the loss is acceptable — we always face a tradeoff between accuracy and size.

🔎 ADDED FOR COMPLETENESS

Number Systems (binary & hex)

The notes lean on base conversion from "Chapter 2" but don't restate it, and this WGU unit tests binary/hex directly, so here is the essential primer.

Positional value. In any base, a digit's worth = digit × (base^position), counting positions from 0 at the right. Binary (base 2) uses digits 0–1; each position is a power of 2: …16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0–9 then A–F (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15).

Binary → decimal: add the place values where a 1 sits. 1011 = 8+0+2+1 = 11.

Decimal → binary: repeatedly divide by 2, writing remainders bottom-up. 13 → 13/2=6 r1, 6/2=3 r0, 3/2=1 r1, 1/2=0 r1 → read up → 1101.

Hex ↔ binary (the shortcut): each hex digit = exactly 4 bits. So 0xB=1011, 0x2F=0010 1111. Group binary in 4s from the right to go back. This is why hex is popular — it's a compact human-readable stand-in for binary.

"Data is dirt, information is a sandcastle." Same sand (facts); only one is shaped to be useful.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — How many bits, and a compression ratio

Problem: (a) A vending machine sells 40 distinct products; each needs a unique binary code. How many bits minimum? (b) A 352-character message compresses to 317 characters. Give the compression ratio.

Part (a) — climb the powers of two. Need 2ⁿ ≥ 40.

2⁵ = 32 → too small (only 32 codes).

2⁶ = 64 → 64 ≥ 40 ✔.

Answer (a): 6 bits. (64 − 40 = 24 codes go unused.)

Part (b) — apply the formula. Ratio = compressed ÷ original = 317 ÷ 352.

317 ÷ 352 = 0.90 (about). Close to 1 → only mild compression.

Worked Example 2 — Decimal → binary → hex (the 🔎 skill)

Problem: Convert decimal 206 to binary, then to hexadecimal.

Decimal → binary by repeated division by 2 (remainders read bottom-up):

206 ÷ 2 = 103 r 0

103 ÷ 2 = 51 r 1

51 ÷ 2 = 25 r 1

25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1

12 ÷ 2 = 6 r 0

6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0

3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1

1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1

Read remainders bottom-to-top: 11001110. Check: 128+64+8+4+2 = 206 ✔.

Binary → hex: group into 4-bit nibbles from the right: 1100 1110.

1100 = 12 = C; 1110 = 14 = E.

Answer: 206 = 11001110₂ = 0xCE.

Wrong way → why → right way: A common error is reading the division remainders top-to-bottom, giving 01110011. That's wrong because the first remainder is the least-significant (rightmost) bit. Right way: always read remainders from the last division up to the first.

📊 FIGURE — one byte in decimal, binary and hex — where every digit’s value comes from
🎯 EXAM TIP

Number-base questions are the highest-volume, most predictable points on this OA, and they are pure procedure — no reasoning required if you drill the two directions.

Binary → decimal: write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits and add the columns with a 1. Decimal → binary: go the other way — subtract the biggest place value that fits, mark a 1, repeat. For 206: 128 fits (78 left), 64 fits (14 left), 32 no, 16 no, 8 fits (6), 4 fits (2), 2 fits (0), 1 no → 11001110. That subtraction method is faster and less error-prone under time pressure than repeated division, because there are no remainders to read in the wrong order.

Anything to hex: never convert through decimal. Go to binary, split into nibbles of four from the right, and read each nibble off the 8-4-2-1 ladder. And when a question asks “how many bits for N things?”, do not compute a logarithm — climb 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 until you pass N and count the rungs.

Choosing the right data type

A large share of the questions here give a scenario and ask which type fits. The reasoning is always the same: what operations must this value support, and what must not be lost?

📘 DEFINITION
An integer is a whole number with no fractional part — 42, 0, −7. 3.0 is not an integer value in type terms: it is a float that happens to be whole.
📘 DEFINITION
A Boolean holds only true or false. A comparison such as x > 3 is guaranteed to produce one, which is why comparisons are what appear inside if-conditions.

Strong typing, and type mismatch

📘 DEFINITION
Strong typing means the language enforces types: a value of one type cannot silently be used as another, and mixing them is reported rather than guessed at.

So in a strongly typed language, adding the integer 200 directly to the string "Total: " raises a type error unless you explicitly convert the number to text first.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
number = "10" for something you intend to count with is a type mismatch. The quotes make it text. Then finalScore = "95" followed by finalScore + 5 does not give 100 — depending on the language it either errors, or concatenates to "955". Neither is the answer expected.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Trace it: integer division versus real division

int a = 7 / 2; and double b = 7 / 2.0;

  1. 7 / 2 — both operands are integers, so the division is integer division: it discards the remainder. a = 3.
  2. 7 / 2.0 — one operand is a float, so the int is promoted and real division happens. b = 3.5.

One character decides it. Whenever a question shows a division, check the types of both sides first.

Precision — why 0.1 ten times is not 1.0

Adding 0.1 ten times can give 0.9999999999999999. Nothing is broken: 0.1 has no exact representation in binary, in the same way 1/3 has no exact decimal representation. Each stored 0.1 is a hair off, and ten additions accumulate the error. This is why money is never stored in a binary float, and why floats are compared with a tolerance rather than with ==.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• Explain why signed-magnitude representation is intuitive but creates the "two zeros" problem.

• Compute the ten's complement and two's complement of a number, and use the invert-and-add-1 shortcut.

• Perform binary addition and subtraction using two's complement, and read the sign bit.

• Recognize overflow and explain why it happens on a finite machine.

• Convert a real number to floating-point form (sign, mantissa, exponent) and back, and convert a fractional decimal to binary.

Plain-English First

A computer has a fixed number of switches for each number — say 8 bits. That's like an odometer with only so many wheels: it can't grow, and it wraps around when it runs out of room. Two puzzles fall out of that: how do you write a negative number when all you have is 0s and 1s (no minus sign)? and how do you write a number with a fractional part like 3.75? This section solves both.

The clever trick for negatives is the complement. Think of a 12-hour clock: moving back 3 hours lands on the same spot as moving forward 9 hours. So on a clock, "9" can stand in for "−3." Computers do exactly this with binary — that stand-in is called the two's complement, and it lets the same simple "add" circuitry do subtraction too.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

Signed-magnitude

Signed-magnitude representation is what you learned in grade school: a sign (+/−) shows ordering and the digits show the magnitude. It's intuitive, but it has a flaw — there are two representations of zero (+0 and −0). Two zeros inside a computer cause needless complexity, so designers prefer complement schemes.

Fixed-size numbers & ten's complement

If we fix the number of digits, we can let the upper half of the values stand for negatives. With two decimal digits (100 values), let 1–49 be +1…+49 and let 50–99 represent −50…−1. Then addition just works (add and discard the carry), and subtraction becomes addition of a negative: A − B = A + (−B). The negative of a value is found with:

📌 MUST-KNOW FORMULA

Ten's complement: Negative(I) = 10ᵏ − I, where k = number of digits. Example (k=2): −3 → 10² − 3 = 100 − 3 = 97. So 97 "means" −3 in a two-digit fixed scheme.

Two's complement (the binary version)

Store everything in binary and the ten's complement becomes the two's complement: negative(I) = 2ᵏ − I. The easy shortcut you'll actually use on the OA:

📌 MUST-KNOW SHORTCUT

Two's complement = invert all the bits, then add 1. The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 = positive, 1 = negative. Example (8-bit): +2 = 00000010 → invert → 11111101 → +1 → 11111110 = −2.

Addition and subtraction work exactly as in ten's complement — add the binary numbers and discard any carry out of the leftmost position. Because a negative number always starts with a 1, you can tell a number's sign at a glance.

Number overflow

Overflow happens when a computed value won't fit in the allocated bits. In 8-bit signed storage, 127 + 3 = 10000010, which our scheme reads as −126, not +130 — the result wrapped past the top of the range. Overflow is the classic symptom of forcing an infinite world onto a finite machine; no matter how many bits you allocate, some number won't fit. How it's handled varies by hardware and programming language.

Representing real numbers (floating point)

A real number has a whole part and a fractional part (either may be zero). In binary the "decimal point" is called the radix point; positions to its right are halves (2⁻¹), quarters (2⁻²), and so on. Computers store a real value using three properties:

📌 MUST-KNOW

A real value = sign × mantissa × base^exponent. The mantissa is the significant digits (radix point assumed at the far right); the exponent says how far to shift the radix point. This is called floating point because the digit count is fixed but the radix point "floats." One common 64-bit standard uses 1 bit sign + 11 bits exponent + 52 bits mantissa.

To convert to floating point: the sign is obvious, the mantissa is the digits with the point removed, and the exponent is how many places the point moved. Example: 148.69 → sign +, mantissa 14869, exponent −2 → 14869 × 10⁻². If only five mantissa digits are allowed, large values lose information (e.g., 155555000 → 15555 × 10⁴ drops the trailing detail).

Converting a fraction to binary: multiply the fractional part by 2 repeatedly; each whole-number carry is the next bit to the right. Stop when the fraction hits 0 (or you have enough bits). Scientific notation is a floating-point form with exactly one digit left of the point (printed with "E", e.g., 1.200132708E+4).

Two's complementBinary negative = invert bits + 1.Standard for signed integers; one zero; easy arithmetic.
Sign bitLeftmost bit: 0=positive, 1=negative.Instantly reveals a number's sign.
OverflowResult exceeds the allocated bits.Causes wrong/wrapped answers; finite-machine limit.
Real numberA value with a potential fractional part.Needed for measurements, money, science.
Radix pointThe "decimal point" in any base.Separates whole and fractional parts in binary.
Floating pointsign × mantissa × base^exponent.How computers store reals in fixed space.
MantissaThe significant digits of a float.Holds precision; too few digits → lost info.
ExponentShifts the radix point.Sets the number's scale/magnitude.
Scientific notationFloat with one digit left of the point.Compact form for very large/small reals.

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

"Flip, then plus one." That's the whole two's-complement recipe. Invert every bit, add 1.

Clock analogy for complements: −3 ≡ +9 on a 12-clock because 12−3=9. In binary, −I ≡ 2ᵏ−I.

Sign bit tells all: leftmost bit 1 → negative, 0 → positive. Check it first.

Overflow smell test: if you add two positives and get a negative (or two negatives and get a positive), you overflowed.

Fraction → binary = MULTIPLY by 2 (whole → binary = DIVIDE by 2). Opposite operations for the two halves of the number.

"Float = point that floats" — the digits are fixed, the radix point moves via the exponent.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Forgetting the "+1" after inverting. Inverting alone gives one's complement, not two's.

Keeping the final carry in two's-complement addition. Discard the carry out of the sign column.

Thinking two's complement has two zeros. That's signed-magnitude. Two's complement has exactly one zero.

Dividing (instead of multiplying) when converting a fraction to binary.

Reporting +130 for an 8-bit 127+3 — the real machine result is the wrapped value −126 (overflow).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Subtract using 8-bit two's complement: 5 − 3

Rewrite as addition: 5 − 3 = 5 + (−3).

Write +5 in 8 bits: 00000101.

Find −3: start with +3 = 00000011.

Invert the bits: 11111100.

Add 1: 11111101 = −3. ✔

Add the two: 00000101 + 11111101.

The sum is 1 00000010 (9 bits) — a carry pops out of the sign column.

Discard the carry → 00000010.

Leftmost bit is 0 → positive → value = 2. Correct (5 − 3 = 2). ✔

Wrong way → why → right way: Keeping the carry gives 100000010 and a confused answer. Why wrong: the result must fit the fixed 8 bits; the carry out of the top is meant to be dropped. Right way: discard the final carry and read the low 8 bits.

Worked Example 2 — Convert 20.25 (decimal) to binary, then to floating-point notation

Whole part 20 → binary by dividing by 2: 20→10 r0, 10→5 r0, 5→2 r1, 2→1 r0, 1→0 r1. Read up: 10100.

Fractional part .25 → binary by multiplying by 2: .25 × 2 = 0.5 → carry 0; .5 × 2 = 1.0 → carry 1; fraction now 0 → stop. Bits (top-down): .01.

Combine: 20.25₁₀ = 10100.01₂.

Now express as floating point (base 2): mantissa = the digits with the radix point pushed to the right = 1010001; the point moved 2 places left of where it "belongs," so exponent = −2.

Result: 1010001 × 2⁻². (Sign +, mantissa 1010001, exponent −2.)

📊 FIGURE — the 8-bit signed wheel — why 127 + 3 comes out negative
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two’s complement is tested three ways, and each has a two-second check.

1. “What is −N in 8 bits?” Write +N, invert, add 1. Then verify without redoing it: add your answer to +N and you must get 00000000 with a carry falling off the end. 00000011 + 11111101 = 1 00000000 ✓. That check catches the missing +1 every time.

2. “What value is this bit pattern?” Look at the leftmost bit first. If it is 0, read it as plain binary and stop. If it is 1, the number is negative — invert, add 1, read the magnitude, and put the minus sign back. Students lose this one by reading 11111101 as 253.

3. “Did it overflow?” Only look at signs, never at magnitudes: positive + positive giving a negative, or negative + negative giving a positive, is overflow. A positive plus a negative can never overflow, so if the question mixes signs the answer is “no overflow” before you compute anything. And the carry that drops off the left end is not overflow — it is discarded on purpose.

Data type selection — picking the type for a stored value

Two cases come up repeatedly:

after this section you will be able to…

• Define a character set and explain why standardizing one made text processing easier.

• Describe the ASCII character set: 7-bit origin, 128 vs. 256 characters, the check bit, and Latin-1 Extended ASCII.

• Explain why ASCII's ordering lets computers alphabetize, and why the first 32 codes are non-printing control characters.

• Describe Unicode, its goal, its typical 16-bit encoding, and why it is a superset of ASCII.

• Convert a character to its numeric/binary code and reason about uppercase vs. lowercase.

Plain-English First

A computer can't store the letter "A." It can only store numbers. So the whole world agreed on a giant lookup table — "let 65 mean A, 66 mean B…" — the way Morse code agrees that "dot-dash" means A. That agreed-upon table is a character set. Once everyone uses the same table, a message typed on one machine reads correctly on another. This section covers the two tables that won: ASCII (great for English) and Unicode (built for every language on Earth).

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

A text document decomposes into paragraphs → sentences → words → individual characters. The document is the continuous (analog) whole; the characters are the discrete (digital) pieces we actually store. Because there are a finite number of characters, we simply list them all and assign each a binary string. (Note: this is separate from word processing, which also stores fonts, margins, and color — here we care only about the characters themselves.)

How many characters must we handle? English has 26 letters, but upper- and lowercase are separate → 52. Add digits ('0'–'9'), punctuation, the space, and other languages, and the list grows fast. A character set is a list of characters and the code for each. Standardizing one let manufacturers make text processing interoperable.

ASCII

ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange. Originally 7 bits per character → 128 unique characters. The 8th bit of the byte was a check bit (error detection during transmission). Later all 8 bits were used for characters, formally the Latin-1 Extended ASCII set → 256 characters (adding accented letters and special symbols).

Two crucial properties:

Ordering. ASCII codes put characters in a definite order — uppercase letters are in sequence, and so are lowercase. Because the codes are ordered, a computer can compare codes to alphabetize a word list.

Control characters. The first 32 ASCII codes are non-printing — reserved for special functions like carriage return and tab. They're interpreted specially by whatever program processes the text.

Unicode

256 characters is enough for English but not the world. Unicode was created with the goal of representing every character in every language, including Asian ideograms and many special-purpose (e.g., scientific) symbols. It generally uses 16 bits per character but is flexible enough to use more space when needed.

📌 MUST-KNOW

Unicode is a superset of ASCII: its first 256 characters correspond exactly to Extended ASCII, using the same codes. So programs written assuming ASCII still work on Unicode systems. A related idea from Bob Bemer is the escape character, which signals that the following character(s) change the standard meaning of the characters that follow.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Encode "Hi" in ASCII (decimal and binary)

Look up each character. 'H' is an uppercase letter. Uppercase 'A' = 65, and H is the 8th letter (A=1…H=8), so 'H' = 65 + 7 = 72.

'i' is lowercase. 'a' = 97, and i is the 9th letter, so 'i' = 97 + 8 = 105.

Convert 72 to 8-bit binary: 64+8 = 72 → 01001000.

Convert 105 to 8-bit binary: 64+32+8+1 = 105 → 01101001.

"Hi" = 72 105 (decimal) = 01001000 01101001 (binary).

Worked Example 2 — Why alphabetizing works, and an uppercase↔lowercase shift

Question: A program sorts "Cat", "Apple", "Banana" by comparing first-letter ASCII codes. In what order do they end up?

First letters: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66, 'C' = 67.

Sorting ascending by code: 65 < 66 < 67 → Apple, Banana, Cat. The built-in ordering of ASCII is alphabetical for same-case letters.

Follow-up: What is the lowercase of 'C'?

Lowercase = uppercase + 32 → 'C'(67) + 32 = 99 → 'c' = 99.

Wrong way → why → right way: Sorting a mixed-case list like "apple", "Banana" naively by code puts "Banana" before "apple" — because uppercase codes (65–90) all come before lowercase codes (97–122). Why: ASCII orders all capitals ahead of all lowercase. Right way: to sort case-insensitively, convert everything to one case first.

If an answer choice says Unicode “replaced” or “conflicts with” ASCII, eliminate it — Unicode’s first 256 codes are Extended ASCII, which is the whole reason old programs still work.

Plain-English First

Compression is like packing a suitcase smarter. Three tricks appear here, each exploiting a different kind of "waste" in text. Keyword encoding is speed-dial: replace a whole common word ("the") with one short symbol. Run-length encoding handles the case where the same thing repeats over and over ("AAAAAAA") — instead of writing it out, you write "A, seven times." Huffman encoding is the cleverest: it notices that some letters (like E and space) appear constantly while others (like X, Z) are rare, so it gives the common ones tiny codes and the rare ones longer codes — like abbreviating the words you say most.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

Keyword encoding

Replace frequently used words with a single character; reverse it to decompress. In the source example, encoding a 352-character paragraph down to 317 characters gives a ratio of 317/352 ≈ 0.90 (modest). Key limitations: (1) the symbols used cannot appear in the original text or decoding is ambiguous; (2) case matters — "The" and "the" are different, needing separate symbols; (3) no gain from encoding one-character words like "a" or "I"; longer words yield more savings, yet the most frequent words are often short.

Run-length encoding (recurrence coding)

Replace a run of one repeated character with: flag character + repeated character + count. With '*' as the flag, AAAAAAA → *A7. So *n5*x9ccc*h6 some other text *k8eee decodes to nnnnnxxxxxxxxxccchhhhhh some other text kkkkkkkkeee (ratio 35/51 ≈ 0.68).

📌 MUST-KNOW

Because each encoded run costs 3 characters, encoding runs of 3 or fewer is pointless (and encoding a run of 2 would make it longer). It only pays off for runs of 4 or more. If the count is read as an 8-bit binary number instead of a single ASCII digit, runs can be counted up to 255 (or 4–259, since runs ≤3 aren't encoded).

Huffman encoding

Named for Dr. David Huffman. It uses variable-length bit strings: frequent characters get few bits, rare characters get more. That's the opposite of a fixed character set (where every character is, say, 8 or 16 bits). Using the source's sample codes, "DOORBELL" encodes to 1011110110111101001100100 — 25 bits versus 8×8 = 64 bits fixed, a ratio of 25/64 ≈ 0.39.

📌 MUST-KNOW

the Prefix Property

In any Huffman code, no character's bit string is a prefix of another's. That's what makes decoding unambiguous: scanning left to right, the moment the bits match a code, that must be the character. This is why 1010110001111011 can only decode to "BOARD."

🔎 ADDED FOR COMPLETENESS

Building a Huffman tree

The source says the construction is "beyond scope," but WGU tests it, so here's the algorithm:

List each character with its frequency.

Repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes, combine them into a new parent whose frequency is their sum.

Repeat until one node (the root) remains.

Label every left branch 0 and every right branch 1 (a consistent choice).

A character's code is the sequence of branch labels from the root down to it.

The two-lowest rule automatically pushes frequent characters near the top (short codes) and rare ones deep (long codes), and it guarantees the prefix property.

Lower ratio = better, so Huffman's 0.39 beats keyword's 0.90 here.

Giving a frequent character a long Huffman code. It's backwards — frequent = short.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Run-length encode and find the ratio

Problem: Encode WWWWWWWWWWKKKAAAAAA using '*' as the flag, then give the compression ratio.

Identify runs: W ×10, K ×3, A ×6.

W ×10 is a long run (≥4) → encode as *W10... but the count must fit the scheme. Reading the count as a binary number allows up to 255, so *W + count(10) is fine → write *W10 conceptually (3 code positions: flag, char, count).

K ×3 → run of 3, not worth encoding (would take 3 chars to save 0). Leave as KKK.

A ×6 → long run → *A6.

Encoded stream: *W10 KKK *A6 → treating each triple as 3 character-positions: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 characters.

Original length = 10 + 3 + 6 = 19 characters.

Compression ratio = 9 ÷ 19 ≈ 0.47.

Wrong way → why → right way: Encoding the K run as *K3 gives no savings (3 chars → 3 chars) and adds decoding overhead. Right way: leave runs of 3 or fewer as-is; only encode runs of 4+.

Worked Example 2 — 🔎 Build a Huffman tree and encode a word

Problem: Characters and frequencies: A:5, B:2, C:1, D:1. Build the tree, list codes, then encode "BAD" and give its bit length vs. a fixed 2-bit code.

Start with four nodes: A(5), B(2), C(1), D(1).

Combine the two lowest: C(1) + D(1) → node "CD"(2).

Now: A(5), B(2), CD(2). Two lowest are B(2) and CD(2) → node "BCD"(4).

Now: A(5), BCD(4). Combine → root(9).

Label branches (left=0, right=1) from the diagram above: A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111.

Verify prefix property: 0, 10, 110, 111 — none begins another. ✔

Encode "BAD": concatenate B + A + D = 10 + 0 + 111 = 100111. Length = 2+1+3 = 6 bits.

Fixed 2-bit code (4 symbols → 2 bits each): 3 chars × 2 = 6 bits. Here they tie because "BAD" happens to use a rare letter (D). Over a whole document dominated by A's, Huffman wins big (each A costs 1 bit instead of 2).

📊 FIGURE — run-length encoding on a real string — and the runs it is not worth using on
🎯 EXAM TIP

Compression questions come in two flavours and both are arithmetic, not theory.

“Encode this / decode this.” For RLE, count each run before you write anything, and only encode runs of 4 or more — the encoded form always costs exactly 3 character positions, so a run of 3 is a tie and a run of 2 makes the file bigger. Decoding is the same rule backwards: every time you meet the flag character, take the next two positions as “which character” and “how many”.

“Give the compression ratio.” Compressed ÷ original, always in that order, always in the same unit. Sanity-check the direction: your answer should be below 1, and the smaller it is the better the compression. If you get 2.1, you inverted the fraction.

For Huffman, the fastest way to check a code set is offered as correct is the prefix test — read the codes and make sure none of them is the opening of another. And if a frequent letter has been given a long code, the tree was built wrong; the two-lowest merge rule always pushes frequent characters near the root.

Explicit conversion

📘 DEFINITION
Converting a float to an integer so the fraction is truncated is an explicit conversion — a cast. You are asking for it, and accepting the data loss: (int) 9.87 gives 9. It truncates towards zero rather than rounding.

The opposite is an implicit conversion, which the language performs by itself and only where nothing is lost, such as promoting an int to a float.

after this section you will be able to…

• Define an algorithm and pseudocode, and explain why we plan before we code.

• Use the foundational pseudocode elements: variables, constants, assignment, and input/output.

• Apply the order of operations and associativity when evaluating expressions.

• Write and read the three control structures: sequence, selection (if/if-else), and repetition (while).

Plain-English First

Before a builder pours concrete, they draw a blueprint. An algorithm is the blueprint for a program — a step-by-step plan to solve a problem in a finite number of unambiguous steps. Pseudocode is how we sketch that blueprint in plain, structured English before translating it into a real programming language. The beauty is that pseudocode has no rigid grammar — it's for humans — so you can focus on logic first and syntax later.

Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory: you can put a value in it, look at what's inside, and swap the contents anytime. That "swappability" is the whole reason computers are useful — write payroll instructions once, then run them with a different employee's numbers in the boxes thousands of times.

Going Deeper — Foundations: Variables, Constants & Operators

A data type classifies a data item by (1) what values it can hold, (2) how it's stored, and (3) what operations are allowed on it. The two broadest types are numeric (numbers usable in arithmetic) and string (nonnumeric text, which cannot be used in arithmetic). A fixed value written directly in code is a constant/literal: a numeric constant like 43, or a string constant in quotes like "Amanda" (strings are also called alphanumeric because they may mix letters, digits, and symbols).

A variable is a named memory location whose contents can change. Before using one, most languages require a declaration providing a data type, an identifier (name), and optionally an initial value (initializing). An uninitialized variable holds garbage (an unknown value) — using it is a logic error.

📌 MUST-KNOW

Assignment

The assignment operator = (or ← / "Set … to …" in pseudocode) is a binary operator that works right-to-left: the expression on the right is evaluated first, then stored into the memory location on the left. The left side must be an lvalue (a name for a memory address); 5 = x is invalid because 5 is not a memory location.

Naming conventions you may see: camelCase (myVariableName), PascalCase (MyVariableName), snake_case (my_variable_name), and kebab-case (my-variable-name). A named constant gives a meaningful name to a fixed value set once (avoiding "magic numbers" — unexplained hard-coded values like 3.14). Rules of precedence (order of operations) decide which operators run first (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction); operators of equal precedence use left-to-right associativity (except assignment, which is right-to-left).

Going Deeper — Pseudocode & the Three Control Structures

To express any algorithm, pseudocode needs just a few concepts: variables, assignment (Set sum to 0), and input/output (Read num / Write "…"; synonyms: Get/Input, Display/Print). Everything else is built from three control structures:

Sequence — statements executed in order, top to bottom.

Selection (branch) — choose an action based on a Boolean expression (true/false). The if-then form does an action or skips it; the if-then-else form chooses between two actions.

Repetition (iteration/looping) — a WHILE loop repeats the indented body as long as its Boolean test is true. Because the test runs before the body, it's a pretest loop; if the test starts false, the body never runs.

📌 MUST-KNOW

A loop needs three things or it breaks: initialize a loop control variable, test it in the condition, and update/increment it in the body. Forget the increment and the condition never changes → an infinite loop.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Desk-check a summing loop

Algorithm: Set sum to 0; Set counter to 0; Read limit; WHILE (counter < limit){ Read num; Set sum to sum+num; Set counter to counter+1 } Print sum. Inputs: limit=3, then nums 5, 10, 2.

Initialize: sum=0, counter=0. Read limit=3.

Test counter(0) < 3 → true. Read num=5 → sum=0+5=5, counter=1.

Test 1 < 3 → true. Read num=10 → sum=5+10=15, counter=2.

Test 2 < 3 → true. Read num=2 → sum=15+2=17, counter=3.

Test 3 < 3 → false. Exit loop.

Print sum = 17. Loop ran exactly limit = 3 times (counter 0,1,2). ✔

Worked Example 2 — Evaluate an expression with precedence & associativity

Problem: Evaluate result = 2 + 3 * 4 - 10 / 2.

Apply higher precedence first (× and ÷, left to right): 3 * 4 = 12.

10 / 2 = 5.

Now left-to-right for + and −: 2 + 12 = 14.

14 - 5 = 9.

Assignment stores the right side into result → result = 9.

Wrong way → why → right way: Reading strictly left-to-right gives 2+3=5, ×4=20, −10=10, ÷2=5. Why wrong: it ignores that × and ÷ bind tighter than + and −. Right way: do all × and ÷ first, then + and −.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Almost every pseudocode question on this OA is answered the same way: build the trace table. One column per variable, one row per pass. It takes ninety seconds and it is the only method that does not lie to you — reading a loop “in your head” is exactly where the marks are lost.

The three things they test with it: how many times does this loop run? (a counter starting at 0 with test counter < limit runs limit times, values 0…limit−1 — write the values out rather than reasoning about them); what is printed? (watch whether the print sits inside or outside the loop body); and what if the condition is false at the start? (a pretest WHILE runs zero times, which is a favourite distractor).

For expression questions, evaluate strictly by precedence — × and ÷ before + and −, ties left to right — and remember assignment is the one that works right to left. If an answer choice matches a pure left-to-right reading, it is the trap answer, not the answer.

Reading an algorithm line by line

Most questions on this section do not ask you to write an algorithm. They hand you one and ask what it produces. That skill is tracing: walking the steps with a table of the variables, writing each new value down rather than holding it in your head.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Tracing nested loops — how many times does the inside run?

An outer loop runs 3 times. Inside it, an inner loop runs 4 times.

  1. The inner loop completes a full set of 4 passes for each single pass of the outer loop.
  2. The outer loop makes 3 passes.
  3. So the innermost statement runs 3 × 4 = 12 times.

Nested loops multiply. Loops one after another add.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Tracing a running total

SET total = 0; SET count = 0; WHILE count < 3: total = total + count; count = count + 1

The loop ends with total = 3 and count = 3. Note the body never ran with count = 3, because the test is checked before each pass.

Building a result up inside a loop like this — a variable that starts at zero and grows each pass — is the accumulator pattern, and total is the accumulator. Initialization matters: had total not been set to 0 first, every addition would build on a meaningless value.

The three control structures

📘 DEFINITION
Every algorithm, in any language, is built from just three: sequence (steps in order), selection (choose a path — if), and repetition (do something again — loops, also called iteration).

Selection comes in three shapes, and the exam names them:

In a chain like if score ≥ 90 → A; else if score ≥ 80 → B; else if score ≥ 70 → C, a score of 95 takes the first branch and stops. The later tests are never reached, even though 95 is also ≥ 80. That "first match wins, then exit" behavior is the whole point of the chain and a favorite exam trap.

Condition-controlled (while)until a condition goes falsethe count depends on the data

A count-controlled loop FOR i = 1 TO 5 runs exactly 5 times. A loop that keeps going until something happens rather than a set number of times is an event-controlled loop.

Sequence, selection and repetition are also called the three constructs. Putting one inside another is nesting, and choosing a construct is simply asking: one path or two (selection), or the same work repeated (repetition)? Every construct carries a small overhead — a loop must test its condition each pass, a call must set up a frame — which is why the cheapest correct construct is preferred.

Modulo — the remainder operator

📘 DEFINITION
% (modulo) gives the remainder after division. 17 % 5 = 2, because 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over.

Its two standard uses are worth memorizing:

  • Even or odd: n % 2 == 0 means n is even.
  • Divisible by / wrapping: n % 12 keeps a value inside 0–11, which is how clocks and circular buffers work.

Operands and operators

📘 DEFINITION
In the expression 3 + 5, the + is the operator and the values 3 and 5 are the operands — the things being operated on.

Operator precedence

Operators are not applied left to right; they have a fixed order, the same one as in arithmetic. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20, because * binds tighter than +. Brackets override it: (2 + 3) * 4 = 20. When a question shows an expression with mixed operators, that is almost always what it is testing.

Rough order, tightest first: brackets → unary NOT → * / % → + - → comparisons → AND → OR.

Short-circuit evaluation

📘 DEFINITION
With AND, if the left side is false the whole thing must be false, so the right side is never evaluated. With OR, if the left side is true the right side is skipped. This is called short-circuiting.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why the order of the conditions matters

if (count != 0 AND total / count > 5)

  1. Suppose count is 0.
  2. The left test count != 0 is false.
  3. Because AND short-circuits, total / count is never run — so the division by zero never happens.
  4. Reverse the two conditions and the program crashes.

The left condition is deliberately acting as a guard for the right one.

Scope, shadowing and lifetime

📘 DEFINITION
Scope is the region of a program where a name is visible. A variable declared inside a function is local — visible only in that function. One declared outside all functions is global — visible throughout the program.

Three consequences the questions lean on:

  • Out of scope is an error. Using a variable declared inside one function from a different function fails, because the name does not exist there. Pass it as a parameter or return it.
  • Shadowing. If a global total exists and a function declares its own local total, the local one hides the global inside that function. Assigning to it changes only the local copy — the global is unchanged.
  • Lifetime. A local variable exists only while its function is running. When the function returns, its memory is released and the value is gone.

Initialization

Reading a variable before assigning it a value is dangerous because it holds no meaningful value yet — depending on the language it is a compile error, a default like 0, or whatever happened to be in that memory. The last case is the worst: the program runs and produces a different wrong answer each time, which is far harder to find than a crash.

Mutability

A mutable object can be changed in place. If a and b both refer to the same mutable list and you call b.append(9), there is only one list — so a shows the 9 too. They are two names for one object, not two copies.

Reading = as "equals". In nearly every language = assigns and == compares. if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x rather than testing it.

ShapeMeans
Ovalstart or end (terminator)
Rectanglea process — a step being carried out
Diamonda decision — two or more ways out

Flowline (arrow)the order — which step comes next, the flow of control

The flowline is the arrow itself. It carries no processing; it shows the sequence.

One question type accounts for a lot of the pseudocode domain: you are given a formula or a described task, and four pseudocode snippets that all look plausible. You are not being asked to write code — you are being asked to spot the one snippet that does exactly what was described. That is a checking skill, and it is quicker and more reliable than reading each option as a whole.

The method — four checks, in this order

Before looking at the options, read the task and write down what the answer must contain. Then test each option against these, stopping the moment one fails:

  1. The operation. Is it adding when the task says add, dividing when the task says divide? Wrong-operator options are the easiest to bin.
  2. The order. Subtraction and division are not reversible. “Subtract d from f” is f − d, never d − f.
  3. The grouping. Does it need parentheses to force the order? x + y / 2 is not the average — division happens first. The average needs (x + y) / 2.
  4. The result. Is the value stored in the right variable, and is it actually displayed or returned if the task asked for that? A snippet that computes correctly and never outputs is still wrong.

Operands swappedd − f where the task said subtract d from f

Which pseudocode calculates the average of val_1 and val_2?

A) SET average TO val_1 + val_2 / 2 B) SET average TO (val_1 + val_2) / 2 C) SET val_1 + val_2 TO average / 2 D) SET average TO (val_1 − val_2) / 2

Check 1, the operation: an average adds, so D is out — it subtracts. Check 3, the grouping: A divides val_2 by 2 before adding, so it is not the average. Check 4, the result: C assigns to an expression, which is not a legal assignment at all. B survives every check.

Notice you never had to “solve” anything. Each wrong option died on a single named check.

💡 The habit to build

Read the task, say out loud what the correct line must look like, then read the options. If you read the options first you will find yourself talking yourself into the plausible-looking one, which is exactly what the distractors are designed for.

after this section you will be able to…

• Distinguish application software from system software, and place the operating system among them.

• Explain booting, multiprogramming, and the three resources an OS manages (memory, process, CPU).

• Contrast batch processing and timesharing, and define a virtual machine.

• Describe the role of device drivers and real-time systems.

• Recognize common operating systems and the idea of a dual-boot setup.

Plain-English First

An operating system is the playground monitor of a computer. Dozens of programs all want the same toys — memory, the CPU, the printer — at the same time. The OS makes sure everyone "shares nicely," takes turns, and doesn't grab someone else's stuff. It's also the front desk: it gives you (the human) a way to interact with the machine, and it gives application programs a way to reach the hardware without each one needing to know the hardware's every detail.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

Software splits into two categories. Application software solves real-world problems (word processors, games, inventory systems). System software manages the computer at a fundamental level and provides the environment in which applications run. The operating system (OS) is the core of system software: it manages resources (memory, I/O devices), provides a user interface, and lets applications reach other system resources.

When you power on, hardware loads a tiny set of instructions from permanent memory (ROM); those load the larger OS from secondary memory (disk) until the system is ready — this is booting ("pull yourself up by your bootstraps"). A machine may offer a dual-boot / multi-boot choice, but only one OS controls the computer at a time. Common OSes: Windows, macOS, UNIX/Linux, and mobile iOS and Android.

📌 MUST-KNOW

the OS's three big jobs

Multiprogramming keeps multiple programs in main memory at once, competing for the CPU. That forces the OS to do (1) memory management — track which programs are where in memory; (2) process management — track each running program's progress and states; (3) CPU scheduling — decide which process gets the CPU next. The OS is itself a program that must take its turn on the CPU too.

Historical/organizational concepts:

Batch processing — jobs (program + system instructions) grouped into batches needing similar resources, run without user interaction. Modern echo: .bat command files; payroll runs.

Timesharing — many users interact at once, each getting a slice of CPU time; it creates the illusion each user has the whole machine. Each user effectively gets a virtual machine ("in effect, though not in essence"). Classic setup: a mainframe with dumb terminals (just a monitor + keyboard).

Device driver — a small program that "knows" how a specific device communicates, so the OS doesn't need built-in knowledge of every device (an example of abstraction).

Real-time system — must guarantee a minimum response time (robots, reactors, missiles).

Key Terms

Batch processingRunning grouped jobs without user interaction.Efficient for large, hands-off jobs.

Virtual machineSoftware emulation of a full computer.Each user "gets" the whole system.

Three OS jobs = M-P-C: Memory management, Process management, CPU scheduling.

Driver = translator. The OS speaks to any device through its driver (abstraction).

Calling a game or word processor "system software." Those are application software.

Thinking a dual-boot machine runs two OSes at once. Only one controls the computer at a time.

Confusing multiprogramming (multiple programs in memory) with timesharing (multiple users).

Believing the OS doesn't use the CPU. The OS is itself a program that takes its turn.

Thinking "real-time" just means fast — it means a guaranteed response time.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Classify the software and the OS job

Problem: For each, name application vs. system software, and (if OS) which of the three jobs applies: (a) Microsoft Word, (b) the part of the OS deciding which process runs next, (c) a device driver for a printer.

(a) Word solves a real-world task → application software.

(b) Deciding which process runs next is CPU scheduling (a core OS job / system software).

(c) A printer driver is system software that interfaces the OS to the device.

Result: (a) application, (b) CPU scheduling, (c) system/driver. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Why timesharing feels private (wrong way → right way)

Scenario: A student claims "on a timesharing system each user truly has the whole CPU to themselves."

Wrong statement: each user literally owns the CPU.

Why it's wrong: the CPU is shared — each process gets small turns; it only seems private.

Right way: each user gets a virtual machine — "in effect, though not in essence" — the OS juggles turns so fast that delays are usually unnoticeable.

Caveat: with too many users, response can visibly degrade. ✔

📊 FIGURE — the three resources the operating system hands out
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two classification questions carry most of the marks here, and both are decided by one word.

Application or system software? Does it solve a real-world problem for a person (word processor, game, browser, payroll) → application. Does it provide the environment other software runs in (the OS, utilities, device drivers) → system. A driver is always system software, no matter what device it drives.

Which of the three OS jobs? Memory management = where a program sits. Process management = what state each program is in. CPU scheduling = whose turn is next. Read the verb in the question and match it.

Then guard the four wordings they build distractors from: multiprogramming means several programs are in memory; timesharing means several users are interacting; a dual-boot machine has two operating systems installed but only one running at a time; and “real-time” means a guaranteed response time, not merely a fast one.

Multitasking, and keeping programs apart

📘 DEFINITION
Multitasking (multiprogramming) is the OS keeping several programs in memory and switching the CPU between them fast enough that a browser, a music player and a word processor all appear to run at once.

Sharing memory between programs needs two registers per partition:

RegisterHoldsGives you
Base registerthe starting address of the program's partitionaddress binding — a logical address is turned into a real one by adding the base
Bounds registerthe size / limit of that partitionprotection — an address beyond the limit is refused

Together they provide address binding and protection: one program cannot read or corrupt another's memory, because every address it produces is checked against its own limit.

🧠 Memory hooks — what an OS actually does

HookWhat it unlocks
“My PC Files Down”Memory, Processor (CPU), Files, Devices — the four things an operating system manages. Almost any “what does the OS do?” question is one of these four.

Going Deeper — how memory is actually allocated

Base and bounds registers say where a program sits and how far it may reach. This is the other half of memory management: deciding which free space a new program gets, and what to do when there is not enough memory at all.

Fixed partitions vs dynamic partitions

SchemeHow memory is dividedThe waste it causes
Fixed partitionsa preset number of blocks of a fixed size, decided in advanceinternal fragmentation — a small program in a big block wastes the leftover inside its own block
Dynamic partitionseach partition is created to fit the program exactlyexternal fragmentation — as programs come and go, the free space breaks into scattered holes too small to use
📌 MUST-KNOW

first fit, best fit, worst fit

With dynamic partitions the OS must pick one of the free holes. Three strategies, and the exam wants you to apply them to a list:

• First fit — the first hole big enough, scanning from the start. Fastest to decide.

• Best fit — the smallest hole that still fits. Wastes least now, but leaves slivers.

• Worst fit — the largest hole. The leftover is big enough to be useful to somebody else.

Worked example. Free holes of 400 KB, 250 KB and 600 KB, in that order. A 200 KB job arrives.

StrategyWhich holeWhy
First fit400 KBthe first one scanned that is at least 200 KB
Best fit250 KBthe smallest hole that still fits — only 50 KB left over
Worst fit600 KBthe largest hole — 400 KB left, still usable by another job

Read the strategy name first, then scan the list once: first = earliest, best = smallest that fits, worst = biggest. Nearly every mark lost here comes from answering with the wrong one of the three.

Paging and virtual memory

Paging divides physical memory into equal frames and each program into equal pages of the same size. A page can then be loaded into any free frame — the program no longer needs one continuous run of memory, which kills external fragmentation.

Virtual memory takes the next step: only the pages actually in use need to be in RAM, and the rest live on disk. That is how a machine runs a program larger than its physical RAM. When the program touches a page that is not resident, the hardware raises a page fault, the OS fetches that page from disk (evicting another if needed) and the instruction resumes.

The cost is speed: disk is far slower than RAM. If a system spends more time moving pages than running programs it is thrashing, and the fix is more RAM or fewer concurrent programs.
