after this section you will be able to…

• Name and describe the five process states and the transitions between them.

• Explain what a process is versus a program.

• Describe the process control block (PCB) and what it stores.

• Define a context switch and why the program counter must be saved.

• Recognize that only one process runs at a time, while many may be ready or waiting.

Plain-English First

A program is a recipe sitting in a cookbook — static text. A process is what happens when a cook actually starts making the dish: ingredients out, a specific step in progress, timers running. The OS is the head chef tracking many dishes at once, but there's only one stove burner (the CPU), so it constantly notes exactly where each dish is, pauses some, and resumes others without losing anyone's place.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

A process is a program in execution — the dynamic entity representing a program while it runs. Through multiprogramming, many processes exist at once, so the OS does process management: tracking each process's progress and intermediate state. Processes move through five process states:

New — the process is being created.

Ready — no barriers; waiting only for a turn on the CPU.

Running — currently executing in the fetch–execute cycle.

Waiting — waiting for a resource other than the CPU (e.g., I/O, a signal).

Terminated — finished; the OS no longer needs its info.

📌 MUST-KNOW

transitions & the one-at-a-time rule

After creation the OS admits a process to ready; the scheduler dispatches it to running. A running process may be interrupted back to ready, may request a resource and go to waiting, or may terminate. A waiting process, once it gets its resource, returns to ready (not directly to running). Many processes can be ready or waiting at once, but only ONE can be running.

The OS stores each process's data in a process control block (PCB). Each state is a list of PCBs; a process's PCB moves between lists as it changes state. The PCB holds the program counter (which instruction is next), all other CPU register values, CPU-scheduling info (like priority), memory-management info (base/bounds or page tables), and accounting info. Because there's only one set of CPU registers, switching processes means saving the current process's registers into its PCB and loading the next process's registers — this exchange is a context switch.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
ProgramA static set of instructions.The recipe, not the cooking.
ProcessA program in execution (dynamic).What the OS actually manages.
Process statesNew, ready, running, waiting, terminated.The lifecycle the OS tracks.
Ready stateWaiting only for the CPU.Eligible to be dispatched.
Waiting stateWaiting for a non-CPU resource.Blocked until I/O/signal arrives.
PCBData structure holding all process info.Lets a process resume correctly.
Program counterAddress of the next instruction.Saved so a process resumes in place.
Context switchSaving one process's registers, loading another's.Enables CPU sharing.

Only ONE runs. Many ready, many waiting, exactly one running (single CPU).

Waiting → Ready, never straight to Running. After getting its resource, a process rejoins the ready line.

PCB = the process's "save file." Program counter + registers let it resume exactly where it left off.

Context switch = swap the save files. Store current registers to PCB, load the next process's.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying a process goes from waiting directly to running. It returns to ready first.

Thinking multiple processes can be "running" simultaneously on one CPU. Only one runs at a time.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Trace a process through the states

Scenario: A newly launched app needs to read a file partway through execution.

The app is created → New.

OS admits it → Ready (waiting for a CPU turn).

Scheduler dispatches it → Running.

It requests a file read (I/O) → moves to Waiting.

File data arrives → back to Ready (not straight to running).

Dispatched again → Running → finishes → Terminated. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Why a context switch needs the PCB

Problem: Process A is interrupted at instruction 5000 so Process B can run. What must happen so A resumes correctly?

Save A's program counter (5000) and all CPU register values into A's PCB.

Load B's saved registers/program counter from B's PCB into the CPU.

B runs; later, reverse the process to bring A back.

Because A's state was saved, A resumes at instruction 5000 as if never interrupted — that swap is the context switch. ✔

Wrong way → why → right way: Skipping the save and just loading B would lose A's place (its registers get overwritten). Right way: always store the outgoing process's registers to its PCB first.

🎯 EXAM TIP

The five states are asked as a sequence question: “a running process requests a file — what happens?” Answer with the transition, not the state: running → waiting (it needs something other than the CPU), then when the data arrives waiting → ready, and only later ready → running when the scheduler picks it.

The counting question is just as reliable: on one CPU there is exactly one running process, and any number of ready and waiting ones. If a question says two processes are running simultaneously on a single processor, it is wrong.

Deadlock is a standstill in which each process holds a resource the other needs and waits for one the other holds, so none can ever proceed.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The classic two-process deadlock

Process A holds resource 1 and waits for resource 2. Process B holds resource 2 and waits for resource 1.

  1. A will not release resource 1 until it gets resource 2.
  2. B will not release resource 2 until it gets resource 1.
  3. Neither condition can ever become true. Both wait for ever: this is deadlock.

Note what it is not: not starvation (where a process is repeatedly passed over but could still run), and not an infinite loop (where a process is busy, not blocked).

🎯 EXAM TIP
The usual practical cure is to break circular wait by requiring every process to request resources in the same fixed order.

after this section you will be able to…

• Define CPU scheduling and distinguish preemptive from nonpreemptive.

• Compute turnaround time and average turnaround time from a Gantt chart.

• Apply FCFS, SJN, and round-robin to a set of processes.

• Explain the trade-offs of each algorithm (fairness, efficiency, knowledge of the future).

• Read a Gantt chart and identify completion/turnaround times.

Plain-English First

Only one process can use the CPU at a time, so the OS is like a checkout clerk deciding who goes next in line. Do you serve people in arrival order (fair but slow if a big cart is first)? Serve the smallest cart first (fast average, but you must guess cart sizes)? Or give everyone a fixed 2 minutes and rotate (nobody waits forever)? Those three policies are FCFS, SJN, and round-robin.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

CPU scheduling decides which ready process moves to running. Scheduling can be nonpreemptive (a new choice happens only when the running process voluntarily leaves — it waits or terminates) or preemptive (the OS can interrupt a running process — e.g., on a timeout or when a higher-priority process becomes ready). A key metric is turnaround time: the time from when a process arrives in ready until it leaves running for the last time. Lower average turnaround is better. (When all arrive at time 0, turnaround = completion time.)

📌 MUST-KNOW

the three algorithms (all arrive at t=0)

Using service times p1=140, p2=75, p3=320, p4=280, p5=125:

FCFS (arrival order p1..p5, nonpreemptive): completions 140, 215, 535, 815, 940 → avg = 529.

SJN (shortest first: p2,p5,p1,p4,p3, nonpreemptive): completions 75, 200, 340, 620, 940 → avg = 435 (provably optimal if service times are known).

Round-robin (time slice 50, preemptive): completions p1=515, p2=325, p3=940, p4=920, p5=640 → avg = 668 (most fair, most widely used).

Notes on each: FCFS is easy but ignores service times, so a long job first delays everyone. SJN gives the smallest average turnaround if you know each job's length — but you can't know the future, so the OS estimates; bad estimates hurt it. Round-robin gives each process a time slice (quantum); when it expires the process is preempted back to ready. Its average turnaround here is highest, but you can't judge an algorithm from one example — round-robin is the most widely used and considered the fairest.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
CPU schedulingChoosing which ready process runs next.Determines efficiency and fairness.
NonpreemptiveRunning process isn't interrupted; it finishes/waits.FCFS and SJN are nonpreemptive.
PreemptiveOS can interrupt a running process.Round-robin is preemptive.
Turnaround timeReady-arrival → last exit from running.The key performance metric.
FCFSRun in arrival order.Simple; can delay everyone.
SJN (shortest job next)Run the shortest service time next.Optimal avg turnaround if times known.
Round-robinFixed time slice, rotate.Fair; most widely used.
Time slice (quantum)CPU time each process gets before preemption.Defines round-robin behavior.

Calling round-robin nonpreemptive. It is preemptive (time slice expiry).

Forgetting SJN needs the service times, which usually must be estimated.

Miscomputing average turnaround — sum the completion times, then divide by the count.

Assuming FCFS can starve a process. It can't; SSTF-style greediness (disk) can — not FCFS.

Declaring one algorithm universally best from a single example.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — FCFS vs. SJN average turnaround

Processes (arrive at t=0): p1=140, p2=75, p3=320, p4=280, p5=125.

FCFS order p1,p2,p3,p4,p5. Completions: 140; 140+75=215; 215+320=535; 535+280=815; 815+125=940.

Average = (140+215+535+815+940)/5 = 2645/5 = 529.

SJN order (shortest first): p2(75), p5(125), p1(140), p4(280), p3(320). Completions: 75; 200; 340; 620; 940.

Average = (75+200+340+620+940)/5 = 2175/5 = 435.

SJN's average (435) beats FCFS (529) — it front-loads short jobs. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Round-robin with time slice 50

Same processes, quantum = 50, order p1..p5, preemptive.

Give each 50 units in turn, subtracting from remaining time, until each hits 0.

p2 needed 75: after two visits (50 + 25) it finishes at time 325.

Working through all rounds, completion times are p1=515, p2=325, p3=940, p4=920, p5=640.

Average = (515+325+940+920+640)/5 = 3340/5 = 668.

Higher average than FCFS/SJN here — but round-robin is the fairest and most widely used; one example doesn't crown a winner. ✔

🎯 EXAM TIP

These questions are arithmetic, and the arithmetic is short if you write the Gantt chart first. With every process arriving at time 0 — which is how this OA words it — turnaround time = completion time, so there is no subtraction to do.

The method: put the jobs in the order the algorithm dictates (arrival order for FCFS, shortest-first for SJN), write a running total across the row, and those running totals are the completion times. Add them, divide by the number of processes, done. For round robin, subtract the quantum from each job in rotation and note the time at which each one hits zero.

Orderwhoever arrived first runs to completioneach process gets a fixed time quantum in turn

after this section you will be able to…

• Define a file, a file system, and the difference between text and binary files.

• Explain file types/extensions and why an extension doesn't change a file's actual contents.

• List the standard file operations and the role of the file pointer.

• Contrast sequential and direct file access, and describe file protection (owner/group/world).

• Navigate a directory tree and write absolute and relative paths (including ..).

Plain-English First

Your computer's disk is a giant filing cabinet. A file is one labeled folder of related data; the file system is the whole organized cabinet plus the rules for finding things. Directories (folders) are drawers that hold files and even other drawers, forming a tree. To tell someone exactly where a document lives, you either give directions from the very top of the cabinet (absolute path) or from where you're currently standing (relative path).

Going Deeper — Files, Types & Operations

Recall main memory is volatile (lost without power) while secondary memory (disk) is nonvolatile — used for permanent storage. A file is a named collection of related data — the smallest unit a user writes to secondary memory. A file system is the logical view the OS provides for managing data as files, usually grouped into directories.

All files are ultimately binary, but we classify them as:

Text file — bytes organized as ASCII/Unicode characters (human-readable; e.g., source code, config).

Binary file — bits interpreted in a specific non-character format (images, executables, Word docs). Only a program built for that format can read it. (A word-processor document is actually binary because it stores formatting, fonts, etc.)

📌 MUST-KNOW

extensions don't define contents

The file extension (after the dot, e.g., .java, .jpg) tells the OS the likely file type so it can pick an application/icon. But an extension is only an indication: renaming photo.txt to photo.gif does not change the file's actual data or make it a real GIF — opening it in a GIF program gives an error.

File operations (via the OS): create, delete, open, close, read, write, reposition the file pointer, append, truncate (erase contents, keep the entry), rename, copy. An open file has a current file pointer marking where the next read/write happens; it advances as you read/write. Truncating deletes contents without removing the file's table entry.

Going Deeper — Access, Protection, Directories & Paths

File access methods:

Sequential access — process the file in order from start to end (simplest, most common).

Direct access — file is numbered logical records; jump to any record by number (great for databases where specific data must be reached fast).

File protection (multiuser systems): UNIX uses three categories — Owner, Group, World — each with read / write / execute permissions (shown as a 3×3 grid). If you can write to a file you can also delete it. World permissions reach the most users, so they're usually the most restricted.

📌 MUST-KNOW

directory trees & paths

A directory can contain files and subdirectories; the top is the root (Windows C:\, UNIX /), forming a directory tree. Your current location is the working directory. An absolute path starts at the root (C:\Program Files\MS Office\WinWord.exe). A relative path starts at the working directory (applications\calState.doc); .. means the parent directory and a single . means the current directory. Files in different directories may share a name; files in the same directory cannot.

Key Terms

Binary fileBits in a specific non-character format.Images, executables, Word docs.
File extensionSuffix indicating file type.OS picks app/icon; only an indication.
File pointerMarks next read/write location.Tracks position in an open file.
Sequential accessRead/write in order.Simple, common.
Direct accessJump to any numbered record.Fast for databases.
DirectoryNamed collection of files (a folder).Organizes files hierarchically.
Root directoryTop of the directory tree.Start of every absolute path.
Working directoryYour current location.Start of every relative path.
Absolute pathFull path from the root.Unambiguous location.
Relative pathPath from the working directory.Shorter; .. = parent.

Diagram — A directory tree with paths

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Extension = label, not contents. Renaming .txt→.gif doesn't make it a GIF.

Text = characters; Binary = special format. A Word doc is binary (it stores formatting).

Absolute starts at the top (root); Relative starts where you stand (working dir).

.. = up one level (parent); . = right here.

Owner > Group > World. World reaches everyone, so it's usually the most restricted.

Truncate keeps the file, empties it; delete removes the entry entirely.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Believing changing a file's extension changes its data/format. It doesn't.

Calling a Word document a text file — it's binary.

Starting a relative path at the root, or forgetting .. to go up a level.

Thinking two files in the same directory can share a name (they can't; different directories can).

Mixing up sequential (in order) and direct (jump to any record) access.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Absolute vs. relative path

Tree: working directory is C:\My Documents\letters. Target file calState.doc is in C:\My Documents\letters\applications. Give both an absolute and a relative path; then reach landscape.jpg in C:\My Documents.

Absolute to calState.doc: start at root → C:\My Documents\letters\applications\calState.doc.

Relative (from letters): the file is one level down in applications → applications\calState.doc.

To reach landscape.jpg in the parent My Documents: go up one level with .. → ..\landscape.jpg.

Check: .. moves from letters up to My Documents, where landscape.jpg lives. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Classify files & the extension trap (wrong way → right way)

Classify: report.docx → binary (stores formatting); notes.txt → text; Game.exe → binary.

Wrong way: a user renames song.mp3 to song.txt expecting to read lyrics in Notepad.

Why it's wrong: the bytes are still MP3 audio; the extension is just a label — the data is unchanged.

Right way: open it with a program that matches the real format; renaming can't convert a file. ✔

📊 FIGURE — UNIX permissions, and sequential versus direct access
🎯 EXAM TIP

The highest-frequency item here is the extension trap, and it has a one-sentence answer: the extension is a label, not the contents. Renaming song.mp3 to song.txt changes nothing about the bytes — it only changes which application the OS offers to open it with.

Path questions are mechanical if you say where you are standing first. An absolute path starts at the root (C:\ or /) and reads the same from anywhere. A relative path starts at the working directory, and .. means “up one level to the parent”. Write out the walk step by step rather than pattern-matching the answer choices.

For permissions, read the nine bits in three groups of three — owner, group, world, each with read, write, execute. World is the broadest audience, so it is normally the most restricted set.

Two more one-mark facts: a text file is bytes interpreted as ASCII/Unicode characters, so a Word document is a binary file (it stores formatting); and truncate empties a file but keeps it, while delete removes the entry altogether.

How a file system is organized, and two failure modes

A file system organizes directories and files into a hierarchical structure — a tree: one root, directories containing files and further directories, each file reached by a path from the root.

📘 DEFINITION
Journaling. A journaling file system writes what it is about to do into a log before doing it. If power is lost mid-write, it replays or discards the log on restart and the file system is consistent again — solving the corruption that an interrupted write used to cause, without a long whole-disk check.
📘 DEFINITION
Thrashing. When too many large programs are open, memory is oversubscribed and the OS spends nearly all its time swapping pages between RAM and disk instead of running programs. The machine slows to a crawl while the disk runs constantly — that symptom is thrashing, and the fix is more RAM or fewer running programs.

🧠 Memory hooks — file systems

HookWhat it unlocks
Path = directions, not the fileAn absolute path starts at the root and works anywhere; a relative path starts where you are and breaks if you move. “Absolute = from the top.”
Extension is a hint, not a factThe extension tells the OS which program to open a file with. Renaming it does not change what is inside — a classic trap answer.

after this section you will be able to…

• Explain why disk I/O is the system's bottleneck and define seek time vs. latency.

• Apply FCFS, SSTF, and SCAN disk scheduling to a request list.

• Define starvation and identify which algorithm risks it.

• Describe the SCAN (elevator), LOOK, and Circular SCAN variations.

• Order cylinder visits and reason about head movement.

Plain-English First

Reading from a spinning disk is the slowest thing a computer does, so the order in which the read/write head visits requested tracks really matters. Picture an elevator with people waiting on many floors. Do you answer call buttons in the exact order they were pressed (fair but lots of zig-zagging)? Always go to the nearest floor next (efficient, but someone far away might wait forever)? Or sweep smoothly top-to-bottom then bottom-to-top (the elevator strategy)? Those are FCFS, SSTF, and SCAN.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

A disk is a stack of platters, each with tracks divided into sectors; the aligned tracks across platters form a cylinder. The heads sit over one cylinder at a time. Seek time is the time to move the heads to the right cylinder; latency is the extra time for the platter to rotate into position. Seek time is the bigger cost, so disk-scheduling algorithms focus on minimizing head movement. Transferring to/from disk is the system's worst bottleneck (far slower than CPU or main memory).

Example request queue (in arrival order): 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35; heads start at cylinder 26.

📌 MUST-KNOW

the three algorithms on this example

FCFS: visit in arrival order → 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35 (lots of back-and-forth; simple, never starves).

SSTF (shortest seek time first): always go to the nearest pending request → 22, 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91, 7 (efficient, but can cause starvation).

SCAN (elevator), moving toward lower cylinders first: sweep down servicing 22, 7, reach the low end, reverse, then service 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91. No starvation.

Starvation: under SSTF, if nearby requests keep arriving, a far-away request might never be served. FCFS can't starve (it honors order). SCAN sweeps to each extreme like an elevator; LOOK is a smarter SCAN that only goes as far as the outermost/innermost actual request (it "looks ahead"), and Circular SCAN (C-SCAN) treats the disk as a ring, jumping back to the start without servicing on the return to improve fairness of wait times.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Seek timeTime to move heads to the right cylinder.The dominant disk cost to minimize.
LatencyTime for platter rotation into position.Secondary cost after seek time.
CylinderAligned tracks across all platters.The unit disk scheduling targets.
Disk schedulingDeciding the order to serve disk requests.Reduces seek time; speeds I/O.
FCFS (disk)Serve requests in arrival order.Simple; no starvation; inefficient.
SSTFServe the nearest pending request next.Efficient but risks starvation.
StarvationA request never served due to closer ones.SSTF's main flaw.
SCAN (elevator)Sweep to one extreme, then reverse.Fair; no starvation.
LOOKSCAN that reverses at the last request.Avoids needless travel to the edge.
Circular SCANTreats disk as a ring; returns without servicing.Evens out wait times.

Diagram — Head movement for the example (start = 26)

Comparison / Reference Tables

FCFSSSTFSCAN (elevator)
BasisArrival orderNearest requestSweep to extremes
EfficiencyLow (zig-zags)HigherGood, steady
Starvation?NoPossibleNo

SCAN vs. LOOK vs. C-SCAN

SCANLOOKCircular SCAN
Travels toThe physical edge/spindleOnly the last requestEdge, then jumps back
Services on return?YesYesNo (ring behavior)

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Seek time > latency. Head movement (seek) is the main cost the algorithms attack.

FCFS = order; SSTF = nearest; SCAN = elevator.

Only SSTF starves. FCFS and SCAN cannot starve a request.

LOOK "looks ahead" and turns around at the last request instead of the physical edge.

C-SCAN = ring. It returns to the start without servicing on the way back.

SSTF ≠ least total movement guaranteed — it's greedy, not globally optimal.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying FCFS or SCAN can starve. Only SSTF risks starvation.

Claiming SSTF always gives the least total head movement — it's greedy, not optimal.

Confusing seek time (head movement) with latency (rotation). Seek time dominates.

Forgetting SCAN needs an initial direction to compute the order.

Mixing up SCAN (goes to the edge) and LOOK (turns at the last request).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — SSTF order and starvation

Requests: 49, 91, 22, 61, 7, 62, 33, 35; head at 26.

From 26, nearest pending is 22 (distance 4) → go to 22.

From 22, nearest is 33 → then 35 → then 49 (49 now closest).

Continue nearest-first: 61, 62, 91, and finally the far-off 7.

Order: 22, 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91, 7.

Starvation note: if new nearby requests kept arriving, cylinder 7 (far away) might be postponed indefinitely — that's SSTF starvation. ✔

Worked Example 2 — SCAN (elevator) going low first (wrong way → right way)

Head at 26 moving toward lower cylinders: service 22, then 7 on the way down.

Reach the low extreme, then reverse and sweep upward.

Going up, service 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91 in order.

Full order: 22, 7, (reverse) 33, 35, 49, 61, 62, 91.

Wrong way → why → right way: jumping straight from 26 up to 33 first ignores SCAN's rule to finish the current direction. Right way: service everything in the current direction (down to 22, 7) before reversing. ✔

📊 FIGURE — track, sector and cylinder — and where seek time and latency come from
🎯 EXAM TIP

Ordering questions are answered by the algorithm’s one rule, applied literally from the starting cylinder. FCFS: arrival order, ignore the head position entirely. SSTF: repeatedly take the nearest pending request — recompute the distances after every move, which is the step people skip. SCAN: keep going in the current direction to the end, servicing on the way, then reverse — so you must be told or must state the initial direction.

The conceptual mark is always starvation: only SSTF can starve a request, because a steady stream of nearby requests can postpone a far-away one indefinitely. FCFS and SCAN both guarantee everyone is eventually served.

Keep the two delays apart — seek time is the arm moving between cylinders, latency is the platter rotating the sector under the head, and access time is the two added together. Seek is the one worth optimising, which is why every algorithm here is about the order of cylinder visits.

Finally, do not upgrade SSTF to “optimal”. It is greedy — nearest next — and greedy is not the same as least total head movement over the whole queue.

Fragmentation

📘 DEFINITION
Fragmentation is a file ending up stored in blocks scattered across the disk rather than in one run.

On a magnetic hard drive the effect is slower reads: the head must physically seek to each separate location instead of streaming one continuous stretch, so seek time dominates. No data is lost — it is purely a performance cost, which is what defragmenting addresses.

It barely matters on an SSD, which has no moving head and reaches any block in the same time.

🧠 Memory hooks — disk scheduling

HookWhat it unlocks
“Fast Seeks Scan Clean Looks”FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK.
SCAN is the liftSCAN sweeps to the end and back like a lift; LOOK is the polite lift that turns round as soon as there are no more requests ahead. C-SCAN always returns the same way, so waiting is fairer.

after this section you will be able to…

• Decode a real laptop spec: CPU/clock speed, cache, RAM, SSD, GPU, ports.

• Explain the clock and what GHz/hertz measure.

• Distinguish RAM (main memory) from SSD (secondary storage).

• Use the computing size prefixes and the powers-of-10 vs. powers-of-2 rule.

• Identify common ports (USB, HDMI) and their uses.

Plain-English First

A computer ad is just a car sticker for a machine — horsepower, fuel tank, trunk space — written in acronyms. The CPU is the engine, its GHz is the RPM, RAM is the desk you spread your work on right now, the SSD is the filing cabinet that keeps everything when you go home, and ports are the plugs on the side. Learn to read the sticker and no spec sheet can intimidate you.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

Walking a real spec: Intel Core i7 (2.8 GHz Quad-Core), 12 MB cache, 20 GB SDRAM, 1 TB SSD, GPU, USB & HDMI ports.

CPU + clock: The processor's speed (2.8 GHz) is set by the clock — a steady stream of electrical pulses that coordinates all actions (like a conductor's baton). Hz = hertz = cycles per second; G = giga = one billion.

Cache: small, very fast memory built into the processor holding frequently used data, so the CPU often avoids slower main-memory trips.

RAM (main memory): random access means any byte can be reached directly. SDRAM = synchronous dynamic RAM. It's where active programs/data live while in use.

SSD (secondary storage): like RAM technology but nonvolatile (keeps data with power off); no moving parts, so faster and lower-power than a spinning hard drive.

GPU: a separate graphics chip that offloads image work from the main CPU, with its own memory.

Ports: USB (universal serial bus) connects almost anything; HDMI sends digital video/audio to displays/TVs.

📌 MUST-KNOW

the prefix rule

Time uses powers of 10 (decimal); storage uses powers of 2 (binary). So K = 1000 for speed but 1024 (2¹⁰) for storage. A byte = 8 bits; KB ≈ 10³, MB ≈ 2²⁰, GB ≈ 2³⁰, TB ≈ 2⁴⁰ bytes. (Milli/micro/nano/pico measure small times in powers of 10.)

Key Terms

CPUMain chip executing instructions.The "engine" of the computer.
ClockPulses coordinating all actions.Sets the processing tempo (GHz).
Hertz (Hz)Cycles per second.Unit of clock frequency.
Cache memorySmall fast memory in the CPU.Speeds access to frequent data.
RAM (main memory)Directly addressable working memory.Holds active programs/data; volatile.
SSDNonvolatile solid-state secondary storage.Fast permanent storage, no moving parts.
GPUSeparate graphics processor.Offloads image work from the CPU.
USB / HDMIPorts for devices / video-audio.Connect peripherals and displays.
Byte8 bits.Basic unit of storage size.

Diagram — Reading a laptop spec

Size prefixes (the powers rule)

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Clock = conductor. GHz is how many billion "beats" per second the CPU marches to.

RAM = desk (temporary), SSD = filing cabinet (permanent).

Time = base 10, Storage = base 2. "K is 1000 for speed, 1024 for storage."

Byte = 8 bits. Always.

Cache is closest & fastest; the CPU checks it before going to main memory.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Thinking RAM keeps data when powered off. It's volatile; the SSD is permanent.

Using 1024 for time or 1000 for storage. Time = base 10, storage = base 2.

Confusing cache (tiny, in-CPU) with main memory (larger, slower).

Calling GHz a storage measure. It's a speed (cycles per second).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Decode a spec line

Problem: Explain "2.8 GHz Quad-Core, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD."

2.8 GHz = clock speed of 2.8 billion cycles/second (speed, base 10).

Quad-Core = four processing cores on the CPU.

16 GB RAM = main working memory, volatile (base 2 sizing).

512 GB SSD = nonvolatile secondary storage for permanent files.

Plain meaning: a fairly fast laptop with roomy working memory and solid permanent storage. ✔

Worked Example 2 — The prefix rule (wrong way → right way)

Question: Is "1 KB of storage" 1000 or 1024 bytes?

Wrong way: assume 1000 because "kilo means 1000."

Why it's wrong: storage is measured in powers of 2, so K = 2¹⁰.

Right way: 1 KB (storage) = 1024 bytes. (For a "1 K" data rate/speed, it would be 1000.) ✔

📊 FIGURE — the memory hierarchy — what a spec sheet is really listing
🎯 EXAM TIP

Spec-decoding questions are answered from three separations. Speed versus storage: GHz is a rate (billions of clock pulses a second), GB is a quantity — if a choice calls GHz a storage measure it is wrong. RAM versus SSD: RAM is the working desk and is volatile; the SSD is the filing cabinet and is nonvolatile. Cache versus main memory: cache is tiny, inside the processor, and checked first.

The prefix rule is a guaranteed mark and is easy to get backwards: time and speed use powers of 10 (1 K = 1,000), storage uses powers of 2 (1 KB = 1,024 bytes = 2¹⁰). Memorise 2¹⁰ = 1,024, 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million, 2³⁰ ≈ 1 billion and you can convert any of them.

And a byte is always 8 bits, so a question giving you bits and asking for bytes (or the reverse) is a division or multiplication by 8 — check which way round before answering.

The pieces, and what each one is for

ComponentWhat it is
Motherboardthe main circuit board that houses the CPU, memory and core components and connects them
Registera very small, very fast storage location inside the CPU, holding the value being worked on right now
Cachesmall fast memory between CPU and RAM, holding recently used data
RAMmain memory — large, fast, and volatile
ROMread-only memory — non-volatile, written at manufacture, holds firmware and start-up instructions
SSD / hard disksecondary storage — slower, much larger, non-volatile
Busthe shared set of wires carrying data, addresses and control signals between components

The speed order, fastest and smallest first: register → cache → RAM → SSD/disk. Every step down is bigger and slower.

Machines have several buses — a data bus carrying the values, an address bus carrying the location, and a control bus carrying the timing and read/write signals. A wider bus moves more bits per transfer, which is a direct performance benefit.

📘 DEFINITION
Volatility. RAM is volatile — its contents are lost when power is removed. An SSD is non-volatile — it keeps its contents with the power off. That, not speed or size, is the defining difference between the two.
📘 DEFINITION
Addressability is the number of bits stored in each addressable location in memory. If a machine is byte-addressable, every address names 8 bits.

Clock speed or more cores?

Given a workload of many independent tasks running at once, more cores helps more than a higher clock speed on a single core: the tasks genuinely run in parallel, one per core. A higher clock speed only helps a single task go faster, which is what matters for work that cannot be split.

Compiler and interpreter

CompilerInterpreter
When it translatesthe whole program, before it runsline by line, as it runs
Producesan executable fileno separate file — it executes directly

Input and Output Devices — including touch screens

The parts above are what the computer thinks with. This is how it communicates. An input device carries data in to the computer (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, camera, barcode reader). An output device carries results out to you (monitor, printer, speakers, projector). A few devices do both — and the exam's favourite example is the touch screen, which displays the picture (output) and accepts your tap (input) in the same surface. Storage devices such as an SSD or a USB drive also count as both, since data flows in and out of them.

The four touch-screen technologies

They differ in what physically detects the touch, and every other difference — gloves, clarity, durability — follows from that one fact. Learn the mechanism and you can derive the rest instead of memorising a table.

TypeHow it detects a touchWorks with a gloved hand?
ResistiveTwo flexible conductive layers with a tiny gap. Pressing pushes them together so they make contact at that point.Yes — it only needs pressure, so a glove, fingernail or any stylus works.
CapacitiveThe glass carries a small electrical charge. A conductive object (bare skin) changes the charge at that spot and the controller locates the change.No — an ordinary glove is not conductive, so no change is registered. Only special conductive "touch-screen" gloves work.
Surface acoustic wave (SAW)Transducers send high-frequency sound waves across the glass. A touch absorbs part of the wave, and the interruption gives the position.Yes — a gloved finger absorbs the wave just as skin does.

Why capacitive is the odd one out

This is the single most tested point. Resistive needs pressure, SAW needs something that absorbs sound, infrared needs something that blocks light — a gloved hand does all three. Clarity and durability, in one line each

  • Resistive — cheapest and resists dust and moisture well, but the extra layers dim the image and it is usually single-touch.

Match the technology to the word in the question: press → resistive · charge / conductive / skin → capacitive · sound wave → SAW · light beam / grid → infrared. And remember one exception: only capacitive fails with gloves.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• State the stored-program concept and why it was revolutionary.

• Name the five components of the von Neumann architecture and each one's job.

• Explain memory addressability and that a bit pattern needs interpretation.

• Describe the ALU, registers, the control unit (IR, PC), the CPU, and the bus.

• Contrast RAM vs. ROM and describe secondary storage (tape, disk) and disk timing.

Plain-English First

The single biggest idea in computing (1944–45): instructions and data can live in the same memory, treated the same way. Before that, "programming" often meant physically rewiring the machine. Once programs became just data you could store and load, the modern computer was born. That design — the von Neumann architecture — still describes essentially every computer today. Think of it as a kitchen: a pantry (memory) holds both recipes and ingredients, a chef's station (ALU) does the work, a door in and a door out (input/output), and a head chef (control unit) directing everything.

Going Deeper — The Five Components

The stored-program concept (von Neumann architecture, credited to von Neumann; ideas also from Eckert, Mauchly, and Atanasoff) separates the units that process information from those that store it, giving five components:

Memory unit — holds both data and instructions.

Arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) — does arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logic (AND, OR, NOT).

Input unit — moves data from the outside world in (keyboard, mouse, scanner).

Output unit — moves results out (monitor, printer).

Control unit — the "stage manager" coordinating everything (runs the fetch–execute cycle).

The ALU and control unit together are the CPU.

📌 MUST-KNOW

memory, registers, and interpretation

Memory is a collection of cells, each with a unique address (numbered from 0). Addressability = bits per addressable cell; most machines are byte-addressable (8 bits). A stored bit pattern (e.g., 10101010) has no inherent meaning — it could be an instruction, an integer, part of an image — you must apply an interpretation. Registers are tiny, ultra-fast CPU storage (one word each) used to hold intermediate results; the control unit has two special ones: the instruction register (IR) (current instruction) and the program counter (PC) (address of the next instruction).

The components connect via a bus (a set of wires) carrying three kinds of information: address, data, and control. Bus width = bits transferable at once (wider = more at once). Speed helpers: cache (fast copy of frequent data, checked before main memory) and pipelining (overlapping instruction steps). All these components sit on the motherboard.

Going Deeper — RAM vs. ROM and Secondary Storage

RAM (random-access memory) is directly accessible and changeable, but volatile (lost at power-off). ROM (read-only memory) is nonvolatile and cannot be changed (its pattern is burned in) — used to store the instructions the computer needs to start. Main memory usually has some ROM plus general RAM.

Secondary (auxiliary/mass) storage keeps programs/data when not in use or when powered off; each device is both input and output. Magnetic tape is sequential (must pass earlier data to reach the middle) — good for backup. Magnetic disks use tracks (concentric circles) divided into sectors (each holding a block). Four disk-efficiency measures: seek time (head to the track), latency (sector spins to the head; avg = ½ rotation — a.k.a. rotation delay), access time (seek + latency), and transfer rate (data speed disk→memory).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Map jobs to components

Problem: Which von Neumann component handles each: (a) adding two numbers, (b) holding a program while it runs, (c) coordinating the fetch–execute cycle, (d) a keyboard press, (e) printing a result?

(a) Add → ALU.

(b) Hold program → Memory unit.

(c) Coordinate cycle → Control unit.

(d) Keyboard → Input unit.

(e) Print → Output unit. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Interpret a bit pattern (wrong way → right way)

Question: Memory address 11111110 holds 10101010. What does it mean?

Wrong way: declare it "equals 170" as if that's the only truth.

Why it's incomplete: the same bits could be an instruction, a signed value, part of an image, etc.

Right way: you must know the intended interpretation first; without it, 10101010 is just a bit pattern. (As an unsigned integer it is 170, but that's only one interpretation.) ✔

🎯 EXAM TIP

The pair most often swapped is PC and IR. The Instruction Register holds the instruction being executed now; the Program Counter holds the address of what comes next. “IR = now, PC = next” is worth writing on your scratch paper.

The stored-program concept itself gets a conceptual question: instructions and data live in the same memory, in the same binary form, which is what makes a general-purpose computer possible. That is also why “what does 10101010 mean?” has no answer without knowing the intended interpretation.

RAM versus ROM: RAM is changeable and volatile; ROM is fixed and permanent. If a choice calls ROM volatile, or says it can be rewritten in normal use, it is wrong.

The four parts of a von Neumann machine

PartJob
Memoryholds both instructions and data
Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU)performs the calculations and comparisons

Input/Outputmoves data in and out

The fourth, and the one usually left blank in the question, is the control unit. The ALU and control unit together make up the CPU.

Storing instructions as data in the same memory is the stored-program concept, and its benefit is that a computer can run different programs without being physically rewired — you load new instructions the same way you load new data.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• List the four steps of the fetch–execute (fetch–decode–execute) cycle in order.

• Explain the roles of the PC and IR during the cycle.

• Describe how the PC is incremented and when it might change.

• Explain why a computer can only run instructions in its own machine language.

• Connect cache and pipelining to speeding up the cycle.

Plain-English First

Everything a computer does boils down to one endlessly repeating loop: get the next instruction, figure out what it means, grab any data it needs, do it — then repeat. As computer scientist Alan Perlis quipped, "the only universal in the computing field is the fetch–execute cycle." Master these four steps and you understand, at heart, how every program runs.

Going Deeper — The Four Steps

Because instructions and data both live in addressable memory (instructions stored contiguously), the cycle begins by loading the address of the first instruction into the program counter (PC). Then it repeats four steps:

📌 MUST-KNOW

the four steps

1. Fetch the next instruction: the control unit reads the address in the PC, copies that memory's contents into the instruction register (IR), and increments the PC to point to the following instruction.

2. Decode the instruction: the control unit determines which operation it is, turning it into control signals (this is why a CPU only runs its own machine language — the operations are built into the circuits).

3. Get data if needed: if the instruction references memory, the control unit fetches that data.

4. Execute: the control unit signals the ALU (or I/O) to carry out the operation; results go to registers or memory. Then the cycle repeats.

Normally the PC just increments by the instruction's size (next contiguous instruction), but a control instruction can change the PC (e.g., a branch/jump based on a result), which is how loops and decisions work. Cache and pipelining both speed the cycle up — cache by avoiding slow memory trips, pipelining by overlapping the steps of successive instructions.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Fetch–execute cycleThe four-step loop every instruction follows.How all programs actually run.
FetchCopy the next instruction into the IR.Step 1; also increments the PC.
DecodeDetermine the operation (control signals).Step 2; ties CPU to machine language.
ExecuteCarry out the operation (often via ALU).Step 4; produces the result.
Program counter (PC)Address of the next instruction.Incremented each fetch; can be changed.
Instruction register (IR)The instruction being executed.Holds what's decoded/executed.
Machine languageThe only instructions a CPU can run.Operations are built into circuits.
PipeliningOverlapping instruction steps.Speeds up throughput.

Diagram — The fetch–execute cycle

StepActionKey part
1. FetchCopy next instruction to IR; increment PCControl unit, PC, IR
2. DecodeIdentify the operationControl unit
3. Get dataFetch needed operandsControl unit, memory/bus
4. ExecutePerform op; store resultALU / registers / memory

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

"Fetch, Decode, Get, Execute" — or simply fetch–decode–execute (the "get data" step folds into it).

PC points to next; IR holds current. Fetch copies PC's target into the IR, then bumps the PC.

Loops/branches = changing the PC. A control instruction rewrites the PC instead of just +1.

CPU only speaks machine language — the operations are literally wired in.

"The only universal is the fetch–execute cycle."

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Putting the steps out of order. It's fetch → decode → (get data) → execute.

Saying the IR is incremented. The PC is incremented; the IR holds the current instruction.

Forgetting the PC can be changed by a control instruction (that's how branching works).

Thinking a CPU can directly run high-level code. It runs only its own machine language.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Trace one pass of the cycle

Scenario: PC = 100, and the instruction at 100 says "add memory[200] to a register." Each instruction is 4 bytes.

Fetch: control unit reads address 100, copies that instruction into the IR, and increments PC → 104.

Decode: control unit recognizes it as an "add from memory" operation.

Get data: fetch the value at memory[200].

Execute: ALU adds that value to the register; result stays in the register.

Cycle repeats using PC = 104 for the next instruction. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Why a branch changes the PC (wrong way → right way)

Question: After a comparison, a program must jump to instruction at address 300 instead of the next one.

Wrong assumption: the PC always just adds the instruction size, so it can't jump.

Why it's wrong: a control instruction can write a new value into the PC.

Right way: the execute step sets PC = 300, so the next fetch pulls the instruction at 300 — that's exactly how branches and loops work. ✔

📊 FIGURE — fetch, decode, get data, execute — one instruction, step by step
🎯 EXAM TIP

The order is the question: fetch → decode → (get data) → execute. Any answer that decodes before fetching, or executes before decoding, is wrong. If only three steps are offered, “get data” has been folded into execute — fetch–decode–execute is the same cycle.

Two register facts settle most of the rest: the PC is incremented during the fetch (never the IR), and the IR holds the current instruction. A choice saying “the IR is incremented” is a distractor built from exactly this confusion.

When a question asks how a loop or an if works at hardware level, the answer is that a control instruction writes a different address into the PC instead of letting it step to the next contiguous instruction. Branching is just PC assignment.

And the conceptual one: a CPU can only run instructions in its own machine language — the operations are physically wired in, which is why high-level source has to be translated first.

after this section you will be able to…

• Define an embedded system and give everyday examples.

• Explain why embedded programs are stored in ROM and often written in assembly language.

• Describe how embedded programs are developed (write on a PC, cross-compile).

• Define the Internet of Things (IoT) and its growth.

• Recognize the range of embedded processors (8-bit → 64-bit RISC/DSP).

Plain-English First

Most computers aren't laptops — they're hidden inside other things. The chip running your microwave, your car's brakes, your smartwatch, a traffic light: those are embedded systems — small computers built to do one narrow job as part of a bigger device, usually with little or no user interaction. When millions of these gadgets also talk to each other over the internet, we call that the Internet of Things.

Going Deeper — The Technical Detail

An embedded system is a computer designed to perform a narrow range of functions as part of a larger system. Typically it lives on a single microprocessor chip with its programs stored in ROM. They're everywhere: watches, microwaves, cars, networking equipment, industrial controls. Some include an operating system; many are so specialized the whole logic is a single program. The term is broad — it covers essentially every computer except desktop PCs — and implies minimal user intervention.

📌 MUST-KNOW

development & language

You can't easily develop/test on the embedded chip itself, so programs are written on a PC and cross-compiled — the executable is generated for the target processor, then burned into its ROM. Because early embedded systems were tight on code size and speed, assembly language was used almost exclusively; even with C available, many stuck with assembly. C programs are about 25% larger and slower than assembly but easier to write; limited ROM size can still force assembly today.

Embedded processors range from 8-bit controllers to 32-bit DSPs (digital signal processors) to 64-bit RISC (reduced instruction set computer) chips, increasingly networked as distributed microprocessors. The Internet of Things (IoT) is the collection of internet-connected devices with embedded electronics/software — phones, vehicles, appliances, cameras, medical implants, animal transponders. Growth: 8.4 billion devices (2017), 13+ billion (2023), predicted 25+ billion by 2030.

Program lives in ROM — nonvolatile, ready the instant power is on.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Is it an embedded system?

Problem: Classify each: (a) a smart thermostat chip, (b) a general gaming desktop, (c) a car's anti-lock brake controller, (d) a fitness tracker.

(a) Thermostat chip → narrow function in a device → embedded.

(b) Gaming desktop → general-purpose PC → not embedded.

(c) ABS controller → dedicated control task → embedded.

(d) Fitness tracker → dedicated, networked → embedded (and part of the IoT). ✔

Worked Example 2 — Language choice (wrong way → right way)

Scenario: A tiny sensor has very limited ROM; a developer wants to use C for convenience.

Wrong assumption: "C is smaller, so it'll fit fine."

Why it's wrong: C programs are about 25% larger and slower than assembly.

Right way: with severely limited ROM, choose assembly to keep the code small enough to fit; use C only when there's ROM headroom. ✔

📊 FIGURE — cross-compiling onto a device, and what turns it into IoT
🎯 EXAM TIP

Classification questions here are one-word decisions: does the machine do a narrow, dedicated job inside a larger device (thermostat chip, ABS controller, fitness band, microwave) → embedded; is it general-purpose (a gaming desktop, a laptop) → not embedded, no matter how small it is.

Three facts are asked almost verbatim. The program is stored in ROM — nonvolatile, so it is there the moment power arrives. Development happens on a PC and is cross-compiled onto the chip, because you cannot practically develop on the device itself. And assembly is smaller and faster than C, with C running roughly 25 % larger and slower but far easier to write — so a severely ROM-limited device forces assembly.

Watch the direction of that last fact; the reversed version (“C is smaller and faster”) is the standard distractor. And IoT is not one device — it is the network of connected embedded devices.

Edge computing, sensors and constraints

📘 DEFINITION
Edge computing processes data near where it is produced instead of sending it to a distant data center. A self-driving car analyzing its sensor feed on board is the standard example: the benefit is much lower latency (plus it keeps working without a network, and sends less data).
ComponentDirectionJob
Sensorinputmeasures the physical world — a thermistor reading temperature
Actuatoroutputacts on the physical world — the relay switching the boiler on

★ NOT IN YOUR COURSE GUIDE

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

A subprogram — also called a function, method, procedure or subroutine depending on the language — is a named block of code you can call by name, hand values to, and get a value back from. It is the first tool for making a program out of parts instead of one long script, and the reasons for using one are worth stating precisely because the OA asks for them.

Reuse removes duplication, so a fix happens in one place rather than five. Abstraction lets you call calculateTax(salary) without holding the tax brackets in your head. Decomposition breaks a large problem into pieces small enough to test separately. Together these are why a well-organised program has a short main routine that calls small named things.

Parameters and arguments

The vocabulary here is tested directly, so keep the two words apart. A parameter is the variable named in the subprogram's definition. An argument is the actual value supplied at the call. The definition is written once; the call can happen many times, each with different arguments.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — definition versus call
FUNCTION square(n)          <- n is the PARAMETER
    RETURN n * n
END FUNCTION

result = square(6)          <- 6 is the ARGUMENT, result gets 36

Parameters are simply local variables initialised from the caller's arguments — which is why reassigning a parameter inside a subprogram never affects the caller's variable. The return value is the one channel back out. A subprogram that returns nothing is often called a procedure or declared void; one that returns a value can have its result stored, compared or passed straight into another call.

That distinction matters more than it first appears. A subprogram that prints its answer can only ever print it. One that returns its answer can be printed, stored, tested or reused — which is what makes it testable at all.

The call, mechanically

When a subprogram is called, execution jumps to it, a stack frame is created holding that call's parameters and local variables, the body runs, and on return the frame is destroyed and execution resumes at the line after the call. This is the same stack from 1.2, and it explains why locals vanish on return and why a value has to be returned to survive.

What makes a good subprogram

Beyond the definitions, the OA asks about the qualities of a well-designed subprogram, and they follow from one idea: it should do one clearly-named thing. That is cohesion. A subprogram called calculateTax that also prints a receipt and updates a database has low cohesion — nobody can reuse it, and its name lies about what it does.

The matching idea is coupling: how much a subprogram depends on the rest of the program. A subprogram that takes what it needs as parameters and returns its result is loosely coupled and can be moved, tested or replaced on its own. One that reads and writes global variables is tightly coupled — it only works in the exact context it was written for. High cohesion and low coupling is the phrase the exam uses, and it is simply the two habits stated together.

This is also why the number of parameters matters. A subprogram needing eight of them is usually doing more than one thing, and the fix is to split it rather than to add a ninth.

Recursion

A subprogram may call itself. That is recursion, and it is the natural shape for any problem that contains a smaller copy of itself — a factorial, a directory tree, a binary search.

Every correct recursive function has exactly two parts. The base case is the smallest input, answered directly with no further call — it is what stops the recursion. The recursive case calls the function again on a smaller input and builds the answer from the result.

FUNCTION factorial(n)
    IF n <= 1 THEN            // BASE CASE — stops the recursion
        RETURN 1
    ELSE                        // RECURSIVE CASE — smaller input
        RETURN n * factorial(n - 1)

factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3)
             = 4 * 3 * factorial(2)
             = 4 * 3 * 2 * factorial(1)   <- base case reached
             = 24

Leave the base case out — or write one the input never reaches — and the function calls itself for ever. Each call takes a frame of memory on the call stack, the stack fills, and the program crashes with a stack overflow. That is the single most tested consequence in this topic: no base case means infinite recursion and a stack-overflow crash, not a wrong answer.

RecursionIteration (a loop)
Repeats bycalling itselflooping
Stops onthe base casethe loop condition
Memorya stack frame per callconstant
Prefer whenthe data is nested — trees, divide and conquerthe depth is large or performance matters

Anything recursive can be written iteratively and the reverse is also true, so the question is never "which works" but which is clearer and which is safe. Choose iteration when the depth could be large, because a loop cannot overflow the stack.

How a parameter is passed

Two conventions decide whether a subprogram can change the caller's variable.

PassingThe subprogram receivesChanging it inside
By valuea copy of the valuedoes not affect the caller's variable
By referencethe address of the caller's variabledoes change the caller's variable

A reference parameter therefore passes the location, not the contents — which is how a subprogram returns more than one result, and also how it causes a side effect the caller did not expect.

📘 DEFINITION

Subprogram: a named, reusable block of code — also function, method, procedure or subroutine

Parameter: a variable in the definition that receives a value

Argument: the actual value passed at the call site

Return value: the result handed back to the caller

Void / procedure: a subprogram that returns no value

Stack frame: the memory holding one call's parameters and locals; destroyed on return

Modularity: building a program from independent, replaceable parts

Decomposition: splitting a problem into smaller solvable pieces

★ ON THE OA

Parameter is in the definition; argument is at the call. The benefits list is reuse, abstraction, modularity and easier testing — and "reduces duplicated code" is the phrasing that appears most often.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Passing arguments in the wrong order is the error no compiler catches. divide(b, a) compiles perfectly when both parameters are the same type, and returns the wrong answer forever.

📊 FIGURE — the call stack for factorial(4) — every call keeps its own n
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — parameters passed by value versus by reference

Two subprograms, identical bodies, one difference in how the parameter arrives. Trace what the caller sees afterwards.

PROCEDURE bumpByValue(x)      // x arrives as a COPY
    Set x to x + 10
END PROCEDURE

PROCEDURE bumpByRef(ref x)    // x arrives as an ADDRESS
    Set x to x + 10
END PROCEDURE

Set total to 40
call bumpByValue(total)
Print total          →  ?
call bumpByRef(total)
Print total          →  ?

Step 1 — the by-value call. total holds 40. The call hands the subprogram a copy of the value 40, which lands in the local variable x. Inside, x becomes 50.

Step 2 — what happens on return. The frame is destroyed and x disappears with it. total was never touched, so the first print is 40.

Step 3 — the by-reference call. This time the subprogram receives the location of total, not its contents. Set x to x + 10 writes 50 into that location — which is total itself.

Step 4 — after return. The frame is gone but the write already happened in the caller’s memory. The second print is 50.

Answer: 40, then 50. The rule to carry away: by value the subprogram can read the caller’s data but not change it; by reference it can do both. That is exactly how a subprogram “returns” more than one result without a return value.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — rewriting a loop as recursion, and reading the base case

Problem: this loop sums the numbers 1…n. Write the recursive version and check it on n = 4.

FUNCTION sumTo(n)                FUNCTION sumTo(n)
    Set total to 0                   IF n = 1 THEN
    Set i to 1                           RETURN 1          // BASE CASE
    WHILE i <= n                     ELSE
        Set total to total + i           RETURN n + sumTo(n - 1)
        Set i to i + 1               END IF
    END WHILE                    END FUNCTION
    RETURN total
END FUNCTION

Step 1 — find the smaller version of the same problem. The sum of 1…n is n plus the sum of 1…(n−1). That sentence is the recursive case, written directly.

Step 2 — find the smallest input you can answer outright. The sum of 1…1 is 1, and no call is needed. That is the base case, and it must be reachable: each call passes n − 1, so any n ≥ 1 walks down to 1.

Step 3 — expand n = 4 on paper. sumTo(4) = 4 + sumTo(3) = 4 + 3 + sumTo(2) = 4 + 3 + 2 + sumTo(1) = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Four frames existed at the deepest point; they then popped in reverse order carrying 1, 3, 6, 10.

Step 4 — compare the two. Identical answers. The loop uses one variable and constant memory; the recursion uses n stack frames. That is the real trade-off the exam asks about — not correctness, but memory and readability.

Break it deliberately: change the base case to IF n = 0 and call sumTo(4) — it still works, returning 0 at the bottom. Change it to IF n = 10 and call sumTo(4) and nothing stops it: n runs 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1 … for ever. A base case that the input never reaches is the same bug as having no base case at all.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Three things are tested here and each has a giveaway.

Vocabulary. Parameter is in the definition; argument is at the call. Remember it by position: the definition declares parameters. Any answer that swaps them is wrong regardless of how the rest reads.

“What does this recursive function return?” Do not reason about it — expand it on paper the way step 3 above does, down to the base case, then fold the answers back up. Four lines of writing beats any amount of staring.

“Why did this crash / never stop?” Look for the base case first. Missing base case, or one the argument never reaches, means infinite recursion and stack overflow. If the base case is fine, check that the recursive call actually moves toward it — factorial(n) calling factorial(n) instead of factorial(n − 1) is the other version of the same bug.

Why break a program into subprograms

The primary benefit is reuse and manageability: logic written once can be called from many places, so it is not duplicated, and a fix has to be made in only one spot. Each piece can also be understood, tested and replaced on its own.

Speed is not the reason — a function call carries a small overhead. The gain is in correctness and maintenance, which is what the exam is looking for.

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

A single variable holds one value. A data structure organises many values so a program can find, add and remove them efficiently. Which structure you pick is a decision about which operation you want to be fast, because none of them is fast at everything — and that trade-off is what the OA actually tests.

StructureOrganisationFast atSlow at
Arrayfixed number of same-type items in contiguous memoryreading item i directlyinserting, deleting, growing
Listordered, dynamic, grows and shrinksadding and removingjumping to position i
Recorda group of named fields of mixed typesholding one entity togethernot a collection at all
Stacklast in, first out (LIFO)push and pop at the topreaching anything but the top
Queuefirst in, first out (FIFO)enqueue at the back, dequeue at the frontreaching the middle
Treehierarchical — parent and child nodesordered search, hierarchyunordered bulk access
Hash tablekey mapped to a slot by a hash functionlookup by key, near-instantordered traversal

The array deserves the most attention because everything else is defined against it. Its items are the same type and physically adjacent in memory, which is what makes arr[i] instant — the machine computes the address arithmetically instead of searching. The price is that its size is fixed at creation, so inserting in the middle means shifting everything after it. A list makes the opposite trade: it grows freely and inserts cheaply, but has no direct index arithmetic.

A record is a different kind of thing from all of these — not a collection of similar items but a group of differently-typed fields describing one entity, like a single row in a table. A CustomerRecord with Name, Address and PhoneNumber is one record; an array of those records is the collection.

Stacks and queues by their discipline

Stacks and queues are defined not by how they store things but by which end you are allowed to touch. A stack is last-in-first-out: the last thing pushed is the first thing popped, like a stack of plates. It is the natural structure for anything nested — undo history, matching brackets, and the call stack that holds function frames. A queue is first-in-first-out: the first thing enqueued is the first dequeued, like a printer queue or a checkout line.

Searching — why the structure matters

The reason to care about all this is what it costs to find something. A linear search checks each item in turn and works on anything, sorted or not, taking up to n comparisons. A binary search repeatedly halves a sorted range and takes about log₂n. On a million items that is a million comparisons against roughly twenty — and it is why a hash table, which computes the location directly from the key, is faster still.

Choosing a structure from a description

Exam questions in this area almost never name the structure. They describe a requirement and expect you to pick. The translation is mechanical once you know it: "must be processed in the order received" is a queue; "the most recent must be handled first" or "undo" is a stack; "look it up instantly by a unique key" is a hash table; "fixed number of same-type items, accessed by position" is an array; "grows and shrinks as items are added" is a list; "organised into a hierarchy" is a tree.

The reason a structure can be fast at one thing and slow at another comes down to whether the machine can compute where something is or has to look for it. An array element's address is the start address plus the index times the item size — one calculation, no searching, which is why it is instant. A linked list has no such formula, so reaching the tenth item means following nine links. A hash table gets back the arithmetic by computing the location from the key itself, which is why it is nearly as fast as an array while still accepting any key you like.

What makes a hash table fast, and where it breaks

A hash table computes the storage slot directly from the key with a hash function, which is why lookup does not depend on the number of items. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across the available slots, so no slot becomes crowded.

When two keys hash to the same slot that is a collision, and every real hash table needs a plan for it. Chaining keeps a list of entries at each slot; open addressing probes for the next free slot instead. Collisions are why the O(1) lookup is an average rather than a guarantee — if every key collided, the table would degrade to a linear search.

📘 DEFINITION

Data structure: an organised collection of values, chosen for which operations it makes fast

Array: a fixed-size collection of same-type items in contiguous memory, accessed by index

List: an ordered, dynamically sized collection that is easy to add to and remove from

Record: a group of named fields of mixed types describing one entity

Stack: a last-in-first-out collection — push, pop, peek

Queue: a first-in-first-out collection — enqueue, dequeue

Tree: a hierarchical structure of parent and child nodes

Hash table: a structure mapping a key to a storage slot with a hash function, for near-instant lookup

Index: the position of an element, counting from 0

★ ON THE OA

Match the discipline to the name: LIFO is a stack, FIFO is a queue. An array is fixed-size and same-type with instant indexing; a list is flexible; a record groups fields of different types. Binary search requires sorted data — on unsorted data you must use linear search.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This is the same trade-off you will meet again as Big-O later in this unit. "Which structure should I use" and "how does this algorithm scale" are the same question asked from two directions.

📊 FIGURE — stack and queue — the same items, different ends
📊 FIGURE — an array and a linked list holding the same five salaries
📊 FIGURE — a hash table, a hash function and a collision
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a stack and a queue fed exactly the same input

Problem: three print jobs arrive — J1, J2, J3, in that order. Push them onto a stack, and separately enqueue them onto a queue. Then remove everything from each. In what order does each hand the jobs back, and which structure should a printer actually use?

Step 1 — the stack, filling. push J1 → [J1]. push J2 → [J1, J2], top is J2. push J3 → [J1, J2, J3], top is J3. Only the top is reachable.

Step 2 — the stack, emptying. pop returns the top: J3, then J2, then J1. Output order J3, J2, J1 — the reverse of arrival. That is LIFO.

Step 3 — the queue, filling. enqueue J1 → front J1. enqueue J2 → [J1, J2]. enqueue J3 → [J1, J2, J3]. Items join at the back; the front never moves except by dequeueing.

Step 4 — the queue, emptying. dequeue returns the front: J1, then J2, then J3 — arrival order preserved. That is FIFO.

Step 5 — choose. A printer must be fair to whoever submitted first, so it needs FIFO: a queue. A stack would print the newest job first and leave the person who queued at 9 a.m. waiting all day. Note also what a stack is right for — the call stack in the recursion section, and “undo”, both of which genuinely want the most recent thing first.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — choosing a structure from a description, four times

Exam questions almost never name the structure; they describe a requirement. Work each one from the operation that must be fast.

(a) “Look up a customer by their account number, instantly, out of two million records.” The access is by key, not by position, and it must not slow down as the data grows. Computing a slot from the key does exactly that → hash table. (An array would need the account number to be the index; a list would need a walk.)

(b) “Hold one student’s name, ID and GPA together.” Three values of different types describing one entity, reached by name rather than by number → record. This is the one that is not a collection at all, which is why it is the answer whenever “different types” appears.

(c) “Store 500 exam scores and read the 200th directly.” Same type, fixed count, access by position → array. The index arithmetic in the figure is precisely the property being asked for.

(d) “Items are added and removed constantly and the count is unknown up front.” Growth and cheap insertion matter; position does not → list. Choosing an array here is the classic wrong answer, because a fixed contiguous block cannot grow and every insertion shifts everything after it.

The method: read the sentence for which operation must be fast — by key → hash table, by position → array, constant change → list, newest first → stack, oldest first → queue, hierarchy → tree. Then check the second half of the sentence for the thing that structure is bad at, which is usually where the distractor lives.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The error is assuming a structure’s strength applies to every operation. Every structure in the table is fast at one thing because it is slow at another, and the exam builds its distractors out of exactly that trade.

The three specific slips: saying a linked list can jump straight to element 7 (it cannot — there is no address to compute, so you walk); saying an array is a good choice when items are constantly inserted and removed (it is not — it is a fixed block, so every insertion shifts the rest); and saying a hash table can list keys in order (it cannot — the hash scatters them deliberately, so ordered traversal is the one thing it is bad at).

How to notice: after you pick a structure, say out loud what it is bad at and re-read the question for that word. If the question contains “in order”, “sorted”, “position” or “grows”, and your structure is bad at that word, you picked the distractor.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Answer the discipline questions from the acronym and stop: LIFO is a stack, FIFO is a queue. If the scenario says “most recent first”, “undo”, “back button” or “nested”, it is a stack; if it says “fair”, “in the order received”, “print jobs”, “waiting line”, it is a queue.

For the array questions, two facts carry nearly all the marks: indexing starts at 0 (so the last element of an array of size n is at n − 1, and asking for index n is the off-by-one they are testing), and an array is fixed size and one type while a record is mixed types reached by field name.

Where a question asks about speed, the one-line answer is: array index and hash lookup do not depend on how much data there is; searching a list one item at a time does. That sentence answers most of the “which is faster and why” items without any calculation.

The vocabulary of data storage

📘 DEFINITION
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) specifies what operations exist and how they behave — not how they are built. "A stack offers push and pop, last in first out" is an ADT. Whether it is implemented with an array or a linked list is a separate choice, hidden behind that interface.
TermMeansExample
Scalarholds a single valuean int, a char, a Boolean
Compositeholds several values as one unitan array, a record, an object
Containeran object whose job is to hold other objectsArrayList, HashMap, a set
Homogeneousevery element is of the same typean array of int — the rule for arrays
Heterogeneouselements may be of differing typesa record/struct with a name and an age

Why array access is O(1) but searching is O(n)

Big-O describes the complexity of an operation — how its cost grows as the data grows. Both of these touch the same array, so the difference is worth understanding rather than memorizing.

  • arr[7] is O(1) because the position is calculated: start address + 7 × element size. One arithmetic step, whatever the array's size.
  • Searching an unsorted array for a value is O(n) because nothing tells you where it might be. You must check elements one by one, and the value could be the last one you look at.

Sort the array and search becomes O(log n) with binary search — the order is what buys the speed.
