This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

An algorithm is a finite sequence of unambiguous steps that solves a problem. Five properties define one formally, and they are worth knowing because questions occasionally ask what disqualifies something: it takes input, produces output, each step is unambiguous, it terminates, and it is effective — each step can actually be carried out.

The two algorithms every intro course tests are searching and sorting, and searching first because it shows why the rest matters.

Searching

AlgorithmHow it worksData must beComparisons (worst case)
Linear (sequential) searchcheck each item in turn until you find itanythingn
Binary searchcheck the middle, discard the half that cannot contain it, repeatsortedabout log₂n

The gap between those two columns is the whole argument of this section. On a list of a million items, linear search may need a million comparisons and binary search needs about twenty — because each step throws away half of what remains. That is also why sorting is worth doing even when you only want to search: sort once, then search cheaply for ever after.

The precondition is not optional. Binary search on unsorted data does not run slowly — it returns wrong answers, because the half it discards may well contain the target.

Sorting

AlgorithmIdeaTypical cost
Bubble sortrepeatedly swap adjacent items that are out of orderO(n²)
Selection sortfind the smallest remaining item, swap it into placeO(n²)
Insertion sorttake each item and slide it back into the sorted partO(n²), but O(n) if already sorted
Merge sortsplit in half, sort each half, merge the sorted halvesO(n log n)
Quicksortpartition around a pivot, sort each sideO(n log n) average

Big-O: how algorithms scale

Big-O notation describes how the work grows as the input grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It answers a question about scaling, not about seconds — which is why 3n + 100 and n/2 are both simply O(n).

ClassNameExampleWork at n = 1,000,000
O(1)constantarray access, hash lookup1
O(log n)logarithmicbinary searchabout 20
O(n)linearone pass over a list1,000,000
O(n log n)linearithmicmerge sort, quicksortabout 20,000,000
O(n²)quadraticbubble, selection, insertion sort1,000,000,000,000

Reading it off code is mostly a matter of counting nesting. One loop over n items is O(n). A loop inside a loop is O(n²). A loop that halves its range each pass is O(log n). And the distinction that catches people: two loops one after another are O(n) + O(n) = O(n) — only nesting multiplies.

Reading Big-O off code

You will not be asked to prove a complexity, but you will be asked to read one off a short piece of code or off a description. Three patterns cover nearly all of it. A single loop over n items is O(n). A loop nested inside another loop, each over n items, is O(n²). A process that halves what remains on each pass — binary search, or repeatedly dividing a number by two — is O(log n).

Two refinements catch people. First, sequential loops add rather than multiply, so two loops one after another are still O(n); only nesting multiplies. Second, a nested loop whose inner bound depends on the outer one — running n, then n−1, then n−2 — does about half the work of a full square, but Big-O drops constants, so it is still O(n²). Doing half as much work does not move you to a better class.

Why sorting is worth the cost

Sorting is expensive and searching a sorted list is cheap, which raises the obvious question of when the trade pays. The answer is: whenever you will search more than a handful of times. Sorting a million items once costs about 20 million operations with merge sort; each subsequent binary search costs about 20 instead of a million. After two searches you are already ahead, and the advantage compounds from there.

Space complexity

Big-O measures time, and the same notation measures memory. Space complexity describes how the extra memory an algorithm needs grows with the input — not counting the input itself.

The two often trade against each other, which is what makes it worth stating separately. Merge sort runs in O(n log n) time but needs O(n) extra space for merging. Quicksort matches its average time and sorts in place, needing only O(log n) for the recursion. Building a lookup table to avoid recomputing values buys speed with memory, and that trade has a name — space–time trade-off — that questions use directly.

What bubble sort does on data that is already sorted

Bubble sort compares each adjacent pair and swaps them when they are out of order, passing over the list repeatedly until a pass makes no swaps. The usual optimisation is to record whether a pass swapped anything and stop early if it did not.

Run that on an already sorted array and the first pass compares every adjacent pair, finds all of them in order and performs zero swaps, so the flag is never set and it stops after that one pass. For n items that is n − 1 comparisons and 0 swaps — its best case, O(n). Without the optimisation it would do the full O(n²) passes regardless.

Choosing test data

Testing is not "does it work on a normal input". Good test inputs come in three kinds, and a scenario that only uses the first proves very little.

KindExample for "accept 1–100"
Typical50 — the ordinary case
Boundary1, 100, and just outside: 0 and 101
Invalida letter, an empty entry, a negative number

Boundaries matter most because that is where off-by-one errors live: a loop or a comparison that is wrong by one only misbehaves at the very edge of the range, and a typical value sails straight past it.

📘 DEFINITION

Algorithm: a finite sequence of unambiguous steps solving a problem

Linear search: checking each item in turn; works on unsorted data; O(n)

Binary search: halving a sorted range each step; O(log n); requires sorted data

Big-O notation: an expression of how running time grows with input size

Best / average / worst case: the fewest, typical and most operations for an input of size n

Count-controlled loop: repeats a known number of times using a counter

Event-controlled loop: repeats until something happens; the count is not known in advance

★ ON THE OA

Linear search checks each item — O(n), works unsorted. Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list — O(log n). If a question offers binary search on unsorted data as an option, it is wrong. Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²); merge sort and quicksort are O(n log n).

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Two sequential loops are O(n), not O(n²). Adding does not change the class; only nesting multiplies.

📊 FIGURE — the five Big-O classes on one pair of axes
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading Big-O straight off four pieces of code

You are never asked to prove a complexity — you are asked to read one off. The rule is: count the loops and see how each one relates to n.

(a)  Set total to 0                      (b)  FOR i FROM 0 TO n-1
     Set total to scores[0] + scores[n-1]          Set total to total + scores[i]
     Print total                              END FOR

(a) O(1). Three statements, and not one of them depends on n. Doubling the array changes nothing about the work done. Constant time — and note that “it touches an array” does not make it O(n); what matters is whether the count of operations grows.

(b) O(n). One loop that runs n times with constant work inside. Doubling n doubles the work.

(c)  FOR i FROM 0 TO n-1                 (d)  Set lo to 0 ; Set hi to n-1
         FOR j FROM 0 TO n-1                   WHILE lo <= hi
             IF a[i] = b[j] THEN count++            Set mid to (lo + hi) / 2
         END FOR                                   IF found THEN stop
     END FOR                                       ELSE discard half
                                               END WHILE

(c) O(n²). A loop inside a loop, each running n times, so the inner body runs n × n times. Nesting multiplies. At n = 1,000 that is a million comparisons — this is the shape the exam wants you to recognise as “does not scale”.

(d) O(log n). Nothing is counted up; the range is halved each pass. From 1,000,000 items: 500,000, 250,000, 125,000 … about 20 steps. Halving is always logarithmic.

The refinement that catches people: two loops one after another — a loop over n, then another loop over n — is n + n = 2n, which is O(n), not O(n²). Sequential loops add and the constant is dropped; only nesting multiplies.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is it worth sorting first? — putting numbers on the trade

Problem: a list holds 1,048,576 (= 2²⁰) customer records. You need to look records up by name. Sorting costs about n log n comparisons; linear search costs about n per lookup, binary search about log₂n. Is sorting worth it?

Step 1 — the cost of one search each way. Linear search, worst case, checks every record: 1,048,576 comparisons. Binary search halves the range each time, so it needs log₂(2²⁰) = 20 comparisons. That is not “a bit faster” — it is roughly fifty thousand times less work.

Step 2 — the entry fee. Binary search only works on sorted data, and sorting is not free: about n log₂n = 1,048,576 × 20 ≈ 21,000,000 comparisons, once.

Step 3 — find the break-even. Doing k searches costs k × 1,048,576 unsorted, versus 21,000,000 + k × 20 sorted. Setting them roughly equal: k ≈ 21,000,000 ÷ 1,048,576 ≈ 20 searches.

Step 4 — answer the actual question. Searching the list once or twice: do not sort, just scan. Searching it repeatedly — which is what a customer database does all day — sorting pays for itself after about twenty lookups and is enormously ahead thereafter.

And the precondition is absolute. Run binary search on unsorted data and it does not merely run slowly; it discards the half that “cannot” contain the target, which on unsorted data may be the half that does. It reports “not found” for records that are sitting right there.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Big-O questions come in three shapes, and none of them needs algebra.

“What is the complexity of this code?” Count nesting. No loop → O(1). One loop over n → O(n). Loop inside a loop → O(n²). Something halving → O(log n). A halving algorithm that also touches every item (merge sort, quicksort) → O(n log n). Loops in sequence add; only nested loops multiply.

“Which is faster for large n?” Order the classes once and reuse the list: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²). Read “large n” as “the curve, not the constant” — an O(n²) algorithm can be quicker on ten items and still be the wrong answer.

“Search / sort matching.” Linear search: O(n), any data. Binary search: O(log n), sorted data only. Bubble, selection, insertion: O(n²). Merge sort and quicksort: O(n log n). And when a question mentions testing rather than speed, the answer it wants is boundary values — 0, 1, the maximum and one past it — because that is where off-by-one errors live.

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

Subprograms group statements. Object-oriented programming goes one step further and groups data together with the subprograms that operate on it. A class is the blueprint describing what every instance will have; an object is one thing built from that blueprint. The class is written once; each object gets its own copy of the fields, so a thousand customers need one class definition and a thousand objects.

WGU words this precisely, and the wording is worth recognising: the object-oriented paradigm organises a program into smaller components that bundle together fields and methods. Fields are the data — also called attributes or properties. Methods are the behaviour.

The four pillars

PillarWhat it meansWhy it exists
Encapsulationdata is kept private and reached only through methodsgives every change one place where a rule can be enforced
Abstractionexpose what something does, hide how it does itlets you use a thing without re-deriving it
Inheritancea class takes on the fields and methods of anotherwrites the shared part once
Polymorphismone interface, many implementationsthe same call runs the right version for each object

Abstraction is the one worth dwelling on, because it appears far beyond OOP. It means focusing on what and hiding the how: you drive a car without knowing how combustion works, and you call sort() without knowing which algorithm runs. Every layer of a computer is an abstraction over the one below it — which is exactly why you can write a program without thinking about voltages.

Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship — a Manager is an Employee, so Manager extends Employee and adds to it. Holding another object as a field is a has-a relationship instead: a Car has an Engine. Getting these the wrong way round is a standard exam item, and the test is to say the sentence out loud. "A Car is an Engine" is nonsense, so it is a field.

Polymorphism is what makes a collection of mixed subclasses useful: a list declared as Employee can hold Managers and Contractors, and calling pay() on each runs that object's own version. The declared type decides what you may call; the actual object decides which version runs.

Where OOP sits among the paradigms

A paradigm is a style of organising a program, and the OA asks you to identify the style from a description and to know which family it belongs to. The split at the top is between saying how and saying what.

FamilyParadigmIdeaLanguages
Imperative (how)Proceduralsteps organised into reusable functions run in sequenceC, Pascal, FORTRAN
Imperative (how)Object-orientedobjects bundling fields and methodsJava, Python, C++
Declarative (what)Functionalcomputation as evaluating functions; avoids mutable stateHaskell, Lisp
Declarative (what)Logicdefine facts and rules, then ask questionsProlog
Declarative (what)Querydescribe the result, not the retrieval stepsSQL, HTML, CSS

Reading an OOP scenario

Most object-oriented questions are scenarios rather than definitions, and they resolve quickly once you know which word to look for. If a description mentions hiding data behind methods or private fields with getters, it is encapsulation. If it mentions a subclass reusing what a parent already has, it is inheritance. If the same method call behaves differently depending on the object, it is polymorphism. If the detail is hidden and only the essential interface is exposed, it is abstraction.

Encapsulation and abstraction are the pair most often confused, because both involve hiding. The difference is what is hidden and from whom. Encapsulation hides data, so that state can only change through methods that enforce the rules. Abstraction hides complexity, so that a user of the thing does not need to understand how it works. A car's locked bonnet is encapsulation; the steering wheel is abstraction.

One structural point worth carrying forward: a class is not an object, and the exam does test the wording. The class is the definition written once in the source; an object is a thing created from it while the program runs. Ten thousand objects share one class.

📘 DEFINITION

Class: a blueprint describing the fields and methods its objects will have

Object / instance: one concrete thing created from a class

Field / attribute: a data item belonging to an object

Method: a subprogram belonging to a class, defining behaviour

Encapsulation: keeping data private and exposing it only through methods

Abstraction: showing what something does while hiding how

Inheritance: a class taking on the fields and methods of another — an is-a relationship

Polymorphism: one interface with many implementations, resolved by the actual object

Paradigm: a style of organising a program

★ ON THE OA

Object-oriented and procedural are both imperative; functional and logic are both declarative. Knowing which family a paradigm belongs to is a common OA item, and "functional is a subset of declarative" is the exact phrasing WGU uses. Functional programming avoids mutable state and side effects.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question describes a program "organised into smaller components that bundle fields and methods", it is describing object-oriented — that is WGU's own wording, close to verbatim.

📊 FIGURE — class, objects, inheritance and the call that resolves itself
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting classes and objects in a sentence

Problem: “A payroll program defines Employee with fields name and salary and a method pay(). It creates records for R. Ortiz, D. Chan and L. Whitfield.” How many classes, how many objects, and what is the difference?

Step 1 — find the blueprint. “Defines Employee with fields and a method” describes a shape, not a person. That is one class.

Step 2 — find the concrete things. Three named people, each with their own name and salary values, all built from the same shape. That is three objects (three instances).

Step 3 — say the difference precisely, because the wording is what is marked. The class is the definition — it exists once, in the source code, and holds no data of its own. Each object is an instance created at run time with its own copy of the fields. salary is a field; pay() is a method; e1 is an object; Employee is a class.

Step 4 — the follow-up they always ask. “If R. Ortiz gets a raise, does D. Chan’s salary change?” No — each object has its own field values. Only something declared as belonging to the class itself (a static or class-level field) would be shared.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — naming the pillar from a four-line scenario

These are the highest-frequency OOP questions on the OA. Each scenario points at exactly one pillar; the trick is knowing which word decides it.

(a) “balance is private. The only way to change it is deposit(), which rejects negative amounts.” → Encapsulation. The deciding words are private and only way in: data is protected behind methods, so the “no negative deposits” rule has exactly one place to live and cannot be bypassed.

(b) “A developer calls sort(list) without knowing which sorting algorithm is inside.” → Abstraction. The deciding words are without knowing how: what it does is exposed, how it does it is hidden.

(c) “SavingsAccount gets all the fields and methods of Account and adds an interest rate.” → Inheritance. The deciding words are gets all of plus adds — and the relationship reads as “a SavingsAccount is an Account”.

(d) “The same draw() call produces a circle for one shape and a square for another.” → Polymorphism. The deciding words are same call, different behaviour: one interface, many implementations, chosen by the actual object.

The separator for the two that get confused: encapsulation hides data (to protect it); abstraction hides implementation (to simplify it). If the scenario mentions private fields or getters and setters, it is encapsulation. If it mentions using something without knowing how it works, it is abstraction.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Three specific slips cost marks here, and all three are wording rather than understanding.

1. Calling a class an object. The class is the definition; the object is the instance made from it. “Employee is an object” is marked wrong even when the rest of the sentence is right. Say blueprint for class and instance for object, and the wording takes care of itself.

2. Using inheritance where composition belongs. Inheritance is an is-a relationship. A Manager is an Employee ✔. A Car has an Engine — that is a field, not a subclass ✘. If you cannot say “X is a Y” without wincing, it is not inheritance.

3. Mixing up the two paradigm families. Object-oriented and procedural are both imperative — they say how. Functional, logic and query languages are declarative — they say what. SQL being declarative is the one people get wrong most often, because writing a query feels like programming a procedure.

Instantiating, and getting to machine code

📘 DEFINITION
To instantiate is to create an object from a class. The class is the blueprint; the instance is one actual object built from it, with its own values in its fields. new Student() instantiates.
📘 DEFINITION
A compiler translates an entire high-level program into machine code before it runs, reporting all errors up front and producing a file that can then be executed on its own.

★ NOT IN YOUR COURSE GUIDE

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

A program is source code written by a person; a computer executes only machine instructions. Something has to bridge that gap, and which mechanism does it is the central distinction of this section.

CompilerInterpreter
Whentranslates the whole program ahead of timeexecutes line by line as it runs
Outputa separate executable fileno separate file — it runs directly
Errorsreported all at once, before it runsfound when that line is reached
Speedfaster to run, slower to start developingslower to run, faster to iterate
ExamplesC, C++Python, JavaScript

Java is the case that does both, and it is the one exams like. Java source is compiled to bytecode — platform-independent instructions in a .class file — and the JVM then executes that bytecode on whatever machine it is installed on. Compile once, run anywhere, which was the whole design goal.

The three kinds of error

Sorting errors by kind tells you where to look, and the OA tests the boundaries.

KindWhen it appearsExample
Syntax (compile-time)before the program runs at alla missing semicolon or bracket
Runtimewhile running, usually stopping the programdividing by zero, reading past the end of an array
Logicnever — it runs fine and is simply wrongusing + where you meant −

The logic error is the dangerous one precisely because nothing reports it. A syntax error stops you immediately; a logic error produces an answer that looks plausible, which is why testing exists and why working an example by hand matters so much.

Putting it together

Everything in Sections 1 and 3 now composes into one picture: a program is data held in variables of some type, combined by operators, arranged with the three control structures, organised into subprograms and — in an object-oriented language — bundled with data into classes. The plan for all of that is written first as pseudocode or a flowchart, then translated into a language, then compiled or interpreted so the machine can run it.

From source code to a running program

The full path is worth having in one line, because questions pick a point on it and ask what happens there. You write source code; a translator — compiler or interpreter — turns it into instructions the machine can execute; the operating system loads it into memory as a process; and the CPU fetches, decodes and executes those instructions one at a time. Every part of that sentence is a topic in this course, and this section is where they join.

Compilation itself has stages the exam occasionally names. The compiler checks the syntax against the grammar of the language, then generates code; a linker then combines your compiled code with the libraries it uses into a single executable. That is why a program can compile successfully and still fail to build — a missing library is a linker error, not a syntax error.

Where a debugger fits

Because logic errors produce no message, you need a way to see inside a running program, and that is what a debugger does: it pauses execution at a breakpoint and lets you inspect variables and step through line by line. The low-tech equivalent, printing values as the program runs, works for the same reason and needs no tools. Either way the goal is identical — make the invisible state visible, because a logic error is by definition something that looks fine from the outside.

Between source code and machine code

A compiler does not usually jump straight from source to a running program. Its output is often assembly language — a human-readable form of machine code where each instruction is a short mnemonic such as MOV, ADD or JMP, standing one-to-one for a machine instruction. An assembler then converts that to binary.

Assembly sits between high-level languages and machine code: far more readable than binary, far more tedious than Java, and specific to one processor family. That last point is why high-level languages exist — assembly written for one architecture will not run on another, which is exactly the portability problem bytecode solves.

How to actually debug

Knowing the three kinds of error is not the same as finding one. Debugging has an order, and the OA asks for the first step.

1  REPRODUCE it reliably      <- always first
2  narrow down WHERE it happens
3  find out WHY
4  fix it
5  re-test, including what used to work

Reproducing comes first because a defect you cannot trigger on demand is one you cannot confirm you have fixed. Only then do you narrow the location — and the technique for that is to inspect the value at points along the path, either by printing it or with a debugger's breakpoints, until you find the first place it is already wrong. Desk checking — walking the code by hand on paper with sample values, keeping a table of each variable — does the same thing without running anything, and it is what catches a logic error the compiler cannot see.

The tools around the code

An IDE (integrated development environment) gathers the editor, the compiler or interpreter, the debugger and the build tools into one program, and adds syntax highlighting and auto-completion. Its value over a plain text editor is exactly that integration: you write, run and debug without leaving it.

Comments are ignored by the compiler and written for people. The useful ones explain why — why this rate, why this order, why this special case — because the code already says what it does. A comment restating the obvious (i = i + 1 // add one to i) is noise, and it goes stale the moment the line changes.

📘 DEFINITION

Source code: the program as written by a person

Compiler: translates an entire program into machine code or bytecode before it runs

Interpreter: executes source code line by line at run time

Bytecode: platform-independent instructions produced by the Java compiler

JVM: the Java Virtual Machine, which executes bytecode on a specific platform

Syntax error: a violation of the language grammar; caught before the program runs

Runtime error: a failure that occurs while the program is executing

Logic error: code that runs successfully and produces the wrong result

IDE: an integrated development environment — editor, compiler and debugger in one tool

★ ON THE OA

A compiler converts the whole program ahead of time and produces an executable; an interpreter executes it line by line. Java compiles to bytecode, which the JVM then runs — that is why Java is described as both compiled and interpreted. Compiled code runs faster; interpreted code is more flexible to develop.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

The error taxonomy is the most reusable thing in this section. When a later question describes a program that "runs but gives the wrong total", the answer is a logic error — no compiler and no exception will ever tell you about it.

📊 FIGURE — compiler, JVM and interpreter — and where each kind of error surfaces
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — classifying five failures, and naming who reports each one

Problem: for each failure, give the kind of error and say what tells you about it.

(a) System.out.println("total: " + total) — the closing bracket is missing. The translator cannot parse the line against the grammar of the language, so it never gets as far as producing a program. Syntax error, reported by the compiler, before anything runs.

(b) The program asks for a divisor, the user types 0, and it stops with a message. The code is grammatically perfect — the problem only exists for that input. Runtime error, reported by the running program (or the JVM) at the moment it happens.

(c) A payroll program computes gross pay as hours − rate instead of hours × rate. It compiles, it runs, it prints a number, and nothing anywhere complains. Logic error — reported by nobody. Only testing against an expected result finds it, which is why this is the dangerous kind.

(d) A loop reads scores[10] in an array of 10 elements. Valid syntax, so it compiles; the array simply has no index 10 (valid indexes are 0–9). Runtime error — and note it is also an off-by-one, the classic boundary bug.

(e) A Python script has a typo on line 40; lines 1–39 run and print output first. Still a syntax error — but the interpreter only reaches it at line 40, which is exactly why interpreted languages can start producing output and then fail. Compiled languages would have refused to run at all.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — debugging a real logic error in the right order

Scenario: a grade program prints an average of 0 for some students but works for others. No error message appears anywhere. Work it in the order the OA asks for.

Step 1 — reproduce it, first, always. Collect the failing cases and find the pattern: it happens for every student with no recorded scores. A defect you cannot trigger on demand cannot be fixed or confirmed fixed, which is why this step comes before any theorising.

Step 2 — narrow down where. The output is wrong, so work back: printing is fine, so the average is wrong; the average comes from total / count. Set a breakpoint there in the debugger, or print total and count just before the division.

Step 3 — find out why. With no scores, count is 0, and the code guards it with IF count > 0 THEN average = total / count ELSE average = 0. So the guard is working — and the guard is the bug. The program is reporting “average 0”, which reads as “this student scored zero”, when the truth is “this student has no scores yet”.

Step 4 — fix it. Report the two situations differently: display “no scores recorded” rather than 0. Note that removing the guard entirely would turn a logic error into a runtime error (divide by zero) — a worse outcome, not a fix.

Step 5 — re-test, including what used to work. Run it for a student with no scores, a student with one score, and a student with a full set. That last group is the regression check: a fix that breaks the cases that already worked is not a fix.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake is treating “it compiled” as “it is correct”. A compiler checks grammar, not meaning. gross = hours - rate; is a flawless sentence in the language and completely wrong as payroll, so it passes every check and ships.

The same confusion runs backwards on exam questions: a divide-by-zero is called a syntax error because “it is written in the code”, and a missing bracket is called a runtime error because “the program stopped”. Sort them by when the failure becomes visible, not by where the text sits: before it runs → syntax; while it runs → runtime; never → logic.

How to notice: ask “would this fail for every input, or only for some?” Every input, before starting → syntax. Only some inputs, mid-run → runtime. No input at all fails, but the answers are wrong → logic.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Compiler-versus-interpreter questions are answered from four words: whole versus line by line, and separate executable versus no separate file. If a choice says an interpreter produces an .exe, it is wrong; if a choice says a compiler finds errors as each line executes, it is wrong.

Java is the one they use to catch you out. javac compiles source to bytecode, not machine code; the JVM then interprets that bytecode on whatever platform it is on. So Java is both, and “platform independence comes from the JVM” is the sentence they want.

For debugging questions, the first step is always reproduce the error — not “read the code”, not “rewrite the function”. And when a scenario says the program “runs but gives the wrong answer”, the words logic error and debugger are the answer; no error message exists to be read.

Translation, selection and comments

Before a high-level program can run it must be translated into machine code — the binary instructions the CPU executes directly — whether by a compiler ahead of time or an interpreter as it goes.

An if that runs a block only when its condition is true, with no else, is a single-alternative selection. Add an else and it becomes dual-alternative.

Comments are the most common form of in-code documentation.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The best use of comments is to explain why the code does what it does — the intent, the constraint, the reason for an unobvious choice. Restating what the line plainly says ("increment i by 1") adds nothing and goes stale as soon as the code changes.

★ NOT IN YOUR COURSE GUIDE

This topic is not in the D684 guide you were given, but the OA asks about it. It sits here because this is the unit it belongs to — study it like the rest.

The ALU introduced in 5.2 performs "logic operations", and this is what those are. Underneath every program and every circuit is Boolean logic — the rules for combining values that are only ever true or false, 1 or 0. It is the bridge between the binary of 3.2 and the hardware that computes with it.

Three operations are fundamental, and every other operation is built from them.

OperationTrue whenSymbol
ANDboth inputs are true∧ · &&
ORat least one input is true∨ · ||
NOTthe single input is false — it inverts¬ · !

Truth tables

A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and the resulting output. Its size is the fact the OA tests: with n inputs there are 2n rows — two inputs give four rows, three inputs give eight, four give sixteen.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — AND, OR and NOT for two inputs
  A     B  |  A AND B   A OR B   NOT A
-----------+-----------------------------
  0     0  |     0         0        1
  0     1  |     0         1        1
  1     0  |     0         1        0
  1     1  |     1         1        0

Reading the table back in words: AND is the strict one — a single false input makes the whole thing false. OR is the generous one — a single true input makes it true. NOT simply flips.

The combined gates

A logic gate is the physical circuit implementing one of these operations, and three combined gates appear on the exam beyond the basic three.

GateEqualsOutput is 1 when
NANDNOT(AND)anything except both inputs being 1
NORNOT(OR)both inputs are 0
XOR (exclusive or)one or the other, not boththe inputs differ
XNORNOT(XOR)the inputs are the same

XOR is the one worth understanding rather than memorising: it answers "are these different?", which is why it appears in error detection, in parity checking and in encryption. And NAND has a remarkable property — every other gate can be built from NAND alone, which is called functional completeness and is why real chips are largely made of them.

Short-circuit evaluation

Programming languages add one behaviour that follows directly from the truth tables. In short-circuit evaluation, if the left operand of an AND is false, the answer is already settled, so the right operand is never evaluated at all. The same happens with OR when the left operand is true.

This is a tool rather than a quirk. Writing IF (x != 0 AND 10/x > 2) can never divide by zero, because the division is skipped whenever x is 0. Put the guard first and the test after it becomes safe.

From gates to arithmetic

The step that makes Boolean logic feel like part of computing rather than a side topic is seeing that these gates can add. Consider adding two single bits: the sum column is 1 when exactly one input is 1, which is XOR, and the carry column is 1 only when both are 1, which is AND. Two gates, and you have built a half adder. Chain a row of them with the carry passed along and you have the circuit that performs the binary addition from 3.2.

That is the whole bridge from physics to programming: switches implement gates, gates implement arithmetic, arithmetic implements everything above it. When 5.2 says the ALU performs "arithmetic and logic operations", these gates are literally what it is made of.

Boolean logic in code

The same three operations appear in every conditional you write. IF (age >= 18 AND hasID) is an AND gate evaluated at run time. That is also why a truth table is the right tool for checking a compound condition you are unsure about: build the small table of every input combination and read the answer off it, instead of arguing with yourself in prose.

Implication — the IF-THEN rule

A rule of the form IF P THEN Q is itself either true or false, and the one case that breaks it is narrower than intuition suggests.

PQIF P THEN Q
truetruetrue — the rule held
truefalseFALSE — the only way to break it
falsetruetrue — the rule said nothing about this case
falsefalsetrue — again, the rule never applied

"IF it rains THEN the ground is wet." It rains and the ground is dry — the rule is broken, and that is the only combination that breaks it. If it does not rain, the rule makes no claim at all, so it cannot be violated whether the ground is wet or dry. A promise is only broken when its condition is met and its result fails.

📘 DEFINITION

Boolean logic: the rules for combining true/false values

AND: true only when both inputs are true

OR: true when at least one input is true

NOT: inverts a single input

Truth table: a table of every input combination and its output; 2ⁿ rows for n inputs

Logic gate: the circuit implementing a Boolean operation

NAND / NOR: the negations of AND and OR

XOR: true when the inputs differ

Functional completeness: the property that every gate can be built from one type — NAND has it

Short-circuit evaluation: skipping the right operand when the left already determines the result

★ ON THE OA

A truth table with n inputs has 2ⁿ rows — three inputs give eight. AND is true only if both; OR is true if at least one; NOT inverts. NAND = NOT(AND), so its output is 0 only when both inputs are 1.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question gives you a compound expression, build the small truth table rather than reasoning in prose. Four rows takes twenty seconds and removes the chance of talking yourself into the wrong answer.

The gates, drawn

Every gate has a fixed shape, and the exam expects you to know it without a legend. Three of them are the operations you already met; the other three are those three with a small circle — a bubble — on the output, and a bubble always means "and then invert".

📊 FIGURE — the six gates you have to recognise on sight

So the shape tells you the operation and the bubble tells you whether the answer is flipped. NAND is AND with a bubble, NOR is OR with a bubble. XOR is the OR shape with a second curved line on the input side, and it means "exactly one of them, not both".

Direction 1 — from an expression to a circuit

You are given (A AND B) OR (NOT C) and asked to draw it. Work from the inside out, exactly the way you would evaluate it.

StepWhat you doResult
1List the inputs, one wire each, down the leftthree wires: A, B, C
2Find the innermost brackets and draw one gate for eachan AND gate fed by A and B; a NOT gate fed by C
3Draw the gate for the operation that joins theman OR gate fed by the two gate outputs
4The last gate drawn is the outputthe OR gate produces Q
📊 FIGURE — step 3 — the finished circuit for (A AND B) OR (NOT C)

Note the shape of the work: one gate per operator. Count the operators in the expression — AND, OR, NOT is three — and your drawing must have three gates. If it does not, you have missed one or drawn one twice.

Direction 2 — from a circuit to an expression

Now the other way, which is the direction the OA asks more often. You are shown a circuit and asked what it computes. Go left to right, naming the output of each gate as you pass it.

📊 FIGURE — read this one out — name every wire, then combine
StepWhat you doResult
1Label the inputs where they enterA, B, C
2Take the leftmost gate and write its output in terms of its inputsw₁ = A OR B
3Move right one gate and substitute what you already namedw₂ = NOT w₁ = NOT(A OR B)
4Keep substituting until you reach the output pinQ = w₂ AND C = NOT(A OR B) AND C
5Sanity-check with one rowA=0, B=0, C=1 → w₁=0, w₂=1, Q=1 ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the truth table for that circuit

Build one column per named wire. Never try to jump straight to the answer column.

ABCw₁ = A OR Bw₂ = NOT w₁Q = w₂ AND C
000010
001011
010100
011100
100100
101100
110100
111100

One row out of eight is 1. That is what "NOR then AND" buys you: the output fires only when A and B are both off and C is on.

Building a truth table, column by column

The same method proves any compound expression. For (A AND B) OR (NOT C) with three inputs there are 2³ = 8 rows — 2ⁿ rows for n inputs, and getting that count wrong is the most common way to lose the mark before you have started.

Fill the input columns in counting order so you cannot skip a case: C flips every row, B every two rows, A every four.

ABCA AND BNOT CQ = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)
000011
001000
010011
011000
100011
101000
110111
111101

Read the last column against the circuit in the figure above and they agree, row for row. That agreement is the proof that your drawing is right — it is also how you check your own work in the exam when you are not sure.

De Morgan's laws — the two you must have

These are the rules for pushing a NOT through a bracket, and they are the most-tested identity in this whole topic:

📘 DEFINITION

NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

In words: negate each part and flip the connective. Negating the parts without flipping AND to OR is the wrong answer the distractors are built from.

📊 FIGURE — De Morgan as bubble-pushing

Drawn, the rule is mechanical: take the bubble off the output, put a bubble on every input, and change the gate shape from AND to OR (or OR to AND). That is why NAND and an OR-with-inverted-inputs are the same component — engineers call it bubble-pushing.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — proving it in four rows
ABA AND BNOT(A AND B)NOT ANOT B(NOT A) OR (NOT B)
0001111
0101101
1001011
1110000

Column 4 and column 7 are identical in all four rows, so the two expressions are equivalent. Two columns matching everywhere is what "equivalent" means — there is nothing more to it, and it is a complete proof.

A plain-English check that catches sign errors: "it is not true that both are on" is the same as "at least one of them is off". "It is not true that either is on" is the same as "both are off".

Why NAND and NOR are special

NAND on its own is functionally complete: AND, OR and NOT can all be built from NAND gates alone, so a whole processor can be manufactured from one part. NOR is complete in the same way.

To buildFrom NAND gates aloneWhy
NOT AA NAND ANOT(A AND A) = NOT A
A AND B(A NAND B) NAND (A NAND B)NAND then invert = AND
A OR B(A NAND A) NAND (B NAND B)De Morgan: NOT A NAND NOT B = A OR B
🎯 EXAM TIP

Three checks, in order, whenever a circuit question appears:

1. Count the gates and count the operators — they must match.
2. Look for bubbles. A bubble you missed turns your answer into its exact opposite, and that opposite is always one of the options.
3. Test one row you can do in your head — usually all inputs 0, or all inputs 1 — against each candidate answer. That single row eliminates most distractors without building the whole table.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake is distributing NOT across AND or OR as if it were a minus sign. It is not. Writing NOT(A AND B) as (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is wrong, and one row of a truth table shows it: take A = 1, B = 0. Then A AND B = 0, so NOT(A AND B) = 1. But NOT A = 0 and NOT B = 1, so (NOT A) AND (NOT B) = 0. Different answers, so the two expressions are not the same thing.

De Morgan’s law says what actually happens: the operator flips when the NOT moves inside. NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). In plain English: “not both” means “at least one is missing”, and “neither” means “not this one and not that one”. Push the bubble in and swap the gate — that is the whole rule.

The same slip has a second form: ignoring precedence. NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR — the Boolean equivalent of “multiply before add”. So NOT A AND B means (NOT A) AND B, not NOT (A AND B), and A OR B AND C means A OR (B AND C). Those are genuinely different functions, and answer choices are built from both readings.

How to notice: never simplify a Boolean expression in prose. Whenever a NOT sits outside a bracket, or an expression mixes AND with OR, build the four-row table for the two candidate readings and compare the output columns. Four rows takes twenty seconds and it is the only method that cannot be argued with.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• Identify major computer types: server, PC/laptop, tablet, smartphone, mainframe, supercomputer.

• Describe server farms and estimate their power needs.

• Explain multicore processors, GPUs, and Moore's Law.

• Define embedded computers and their prevalence.

• Define the Internet of Things (IoT) and its impact.

Plain-English First

"Computer" isn't one thing — it's a whole family, from the phone in your pocket to warehouse-sized supercomputers. Meanwhile, chips keep getting more powerful (that steady doubling is Moore's Law), so today's single chip packs many processors (cores), and tiny computers hide inside almost everything, quietly talking to the internet as the Internet of Things.

Going Deeper — Types of Computers

Common types today:

Server — serves web pages/files/videos to other computers over a network; usually no keyboard/screen; fast but large, costly, power-hungry (kept in closets/labs/warehouses).

PC (desktop) — used by a few people; has keyboard and screen; runs varied applications. A laptop is a portable PC (smaller, battery-powered).

Tablet — book-sized, mostly screen (input + output); a book reader is a tablet specialized for reading.

Smartphone — pocket-sized phone with computer functionality; low-cost, low-power, but slower than larger types.

Mainframe — large centralized computer (1950s–1980s) shared by hundreds via terminals; now largely faded.

Supercomputer — extremely fast; executes trillions of instructions/second on big data; much faster than the others.

Going Deeper — Hardware Trends

📌 MUST-KNOW

server farms, cores, GPUs, embedded

A server farm is a collection of thousands of servers in specially equipped buildings (power, cooling, security). Power adds up: 2,000 servers × 500 watts = 1 megawatt — so farms are built near cheap electricity. Thanks to Moore's Law (growing chip capacity), a chip that held one CPU in the 1980s–2000s now holds many cores: dual-core (2 CPUs, ~2005), quad-core (4), and 8-/16-core (~2015). A GPU is a special-purpose chip for fast graphics/video (also parallel work). An embedded computer is one built inside a device (car, appliance) for a dedicated function — about 25% of a car's cost is its computers, and billions of embedded computers are made yearly.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of interconnected devices — from smart thermostats and refrigerators to industrial machines and wearables — that communicate and exchange data over the internet, enhancing automation, efficiency, and real-time analysis.

Key Terms

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Size spectrum: smartphone → tablet → laptop → desktop → server → supercomputer.

Core count: dual = 2, quad = 4; more cores = more simultaneous tasks (Moore's Law drives it).

Server power math: servers × watts each = total watts (2000 × 500 = 1 MW).

GPU = graphics specialist (also great at parallel work).

Embedded = inside a device; IoT = those devices networked together.

Mainframe = old & centralized; supercomputer = fastest.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Confusing a mainframe (large, shared, older) with a supercomputer (fastest, computation-focused).

Thinking a server always has a keyboard/monitor — usually it doesn't.

Mixing up cores and chips — a multicore chip has multiple CPUs on one chip.

Calling a GPU a general-purpose CPU — it's specialized for graphics/parallel tasks.

Confusing an embedded computer (single device) with IoT (the network of devices).

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Server farm power

Problem: A server farm has 3,000 servers, each drawing 400 watts. What is the total power draw (ignoring cooling)?

Multiply servers × watts each: 3,000 × 400 = 1,200,000 watts.

Convert to megawatts: 1,200,000 W = 1.2 MW.

This is why farms sit near cheap power (e.g., hydroelectric). ✔

Worked Example 2 — Classify the computer (wrong way → right way)

Classify: (a) a warehouse machine running trillions of ops/sec for climate simulation → supercomputer; (b) a keyboard-less box serving web pages → server; (c) a chip inside a microwave → embedded computer.

Wrong way: calling the climate machine a "mainframe."

Why it's wrong: mainframes are large shared business machines (mostly faded); the fastest computation machine is a supercomputer.

Right way: match "trillions of ops/sec, computation-heavy" → supercomputer. ✔

📊 FIGURE — Moore’s Law on a log scale, and the family of machines it produced
🎯 EXAM TIP

Identify machines by who uses them and for what, not by size alone. Server: serves files, pages or video to other computers, usually with no keyboard or screen of its own. Mainframe: one large centralised machine shared by hundreds of users through terminals. Supercomputer: extreme speed, trillions of instructions a second, on one enormous problem. Mainframe and supercomputer are the pair that get swapped — shared-by-many versus fastest-possible.

Moore’s Law is the statement that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years. It is an observation about a trend, not a law of physics — and note it is about transistor count, not clock speed, which is why the answer to “chips stopped getting faster” is multicore: several processing cores on one chip.

Two supporting facts round it out: a server farm is thousands of servers in a purpose-built building, which is why power and cooling dominate its cost; and a GPU is a separate processor with its own memory that takes graphics work off the main CPU.

after this section you will be able to…

• Use simple (atomic) variables and nested selection (if / else-if / else) correctly.

• Distinguish count-controlled from event-controlled loops and their three required parts.

• Explain composite variables: arrays (homogeneous, indexed) and records (heterogeneous fields).

• Compare sequential (linear) and binary search, and know when each applies.

• Describe bubble, selection, and insertion sort at a high level.

Plain-English First

Now we put the building blocks to work. A simple variable holds one value in one place (like a single labeled box). Real programs also need to hold many values — that's an array, a row of numbered boxes. Two everyday jobs dominate: searching (find a value) and sorting (put values in order). There are slow-but-simple ways and fast-but-pickier ways to do each, and knowing which to use is a core CS skill. Analogy: finding a word in a shuffled pile means checking every slip (sequential search); finding it in a sorted dictionary lets you flip to the middle and cut the problem in half each time (binary search).

Going Deeper — Selection & Loops

Simple (atomic) variables cannot be divided — one value in one place. A chain of else-if tests handles multiple ranges: only reaching the second IF means the first was false, so each branch implies a specific range (e.g., a temperature between 71 and 90). Any branch may hold a sequence of statements.

There are two basic loop types:

Count-controlled loop — repeats a specific number of times using a loop control variable with three parts: initialization (set start value), testing (has it reached the limit?), and incrementation (add 1 in the body). Set count to 0; WHILE(count < limit){ … Set count to count+1 } runs exactly limit times (count = 0,1,…,limit−1). It's a pretest loop; omit the increment and you get an infinite loop.

Event-controlled loop — repeats until an event inside the body occurs (user input, a sensor value, quotient becoming 0). It also has three parts: the event is initialized, tested, and updated. The base-conversion loop ("while quotient is not zero") is event-controlled.

Going Deeper — Composite Variables, Searching & Sorting

Composite variables hold multiple values. An array is a collection stored at contiguous memory locations, each reached by an index (position number); arrays are homogeneous (all elements the same type). A record stores multiple fields of different types (heterogeneous) about one entity.

📌 MUST-KNOW

Searching

Sequential (linear) search checks each element one by one until found or the list ends — works on any list. Binary search requires a sorted array and repeatedly halves the search interval (check the middle, discard half). Binary is far faster but only works if the data is already sorted.

Three simple sorting algorithms: bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps out-of-order pairs (largest "bubbles" to the end each pass); selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted part and moves it to the front; insertion sort builds the sorted portion one element at a time, inserting each into its correct place. A concrete step is a fully specified action (versus an abstract step that says what, not how).

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Simple/atomic variableHolds a single indivisible value.The basic storage unit.
Count-controlled loopRepeats a set number of times.Use when you know the count.
Event-controlled loopRepeats until an event occurs.Use when the count is unknown.
Loop control variableVariable that governs loop continuation.Must be initialized, tested, updated.
ArrayHomogeneous, indexed, contiguous collection.Stores many like values efficiently.
IndexNumeric position of an array element.How you access a specific element.
RecordComposite of differently typed fields.Groups related data about one entity.
HomogeneousAll items the same type.Describes arrays.
HeterogeneousItems of different types.Describes records.
Sequential (linear) searchCheck each element in turn.Works on unsorted data.
Binary searchHalve a sorted interval repeatedly.Fast, but needs sorted data.
Bubble sortSwap adjacent out-of-order pairs.Simple sorting method.
Selection sortMove the min of the rest to the front.Simple sorting method.
Insertion sortInsert each item into its sorted place.Simple sorting method.

Diagram — Binary search halving a sorted array

Comparison / Reference Tables

Count-controlledEvent-controlled
Stops afterA fixed number of iterationsAn event occurs in the body
Driven byA counter (loop control variable)A condition/event (input, sensor)
Three partsInitialize, test, incrementInitialize, test, update the event
ExampleSum 10 numbersRead until quotient = 0

Sequential (linear)Binary

ArrayRecord
Element typesHomogeneous (same)Heterogeneous (mixed)
Accessed byNumeric indexNamed field

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Count = known, Event = unknown. If you know how many times up front, use a count loop; otherwise an event loop.

Binary needs order. If the list isn't sorted, you cannot use binary search — you must sort first or use sequential.

Array = All same (homogeneous, indexed). Record = Ranges of types (heterogeneous, fields).

Bubble = adjacent swaps; Selection = pick the min; Insertion = insert into place. Three sorts, three verbs.

Loop runs limit times: a count < limit loop starting at 0 runs exactly limit times (0…limit−1).

Halving is powerful: binary search on 1,000,000 items needs only ~20 checks.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Using binary search on an unsorted array — it only works when sorted.

Off-by-one on loop counts. count = 0; while(count < 5) runs 5 times, not 4 or 6.

Calling an array "heterogeneous." Arrays are homogeneous; records are heterogeneous.

Confusing count-controlled with event-controlled loops.

Forgetting that a pretest loop can run zero times if the condition starts false.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Trace a binary search

Problem: Find 16 in the sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56] (indices 0–7).

low=0, high=7. mid=(0+7)/2 = 3 → value 12. Target 16 > 12 → search right: low=4.

low=4, high=7. mid=(4+7)/2 = 5 → value 23. Target 16 < 23 → search left: high=4.

low=4, high=4. mid=4 → value 16. Match at index 4. ✔

Only 3 comparisons for 8 elements — sequential could take up to 8.

Wrong way → why → right way: Running binary search on the unsorted list [16,2,38,5] may report "not found" even though 16 is present. Why: halving logic assumes order. Right way: sort first, or use sequential search on unsorted data.

Worked Example 2 — One pass of bubble sort

Problem: Show the first full pass of bubble sort on [5, 1, 4, 2].

Compare (5,1): out of order → swap → [1, 5, 4, 2].

Compare (5,4): out of order → swap → [1, 4, 5, 2].

Compare (5,2): out of order → swap → [1, 4, 2, 5].

End of pass 1: the largest value 5 has "bubbled" to the last position. ✔

(Later passes sort the rest → final [1, 2, 4, 5].)

📊 FIGURE — bubble, selection and insertion — what one pass actually does
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two question types dominate here, and both are traceable rather than memorisable.

“Show the list after pass k.” Identify the sort by its verb — bubble swaps adjacent pairs, selection picks the smallest and swaps it into place, insertion slides one item back into the sorted prefix. Then perform exactly one pass and stop. Answer choices are usually built from “one pass too many” and “fully sorted”, so stopping on time is the whole test.

“Trace the binary search.” Write low, high and mid in a column and use integer division: mid = (low + high) / 2 rounded down. If the target is bigger, low = mid + 1; if smaller, high = mid − 1. The count of comparisons is the answer they want.

Before any binary-search question, check the array is sorted. If it is not, the answer is not “slower” — it is that binary search may report “not found” for a value that is present.

after this section you will be able to…

• List Polya's four problem-solving steps and the classic strategies (ask questions, look for familiar things, divide and conquer).

• Describe the four phases of the computer problem-solving process and how they map to Polya.

• Explain top-down design and why algorithms must be tested before implementation.

• Order and describe the phases of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

• Recognize why understanding the problem (and asking the user clarifying questions) comes first.

Plain-English First

Big problems feel paralyzing until you have a method. In 1945 mathematician George Polya wrote How to Solve It, boiling problem-solving down to four moves that work for math, code, or cleaning a house: (1) understand it, (2) make a plan, (3) do the plan, (4) look back. Computer scientists borrowed this directly. The single most important habit hiding in here: you cannot solve a problem you don't understand — so the first move is always to ask questions until the task is crystal clear.

Going Deeper — Polya's Strategies

Polya's list is general because you can swap "unknown → problem," "data → information," "theorem → solution." The heart of it is step 2: finding the connection between the information and the solution. Key strategies:

Ask questions — clarify until the task is fully specified: What do I know? What does the solution look like? What special cases exist? How will I know I'm done?

Look for familiar things — "don't reinvent the wheel." Finding the daily high/low temperature is the same problem as finding the highest/lowest test score.

Divide and conquer — break a large problem into smaller, manageable subtasks (applying abstraction); repeat until each piece is solvable.

An algorithm (formally) is a set of instructions for solving a problem in a finite amount of time using a finite amount of data, and the instructions must be unambiguous.

Going Deeper — The Computer Problem-Solving Process & SDLC

The computer problem-solving process has four phases, each producing an output:

Analysis & specification → output: a clearly written problem statement.

Algorithm development → output: a general solution plan (pseudocode).

Implementation → output: a working program (the specific solution).

Maintenance → no output unless errors/changes arise, which are sent back to the appropriate earlier phase (backtracking).

This maps onto Polya: understand (analysis), plan (algorithm), carry out (implementation), look back (maintenance). The strategy that parallels Polya is top-down design, producing a hierarchy of tasks via successive refinement. Crucially, algorithms must be tested before implementation (desk checking) — the earlier a problem is found, the cheaper it is to fix.

📌 MUST-KNOW

the SDLC (7 phases)

The Software Development Life Cycle extends the problem-solving process into: Planning → Analysis → Design → Implementation → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance. Following it lets teams catch issues early and deliver software that meets requirements.

Understanding the problem means understanding the end user's real need. When planning, think of the output first, then work back to the input and processing needed to produce it. A vague request ("list employees here over five years") hides decisions only the user can make (full-time only? which cutoff date? what fields? what order?). Documentation — the supporting paperwork (requests, sample output, data descriptions) — helps the programmer understand the problem.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
AnalysisThoroughly understanding the problem's requirements.You can't solve what you don't understand.
DesignPlanning the solution (algorithms, structures).Turns understanding into a plan.
ImplementationWriting the code for the design.Produces the working program.
TestingRunning with varied inputs to verify behavior.Confirms correctness before release.
MaintenanceKeeping software working and updated.Software lives long after launch.
Top-down designBreak a problem into a task hierarchy.Makes big problems tractable.
Divide and conquerSplit a problem into smaller subproblems.Core problem-solving strategy.
SDLCStructured multi-phase software process.Systematic quality & risk management.
End userThe person who ultimately uses the software.Their needs define "correct."
DocumentationSupporting paperwork for a program.Clarifies requirements and use.
DebuggingFinding and fixing errors ("bugs").Restores correct behavior.

Diagram — The four-phase process (with backtracking)

Comparison / Reference Tables

Polya, Computer process, and SDLC aligned

Polya (1945)Computer process (4 phases)SDLC (7 phases)
Understand the problemAnalysis & specificationPlanning, Analysis
Devise a planAlgorithm developmentDesign
Carry out the planImplementationImplementation, Testing, Deployment
Look back / examineMaintenanceMaintenance

Certification vs. Licensing

CertificationLicensing
Granted byNongovernmental organizationsGovernment
Voluntary?YesNo (legal authority)
Computer pros?Often certifiedGenerally not required to be licensed

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Polya = "U-P-C-L": Understand, Plan, Carry out, Look back.

4 computer phases = "A-A-I-M": Analysis, Algorithm, Implementation, Maintenance.

SDLC = "Please Analyze Design In Time, Deploy, Maintain" → Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance.

Output first. When planning, decide what the result should look like, then work back to inputs/processing.

Cheaper early. The earlier you catch a defect (desk checking), the less it costs — test algorithms before coding.

Certification is not Licensing: certification is voluntary (a private org); licensing is government and mandatory.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Jumping to code before understanding the problem. Analysis is always first.

Confusing the 4-phase computer process with the 7-phase SDLC — know both lists.

Thinking maintenance produces new output every time. It only does when errors/changes appear, which loop back to earlier phases.

Believing a programmer should decide ambiguous requirements. The user must resolve those.

Swapping certification and licensing — licensing is the government, mandatory one.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Apply the four phases to a real request

Problem: HR asks for "a list of employees here over five years." Walk the process.

Analysis & specification: ask clarifying questions (full-time only? cutoff date = today or dinner date? which fields? sort order?). Output a precise problem statement once the user answers.

Algorithm development: plan in pseudocode — read employee records, select those with tenure > 5 years by the agreed cutoff, sort as requested, output chosen fields.

Implementation: code the algorithm in a language and run it.

Maintenance: if HR later wants part-time employees too, that change loops back to analysis.

Result: a correct, user-approved report — because ambiguity was resolved before coding. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Divide and conquer + "look for familiar things"

Problem: Build a program that reports the warmest and coldest day from a month of temperatures.

Look for familiar things: "largest and smallest in a list" is a solved pattern — the same as highest/lowest test scores.

Divide and conquer: subtask A = find max; subtask B = find min; subtask C = read the data.

Reuse the known max/min scan for A and B rather than inventing new logic.

Assemble subtasks under a main module (top-down): read data → find max → find min → report.

Desk-check with a few sample temperatures before coding. ✔

📊 FIGURE — why every process puts understanding first — the cost of a late fix
🎯 EXAM TIP

This section is pure recall, and the questions are almost always “which phase / which step comes next?”. Fix the two lists so you can write them in the margin the moment the exam starts:

Polya (4): Understand → Plan → Carry out → Look back. Computer process (4): Analysis & specification → Algorithm development → Implementation → Maintenance. SDLC (7): Planning → Analysis → Design → Implementation → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance. The 4-phase and the 7-phase lists are different questions; do not answer one with the other.

Scenario questions have a reliable tell. If the scenario contains an ambiguity (“employees here over five years” — measured from when?), the correct answer is always ask the user, never “the programmer decides”. If it contains a new requirement after delivery, the answer is maintenance looping back to the earlier phase, not “start a new project”.

The four pillars of computational thinking

PillarWhat it means
Decompositionbreak a large problem into smaller sub-problems that can each be solved on their own
Pattern recognitionspot what repeats, within this problem or from ones solved before
Abstractionignore the detail that does not matter, keep what does
Algorithm designwrite the ordered steps that solve it

Those four, and only those four. Questions ask which item is not one of them — candidates like "debugging", "compilation" or "testing" are real activities but not pillars.

Recursion and iteration

📘 DEFINITION
Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller version of itself, stopping at a base case. Iteration does the same work with a loop.

Compared with iteration, recursion is often shorter and closer to the definition of the problem, but uses more memory: every outstanding call occupies a frame on the call stack until it returns.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
A recursive function that crashes with a stack overflow almost always has a missing or unreachable base case, so it recurses for ever and the call stack runs out of room. Check the stopping condition first, not the recursive step.

Waterfall and Agile

WaterfallAgile
Shapeone pass through the stages in ordershort repeated cycles (iterations/sprints)
Requirementsfixed up frontexpected to change
Customersees it near the endgives feedback every cycle
Deliversonce, at the endworking software every few weeks
Best whenrequirements are stable and well understoodrequirements evolve, feedback is needed early

So for a client whose requirements will evolve and who wants working software every few weeks, the answer is Agile. Waterfall suits a stable, fully specified project such as one bound by a fixed contract.

after this section you will be able to…

• Identify the ACM and IEEE and what each traditionally represents.

• State the purpose of a code of ethics and the four categories of the ACM Code.

• Recognize the core general ethical principles (avoid harm, be honest, be fair, respect privacy, honor confidentiality).

• Apply ethical principles to real-world scenarios (privacy, security, public interest, professionalism).

• Distinguish key IEEE commitments (safety paramount, reject bribery, honest claims, no discrimination).

Plain-English First

A code of ethics is a profession's shared promise about how to behave — like the doctor's "do no harm," but for people who build software and hardware. Because computing touches money, privacy, safety, and infrastructure, the two big professional bodies wrote down principles their members agree to follow. You don't memorize all of them word-for-word; you learn the themes so you can recognize the right choice in a scenario question, which is exactly how the OA tests this.

Going Deeper — The Two Organizations & the ACM Code

There are two major computing organizations: the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), traditionally the software side, and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), traditionally the hardware side. A code of ethics is a professional code of conduct governing the behavior of computing professionals.

The ACM Code of Ethics has four categories:

General Ethical Principles (1.x): contribute to society and human well-being; avoid harm; be honest and trustworthy; be fair and don't discriminate; respect the work required to produce ideas/IP; respect privacy; honor confidentiality.

Professional Responsibilities (2.x): strive for high quality; maintain competence; know and respect existing rules; accept/provide review; give thorough evaluations including risks; work only in areas of competence; foster public awareness; access resources only when authorized; design systems that are robustly and usably secure.

Professional Leadership Principles (3.x): keep the public good central; support social responsibility; enhance quality of working life; apply the Code's policies; grow others professionally; use care when modifying/retiring systems; take special care of systems integrated into society's infrastructure.

Compliance (4.x): uphold and promote the Code; treat violations as inconsistent with ACM membership.

📌 MUST-KNOW

IEEE highlights

The IEEE Code commits members to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public; avoid/disclose conflicts of interest; be honest and realistic in claims; reject bribery; maintain and improve technical competence; offer/accept honest criticism and credit others; treat all people fairly with no discrimination; avoid injuring others' person, property, reputation, or employment; and help colleagues follow the code.

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

General principles = "HARP-CP": Harm-avoid, honest, fair, Respect-IP, Privacy, Confidentiality, Contribute to society — the human-decency core.

IEEE's first commandment: public safety, health, welfare paramount. If a scenario risks the public, that principle wins.

Scenario tip: pick the answer that protects people, tells the truth, and stays within your competence/authorization.

Reject bribery & disclose conflicts — classic IEEE test triggers.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Swapping ACM and IEEE — ACM is software, IEEE is hardware (though the line blurs in practice).

Choosing a "profitable but harmful" option. Codes put public welfare and honesty above convenience.

Thinking accessing any system you can reach is fine. You must be authorized.

Ignoring "credit others" — using someone's work without attribution violates the codes.

Assuming ethics are optional guidelines with no membership consequences — violations conflict with ACM membership.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Map a scenario to the right principle

Scenario: A developer discovers the app stores users' full credit-card numbers in plain text. What does the Code require, and which principles apply?

Identify the risk: exposed personal/financial data → potential harm and a privacy/security failure.

Applicable ACM principles: Avoid harm (1.2), Respect privacy (1.6), and design robustly and usably secure systems (2.9).

Required action: report the flaw and fix it (encrypt/limit data), not hide it — being honest and trustworthy (1.3).

Correct ethical choice: remediate and disclose responsibly. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Competence & honesty (wrong way → right way)

Scenario: You're offered a contract to build medical-device firmware, an area you've never worked in, on a tight deadline.

Wrong way: accept quietly and figure it out, overstating your experience to win the job.

Why it's wrong: violates "perform work only in areas of competence," "be honest," and risks public safety (IEEE paramount clause).

Right way: disclose your limitations, decline or bring in qualified help, and be honest about timelines.

Outcome: protects users and your integrity — the codes value honesty and competence over the paycheck. ✔

📊 FIGURE — the order to apply the principles in when a scenario gives you two bad options
🎯 EXAM TIP

Nearly every ethics item is a scenario with four plausible-sounding actions, and they are answered by ranking, not by recall. Apply the ladder in the figure and take the first rule that fires: harm to people beats honesty beats competence beats credit and privacy beats convenience and profit.

Eliminate first — it is faster than choosing. Strike any option that conceals a defect, that proceeds without authorisation, that takes on work outside your competence, or that puts cost or schedule above someone’s safety. That usually leaves one answer standing before you have thought about it properly.

Know the two organisations apart, because a question will simply ask: ACM is the software body, and its Code has four categories — general principles, professional responsibilities, leadership principles, compliance. IEEE is the hardware/electronics body, and its signature commitments are hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public and reject bribery in all its forms.

Finally, keep certification and licensing straight — they appear as a one-mark freebie. Certification is voluntary and granted by a non-governmental body; licensing is mandatory and granted by government. Computing professionals are commonly certified and rarely licensed.

Intellectual property theft at national scale

IP theft is not only an individual act. Governments have publicly accused state-backed actors of large-scale commercial espionage — most prominently, US and European accusations against China over the theft of trade secrets and industrial designs, which both the ACM and IEEE codes treat as a professional and societal harm rather than a merely legal one.

The point the codes make is one of scale: the same principle that forbids copying a colleague's work forbids it when the actor is an organization or a state.
