🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• Define intellectual property and distinguish copyright, patent, trademark, fair use, and public domain.

• Compare common software licenses: GNU GPL (copyleft), Creative Commons, MIT, and public domain.

• Explain piracy, file sharing, P2P networks, and the malware risk of piracy.

• Identify major cybercrime types, who investigates them, and how they're punished.

• Define cyberbullying, why it can be worse than in-person bullying, and the correct responses.

Plain-English First

Ideas can be owned. Intellectual property (IP) is "creations of the mind" — songs, code, inventions, logos — and the law gives creators certain rights over them. Different protections cover different things: copyright for creative works, patents for inventions, trademarks for brand identifiers. When people copy or share protected work without permission, that's piracy. Two darker corners of the online world round out this section: cybercrime (crimes committed with computers) and cyberbullying (online harassment). The OA tests whether you can classify a scenario and pick the responsible action.

Going Deeper — Intellectual Property & Licensing

Intellectual property = creations of the mind (inventions, works, designs, symbols, names, images). The main protections:

Copyright — protects original creative works (literature, music, art) from use without permission.

Patent — gives an inventor exclusive control over an invention for a limited period.

Trademark — a symbol, word, or phrase representing a company or product.

Fair use — a legal doctrine allowing limited use of copyrighted material (e.g., commentary, education).

Public domain — works not (or no longer) copyrighted, free for anyone. 🔎 Per the source, works published before 1923 are treated as public domain.

📌 MUST-KNOW

License types

GNU GPL — free software license; copyleft means any derivative must use the same license (ex: Linux kernel, Ubuntu, MySQL). Creative Commons (CC) — variations include CC0 (no restrictions), CC BY (credit the author), CC BY-SA (credit + share-alike license), CC BY-NC (credit + non-commercial). MIT license — reuse freely as long as the license and copyright notice are included (ex: Bitcoin Core, jQuery, Ruby on Rails). Public domain — no license needed.

Going Deeper — Piracy, Cybercrime & Cyberbullying

Piracy is the unauthorized copy, distribution, or sale of copyrighted work. File sharing and the Internet make it easy; a common method is a peer-to-peer (P2P) network, where peers share files directly with no central server (Napster, Kazaa, LimeWire — Napster was shut down in 2001 for copyright infringement). Piracy also spreads malware (malicious software) because pirated files are unregulated — piracy-site visitors are far more likely to be infected.

Cybercrime is any crime involving a computer and network — the computer can be the target, the tool, or both. Common types: identity theft, fraud, data breaches, trafficking, extortion (e.g., ransomware), malware, and harassment. Investigators use digital forensics (recovering data as evidence), decryption, and surveillance. Local police handle individual crimes (harassment, identity theft); the FBI and Secret Service handle larger cases (extortion, trafficking); Interpol handles international ones. Crimes are reported to the FBI's IC3. Punishment (fines, jail, loss of computer-use rights) depends on severity, monetary damage, and jurisdiction; offenders may be extradited to where the crime occurred.

📌 MUST-KNOW

Cyberbullying

Cyberbullying is the willful use of electronic technology to repeatedly threaten, abuse, or dominate others, often anonymously — a form of harassment. It can be worse than face-to-face bullying because the victim can't easily escape it, it reaches more people, and anonymity makes the bully hard to trace. Effects include lower academic performance, low self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts.

Correct responses to cyberbullying: tell someone (parent, teacher, friend), block the abuser, keep evidence, and never retaliate; notify the school principal for student-on-student cases. Contact law enforcement if there are threats of violence/death, physical stalking or attack, prolonged harassment based on protected traits (race, religion, sexuality, disability), or explicit images of a minor. Parents should not remove a child's technology (it increases isolation) — instead encourage behavior changes like spending less time online.

Key Terms

TermDefinitionWhy it matters
Intellectual propertyCreations of the mind.The thing IP law protects.

PatentExclusive control of an invention for a time.Protects inventions, not expression.

(b) A new physical invention → patent (exclusive control for a period).

(c) Source code is an original creative/authored work → copyright.

Identify severity: it escalated to a threat of violence.

Standard first steps still apply: tell a trusted adult, block the sender, and save evidence (don't delete the threatening messages before documenting).

Because there's a violent threat, this crosses into contact law enforcement territory.

Do not retaliate, and parents should not confiscate the teen's technology (it increases isolation).

Correct response: preserve evidence + involve police. ✔

For licences, only one distinction is really tested: copyleft versus permissive. GPL is copyleft — anything derived from it must carry the same licence. MIT is permissive — reuse it almost anywhere, just keep the notice. If a question describes a company building a closed product on top of GPL code, the answer involves the copyleft obligation.

Cybercrime items usually ask who investigates: local police for personal crimes, the FBI or Secret Service for large or national ones, Interpol when it crosses borders. And remember the framing that the answer choices are built from: the computer can be the target, the tool, or both.

Cyberbullying scenarios have four fixed correct actions — tell someone, block the abuser, keep the evidence, never retaliate — and two fixed wrong ones: taking the child’s technology away (it isolates them) and deleting the messages (it destroys the evidence). Escalate to police only for threats of violence, stalking, harassment on protected traits, or explicit images of a minor.

📘 DEFINITION
Hashing is one-way. It turns any input into a fixed-length value that cannot be reversed back into the original. Encryption is two-way by design — the whole point is to get the data back. That is why passwords are hashed, not encrypted: a stolen database of hashes does not hand over the passwords.

In the United States, financial and payment-system cybercrime falls to the Secret Service, whose original remit was currency counterfeiting. The FBI leads on computer intrusion, espionage and terrorism, and runs the IC3 complaint center.

Cybercrime complaints and reported dollar losses to the FBI have been rising steadily year on year.

after this section you will be able to…

• Define a computer network, node/host, and data transfer rate/bandwidth.

• Contrast the client/server and peer-to-peer (P2P) models.

• Distinguish LAN, WAN, and MAN, and the ring / star / bus topologies.

• Compare Internet connection types (phone modem, DSL, cable, broadband) and the roles of ISP, backbone, router, repeater.

• Explain packet switching and why packets may arrive out of order.

Plain-English First

A network is just computers that can talk to each other and share stuff — files, printers, web pages. The magic trick that makes the whole internet work is packet switching: instead of sending a message as one big stream, your computer chops it into little numbered envelopes (packets), fires them off — possibly by different routes — and the far end reassembles them in order. Think of mailing a book one page at a time in separate envelopes; even if they arrive scrambled, the page numbers let the recipient rebuild it.

Going Deeper — Models & Network Types

A computer network is a collection of computing devices connected to communicate and share resources. Any device on it is a node (or host) — computers, printers, traffic-handling devices. Key metric: the data transfer rate (a.k.a. bandwidth) — how fast data moves, in bits per second. Communication follows protocols (rules for formatting/processing data).

Two interaction models:

Client/server — a client requests; a server responds (e.g., a web server answering a browser, a file server storing shared files). Can support parallel processing.

Peer-to-peer (P2P) — decentralized; each node can act as client or server, sharing resources directly. No single server, but harder to administer and more prone to security problems.

📌 MUST-KNOW

LAN / WAN / MAN & topologies

LAN = small area (room/building). WAN = connects LANs over large distances (the Internet is the ultimate WAN). MAN = city/campus scale. A LAN node set up to link a LAN to other networks is a gateway. LAN topologies: ring (closed loop, messages travel one direction), star (all nodes connect to one central node — huge burden; if it fails, no communication), bus (all nodes on one shared line carrying messages both directions; nodes ignore messages not addressed to them).

Going Deeper — Wireless, Internet Connections & Packet Switching

Wireless networks use a wireless access point (usually wired to the rest) so devices connect via radio waves — flexible and cheap to install, but more prone to interference and access-control issues. Bluetooth is short-range wireless for peripherals.

No one owns the Internet. Latency (delay between request and receipt) defines speed; the goal is to minimize it. The Internet backbone is a set of high-capacity routes (with heavy redundancy — no true center). An ISP (Internet service provider) connects you to the backbone. Connection types: phone modem (modulator/demodulator; converts data to analog audio over phone lines, ~64 kbps max), DSL (digital over copper phone lines, always-on, distance-limited), and cable modem (over TV cable). DSL and cable are broadband (generally ≥25 Mbps download; always on). For both, download (data to you) is usually faster than upload (data from you), since download traffic dominates.

Packet switching: messages are split into fixed-size numbered packets sent individually, possibly by different routes, then reassembled in order at the destination. Routers direct packets between networks (each knows only the best next hop, not the whole route, and can reroute around congestion/failures). Repeaters strengthen a signal over long distances so it doesn't degrade too much.

ISPProvides Internet access.Your on-ramp to the backbone.

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Node = any device; "host" is the same idea.

Star = single point of failure. Kill the hub, kill the network.

LAN < MAN < WAN by geographic size; the Internet is the biggest WAN.

Packets are numbered so out-of-order arrival can be reassembled.

Router = next hop; Repeater = signal booster.

Download > upload speed on most home broadband (download traffic dominates).

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Confusing LAN and WAN — LAN is local (building), WAN spans large distances.

Thinking a router knows the entire path. It only knows the best next hop.

Saying packets always arrive in order. They may not; numbering fixes this.

Mixing up client/server (central) with P2P (decentralized).

Calling a repeater a router — a repeater just boosts the signal.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Classify the network and model

Problem: A university links every building's LAN across campus; students' browsers request pages from a central library catalog computer. Identify the network scope and the interaction model.

Scope: connects many LANs across a campus/city area → MAN (a WAN if it spanned larger distances).

Browsers requesting from a central catalog computer = requests to a responder → client/server model (the catalog is the server).

If instead students shared files directly among their laptops with no central host, that would be P2P. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Packet switching & a star weakness (wrong way → right way)

A 3-packet message is sent; packets take different routes and arrive as #2, #3, #1.

The destination uses the packet numbers to reorder them → #1, #2, #3 → original message. ✔

Wrong way → why → right way (star topology): a team assumes a star network is the most fault-tolerant. Why wrong: the central node is a single point of failure — if it dies, no one can communicate. Right way: recognize the star's central-node risk when judging reliability. ✔

📊 FIGURE — packet switching — why packets arrive out of order and why it does not matter
🎯 EXAM TIP

Two vocabulary pairs supply most of the questions. LAN / MAN / WAN is purely about geographic size — one building, one city or campus, one large distance — and the Internet is the biggest WAN. Client/server versus peer-to-peer is about whether there is a central responder: if one machine answers requests it is client/server; if every node can be both, it is P2P.

Topology questions almost always want a weakness. Star = a single point of failure at the hub. Ring = a break disrupts the loop. Bus = one shared line, so everybody contends for it. If the question asks which is most vulnerable to one device failing, it is the star.

The packet-switching item is worded as a puzzle: “packets arrived in the order 2, 3, 1 — what went wrong?” Nothing. Packets are sent individually and may take different routes; the numbers let the destination reassemble them. Any answer implying the message is corrupted or must be resent is wrong.

Keep the devices apart, too: a router chooses the next hop toward a destination; a repeater only boosts a weakening signal. And a router never knows the whole path — only the best next step.

Reading a network complaint

When a call connects but voices arrive noticeably late, the metric to blame is latency — the delay in getting each packet there. Bandwidth is capacity, and a connection can have plenty of it while still being slow to respond.

after this section you will be able to…

• Contrast proprietary and open systems, and explain interoperability.

• Describe the OSI Reference Model (7 layers) and a protocol stack.

• Explain TCP/IP and how TCP and IP divide the work; contrast UDP.

• Identify the high-level protocols (SMTP, FTP, Telnet, HTTP) and the role of ports.

• Explain ping, traceroute, MIME types, and firewalls.

Plain-English First

For computers from different companies to talk, they need shared "manners" — protocols (rules of etiquette for communication). Early vendors built proprietary systems that couldn't talk to each other; the fix was open systems built on common standards so anything can interoperate. The most famous rulebook is TCP/IP, a team of two: IP is the mail carrier that routes packets, and TCP is the meticulous shipping clerk that numbers packets, checks nothing got lost, and reassembles them in order.

Going Deeper — Open Systems & the OSI Model

A proprietary system is privately controlled and often can't talk to other vendors' networks. As networking grew, the need for interoperability (different systems working together) drove open systems — based on common architecture and protocol suites. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) created the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Reference Model: seven layers, each handling one aspect of communication. The highest layer is closest to the application; the lowest handles the physical medium (wiring); the network layer, for example, handles routing/addressing of packets.

📌 MUST-KNOW

protocol stacks & TCP/IP

Protocols are layered — each relies on the ones beneath it — forming a protocol stack. This lets new protocols be added without disturbing lower layers. TCP/IP is the core Internet suite: IP (Internet Protocol) routes packets to their destination; TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) breaks messages into packets, hands them to IP, then orders/reassembles them and handles errors (very reliable, a bit slower). UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is TCP's alternative — connectionless, less reliable but faster. Ethernet spans the physical/data-link layers.

Going Deeper — Utilities, High-Level Protocols, Ports & Firewalls

Two TCP/IP utilities: ping tests whether a host is reachable (like a sonar "ping"/echo); traceroute lists the intermediate computers (hops) a packet passes through to a destination. High-level protocols build on TCP/IP:

SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (sending email).

FTP — File Transfer Protocol (transferring files between computers).

Telnet — log into a remote computer.

HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol (exchanging Web documents, usually HTML).

A port is a numeric designation for a particular high-level protocol; servers/routers use it to control traffic (HTTP has a default port; Telnet uses port 23). A MIME type (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extension) is a standard identifying a file's format so a program knows how to handle it (e.g., an email attachment). A firewall is a gateway machine/software that filters traffic and enforces an organization's access control policy — commonly by denying traffic on particular ports (e.g., blocking inbound Telnet on port 23).

Key Terms

Open systemBuilt on common standards.Maximizes interoperability.
InteroperabilityDifferent systems working together.Goal of open standards.
OSI Reference Model7-layer conceptual network framework.Standardizes network functions.
Protocol stackLayered set of protocols.Add protocols without breaking lower ones.
TCPSplits/orders/reassembles packets; reliable.Reliable delivery.
IPRoutes packets to destination.Delivery/addressing foundation.
UDPConnectionless; faster, less reliable.Speed over reliability.
ping / tracerouteReachability test / hop path.Network diagnostics.
PortNumber for a high-level protocol.Controls/identifies traffic.
FirewallFilters traffic per access policy.Protects a network.
MIME typeIdentifies a file's format.Tells programs how to handle data.

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

IP routes, TCP reassembles. IP = the road; TCP = the careful courier.

TCP = reliable/slower, UDP = fast/less reliable. "U" for "Unreliable but fast."

OSI = 7 layers (physical at the bottom, application at the top).

Open beats proprietary for interoperability.

Ping = "are you alive?"; Traceroute = "what path did you take?"

Firewall = port bouncer. It commonly blocks traffic on specific ports.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Swapping TCP and IP jobs. IP routes; TCP splits/orders/reassembles and handles errors.

Calling UDP more reliable than TCP. UDP is faster but less reliable.

Thinking the OSI model has a different number of layers — it has 7.

Confusing ping (reachability) with traceroute (hop-by-hop path).

Believing a firewall stores files — it filters traffic.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Who does what in TCP/IP?

Problem: A large file is emailed. Which protocol (a) breaks it into ordered packets and checks for loss, (b) routes each packet, (c) actually sends the email between mail servers?

(a) Break into packets, order, error-check → TCP.

(b) Route packets to destination → IP.

(c) Transfer the email between servers → SMTP (a high-level protocol built on TCP/IP). ✔

Worked Example 2 — Choose the diagnostic / firewall action (wrong way → right way)

An admin wants to know whether a server is reachable → use ping.

To see which route packets take to it → use traceroute.

To block outside users from remotely logging in via Telnet → deny inbound traffic on port 23 at the firewall.

Wrong way → why → right way: using UDP for a banking transaction "to be faster." Why wrong: UDP is unreliable; lost data could corrupt the transaction. Right way: use TCP for accuracy-critical transfers. ✔

📊 FIGURE — a message going down the sending stack and back up the receiving one
🎯 EXAM TIP

The division of labour is the exam’s favourite question, and one sentence settles it: IP routes, TCP reassembles. IP puts an address on each packet and gets it to the next hop; TCP splits the message, numbers the pieces, checks for loss and puts them back in order. If a choice gives TCP the routing job, it is wrong.

TCP versus UDP is a trade, not a ranking: TCP is reliable and slower, UDP is fast and connectionless with no guarantee of delivery or order. Money, mail and file transfers want TCP; live streaming and games can afford UDP.

Memorise the four high-level protocols by their verb: SMTP sends mail, FTP transfers files, Telnet logs in remotely (port 23), HTTP exchanges web documents. Ports are how a firewall filters — “block remote logins” means deny inbound traffic on the Telnet port.

And two number facts they ask directly: the OSI model has seven layers, physical at the bottom and application at the top; and the reason layering exists at all is that a new protocol can be slotted in without rewriting the ones below it.

Naming, capacity and delay

📘 DEFINITION
DNS (Domain Name System) translates a human-readable name such as wgu.edu into the numeric IP address a machine needs in order to connect. It is the internet's phone book.
TermMeansAnalogy
Bandwidthmaximum data capacity of a path — how much can flow at oncelanes on a motorway
Latencydelay — how long one piece takes to get therehow long the journey takes

They are independent, which is the point of the classic question: a connection can advertise very high bandwidth and still give a choppy video call, because the call is ruined by high latency (and jitter), not by lack of capacity. Equally, a call where voices arrive noticeably late is a latency problem.

Choosing a transport protocol

TCPUDP
Guaranteesevery byte arrives, in order, re-sending what is lostnone — best effort
Costslower, more overheadfast, minimal overhead
Use forfile transfer, web pages, emaillive video/voice, gaming, where late data is useless

An application that must have every byte arrive reliably and in the correct order uses TCP.

Client and server

The client requests; the server provides. A web browser asking for a page is the client, and the remote machine that sends the page back is the server.

HTTP status codes

CodeMeans
200OK — the request succeeded
404Not found — the server was reached, but has nothing at that address
403Forbidden — it exists, you may not have it
500Server error — the fault is at the server end

404 is the one to know: the server answered, so the network and the server are fine. The resource is what is missing.

after this section you will be able to…

• Distinguish a hostname from an IP address.

• Compare IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit) and know why IPv6 exists.

• Explain the domain name system (DNS) and how names resolve to IP addresses.

• Identify domain names, top-level domains (TLDs), and ICANN.

• Define domain squatting and network neutrality.

Plain-English First

Every computer on the Internet needs an address — but humans hate memorizing numbers. So we use friendly hostnames like villanova.edu, and a giant behind-the-scenes phone book called DNS translates them into the numeric IP addresses computers actually use. When you type a web address, DNS quietly looks up the number and connects you.

Going Deeper — Hostnames, IP Addresses, DNS

A hostname is a unique, human-readable name (e.g., matisse.csc.villanova.edu) — the computer name plus the domain name. Network software translates it to an IP address the computer uses.

📌 MUST-KNOW

IPv4 vs. IPv6

IPv4 stores addresses in 32 bits = four bytes shown as four decimal numbers 0–255 separated by dots (e.g., 205.39.155.18), giving only about 4 billion addresses — which ran out (last block assigned in early 2011). IPv6 uses 128 bits = eight groups of 16, written in hexadecimal (e.g., FE80:0000:...:8329), giving vastly more addresses. The IPv4 scheme is hierarchical: first numbers = network, then subnetwork, then host.

The domain name system (DNS) translates hostnames into IP addresses. It's a distributed database (designed 1984) — no single organization holds all mappings. When you enter a hostname, your software asks a nearby domain name server; if it can't resolve the name, it asks another, propagating until the name resolves or the request expires. (Before DNS, a single Stanford-maintained host table was used — it didn't scale.)

Going Deeper — Domains, TLDs, ICANN & Neutrality

A domain name narrows to a particular organization's networks. Its last section is the top-level domain (TLD) — .com (commercial), .edu (universities; tightly controlled), .org, .net, or two-letter country codes. ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) is the international authority managing TLD names and IP assignments. Because early .com/.org/.net were unrestricted, people practiced domain squatting — registering names (often trademarks) hoping to resell them at a profit — generally considered unethical; more TLDs (now 1,500+) were added to relieve pressure. Finally, network neutrality is the principle that ISPs should treat all Internet traffic equally, without favoring or throttling based on user, content, or application.

💡 Tips, Tricks & Mnemonics

Hostname = for humans; IP = for computers. DNS is the translator.

IPv4 = 4 numbers (32 bits); IPv6 = hex (128 bits). "4 = four numbers."

Each IPv4 number is 0–255 (one byte).

DNS is distributed — no single owner; requests propagate until resolved.

TLD = the last part (.com/.edu). ICANN runs the naming system.

Net neutrality = equal treatment of all traffic.

⚠️ COMMON EXAM MISTAKES

Saying an IPv4 number can exceed 255. Each byte maxes at 255.

Mixing up IPv4 (32-bit, decimal) and IPv6 (128-bit, hex).

Thinking DNS is one central server — it's a distributed database.

Confusing the hostname (human-readable) with the IP address (numeric).

Calling domain squatting ethical — it's generally considered unethical.

Step-by-Step Worked Examples

Worked Example 1 — Read an address and pick the version

Problem: Classify each: (a) 193.133.20.4, (b) FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329. Is 256.10.10.1 a valid IPv4 address?

(a) Four decimal numbers separated by dots → IPv4 (32-bit).

(b) Eight hex groups separated by colons → IPv6 (128-bit).

(c) 256 exceeds the 0–255 range of one byte → invalid IPv4 address. ✔

Worked Example 2 — Trace a DNS lookup (wrong way → right way)

You type example.edu; the browser sends the name to a nearby domain name server.

If that server knows the mapping, it returns the IP address; if not, it asks another server, and the request propagates.

Once resolved, the browser connects to the returned IP.

Wrong way → why → right way: assuming one master DNS server holds every mapping. Why wrong: DNS is a distributed database; no single server has everything. Right way: understand requests hop between servers until resolved. ✔

📊 FIGURE — an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, and what DNS is for
🎯 EXAM TIP

Spot-the-invalid-address is the most common item, and it has one rule: each IPv4 number is one byte, so 0–255. Anything with 256 or above in it is not a valid IPv4 address. Scan the four numbers before reading the answer choices.

Tell the versions apart by shape rather than by counting bits: four decimal numbers separated by dots → IPv4 (32 bits); hexadecimal groups separated by colons → IPv6 (128 bits). IPv6 exists because IPv4’s roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out.

DNS questions test one property: it is a distributed database, not a single master server. If your nearby name server does not know a mapping, the request propagates to others until it is resolved. Any choice describing “the DNS server that holds every mapping” is wrong.

The last-mark facts: the TLD is the final part of a domain name (.com, .edu, a two-letter country code), ICANN administers the naming system, domain squatting — registering a name purely to resell it — is regarded as unethical, and network neutrality means all traffic is treated equally regardless of what it is or who sent it.

Two kinds of address, and the firewall

IP addressMAC address
What it identifiesa device's logical position on a networkthe physical network adapter itself
Assigned bythe network (often DHCP) — it changes when you move networksthe manufacturer, burned into the hardware
Scoperoutable across networks, worldwidethe local network segment only

Both are needed: IP gets a packet across the internet to the right network, MAC delivers it to the right machine on that final segment. That two-level addressing scheme is what lets one design scale from a home network to the whole internet.

📘 DEFINITION
A firewall filters network traffic against a set of rules, allowing or blocking it by address, port or protocol. It controls what may cross the boundary — it is not antivirus, and it does not encrypt.

🎯 LEARNING OBJECTIVES

after this section you will be able to…

• Explain what cloud computing is and why organisations use it.

• Tell IaaS, PaaS and SaaS apart from a scenario, and say who manages what.

• Distinguish public, private and hybrid deployment.

• Say when edge computing beats sending data to the cloud.

• Identify the common attacks — DDoS, malware, phishing, man-in-the-middle, brute force — and the defence for each.

Plain-English First

The last section ended with server farms — warehouses of servers. Cloud computing is simply renting space on somebody else's server farm, over the internet, instead of buying and running your own. You pay for what you use and give it back when you are done.

The only real question is how much of the stack you rent. Rent bare machines and you still install everything yourself. Rent a ready-made platform and you supply only your code. Rent a finished application and you just log in. Those three levels are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and telling them apart from a short scenario is the single most commonly tested idea here.

Going Deeper — the three service models

ModelYou manageThe provider managesTypical example
IaaS
Infrastructure as a Service		the operating system, runtime and your applicationhardware, storage, network, virtualisationrenting virtual machines and disks
PaaS
Platform as a Service		your application code and data onlyeverything below your code — OS, runtime, scaling, patchingpush code, the platform runs it
SaaS
Software as a Service		nothing but your own data and settingsthe entire stack including the applicationweb email, online documents
📌 MUST-KNOW

reading the scenario

Every one of these questions is answered by finding the highest thing the customer still manages:

• They mention installing or patching an operating system, or renting virtual machines → IaaS.

• They deploy their own code but no OS is ever mentioned → PaaS.

• They just use a finished application in a browser → SaaS.

It is one sliding scale: from IaaS to SaaS, what the customer manages goes down and what the provider manages goes up.

Going Deeper — deployment models

DeploymentWho the infrastructure servesChosen when
Publicmany unrelated customers share the provider's hardwarecost and elasticity matter most
Privateone organisation only, dedicatedregulation or sensitivity demands isolation
Hybridboth, connected togethersensitive systems stay private while public services scale in the public cloud

Going Deeper — why it is worth it, and what it costs you

The gains. Elasticity — add capacity for the busy week and release it afterwards. Pay-as-you-go — an operating cost instead of buying hardware up front. No data centre to power, cool, secure or replace. Someone else handles hardware failure.

The costs. You now depend on the provider and on your own internet link: their outage is your outage. Data lives somewhere you do not own, which can matter legally. Heavy long-running workloads can end up dearer than owning. Moving to another provider later is rarely easy.

Going Deeper — edge computing

Edge computing processes data near where it is produced — on the device or a local gateway — instead of shipping everything to the cloud. A factory gateway that reads its own sensors, or a camera that recognises a face on-device, is doing edge computing.

📌 MUST-KNOW

edge or cloud?

• Edge when the answer is needed fast (low latency, milliseconds), when bandwidth is limited or costly, or when raw data should not leave the site.

• Cloud when the work needs heavy computation or must combine data from many places. One site's gateway cannot see the other thousand sites.

Going Deeper — network & IoT security

Connecting everything to the internet — including the billions of embedded and IoT devices from the previous unit — is what makes these attacks possible. Learn each one by what it targets.

AttackHow it worksWhat stops it
DoSone machine floods a server so real users cannot get througha firewall filtering and rate limiting at the boundary
DDoSthe same flood from many hijacked machines at once — a botnetupstream scrubbing; and securing the devices so they are never recruited
Malwarea virus needs a host file to be run; a worm spreads by itself; a trojan is disguised as something wanted; ransomware encrypts your files for paymentpatching, anti-malware, least privilege, backups
Phishinga message imitates someone trusted to get credentials — it attacks the persontraining, and 2FA so a stolen password is not enough
Man-in-the-middlethe attacker sits in the path and reads or alters traffic while both sides think they are talking directlyencryption in transit (HTTPS) makes what is intercepted useless
Brute forceguessing passwords over and over until one worksaccount lockout or rate limiting — it removes the unlimited guesses
📌 MUST-KNOW

why IoT devices end up in botnets

Not because they are powerful — because they are neglected. They ship with default passwords nobody changes and firmware nobody ever updates, and there are billions of them. Change the credentials and keep the firmware current and the whole attack falls apart.

Key Terms

TermDefinition
Cloud computingrenting computing resources over the internet instead of owning them
IaaSyou rent virtual machines, storage and networking; you manage the OS upward
PaaSyou rent a managed platform and supply only your application code
SaaSyou use a finished application; the provider manages everything
Hybrid cloudprivate infrastructure for sensitive systems combined with public cloud services
Elasticitycapacity can be added and released on demand
Edge computingprocessing data near its source rather than sending it to the cloud
Botneta network of compromised machines controlled by an attacker
DDoSa denial-of-service flood coming from many machines at once
Phishinga message impersonating a trusted party to obtain credentials
Man-in-the-middlean attacker secretly relaying traffic between two parties
Firewalla filter at the network boundary that allows or blocks traffic by rule
Two-factor authenticationproof from two different categories — knowledge, possession or biometrics

🧠 Memory hooks

HookWhat it unlocks
“Infrastructure, Platform, Software”IaaS → PaaS → SaaS is bottom to top of the stack. The further up you rent, the less you manage. Read the scenario for the highest layer the customer still touches.
OS mentioned = IaaSIf the customer installs, patches or chooses the operating system, it is IaaS. PaaS and SaaS both hide the OS completely.

Fast or local → edgeMilliseconds, weak link, or data that must not leave the site → edge. Heavy computation or combining many sites → cloud.

◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Write the variable and its value in the margin. Read the condition out loud with the real number substituted in — "is 65 greater than 65?" — and answer it before you look at the options.

The one that decides these questions

> is strict. A value equal to the cut-off FAILS a > test and falls to ELSE. >= includes the cut-off. Most "what prints" items are built on exactly that difference, so the test writer will hand you the boundary value on purpose.

Two rules that never change

An IF/ELSE runs exactly one branch — never both, never neither. And quoted text prints literally: OUTPUT "Continue" prints Continue, it does not look up a variable called Continue.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t2":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Test the branches top to bottom and stop at the first true one. Everything below it is skipped, even if it would also be true.

Why order matters

In a grade chain, 95 is greater than 90 AND 80 AND 70 — but only the first match runs. That is why the chain is written highest cut-off first. Reversed, every score would print the lowest grade.

Nested IFs

An inner IF is only reached if the outer condition passed. If the outer test fails, the whole inner block — both its branches — is skipped without being evaluated at all.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t3":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Write out the values the loop variable actually takes: 1, 2, 3 … Do not divide the range and estimate. For short loops, tracing every pass is faster and safer than reasoning about it.

Inclusive ends

FOR i = 1 TO 10 runs 10 times — both endpoints are included. That is where off-by-one answers come from, and the wrong options are usually the count ±1.

Accumulators

A running total must be initialised before the loop. Set it inside and it resets on every pass, leaving only the last value.

Nested loops

The inner loop runs completely for each pass of the outer one, so the body runs outer × inner times — nested loops multiply, they never add.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t4":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Keep a two-column table: the variable, and whether the condition is still true. Stop the moment it turns false — the value it holds then is the answer.

The overshoot

A WHILE checks its condition before each pass, so it exits with the first value that fails the test. x = 4, x < 11, x = x + 3 ends at 13, not 11 — the limit itself is rarely the answer, which is why it is always offered as a distractor.

Infinite loops

If nothing inside the body changes the variable in the condition, the loop never ends. Every WHILE needs its own update line.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t5":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Give each variable a column and cross out the old value on every assignment. Assignment replaces; it is not an equation that stays true.

Order is everything

SET x = x + 5 means "take the current x, add 5, store it back". The right-hand side is worked out first, using the values as they are at that moment.

The classic swap

Swapping needs a third variable: temp = a; a = b; b = temp. Without temp, the first line overwrites a and both variables end up holding b — a favourite exam trap.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t6":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

Work the expression in precedence order and write down each intermediate value rather than doing it in your head.

MOD is the remainder

17 MOD 5 = 2 (17 = 3×5 + 2), not 3. The quotient is the distractor. MOD is the standard test for divisibility: n MOD 2 = 0 means n is even.

Division

In this course’s pseudocode, / is ordinary division and keeps the fraction: 33 / 4 = 8.25. Some real languages truncate to 8 when both operands are integers — read which convention the question is using.

Precedence

Multiply and divide before add and subtract: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20. Brackets override it.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t7":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

For strings, copy the output character by character — including the spaces. For lists, write the index above each value before you answer.

Concatenation

first + " " + last joins in written order and the " " supplies the space. Drop it and the words run together.

Indexing starts at 0

In a list of 6 values the valid indexes are 0–5. nums[2] is the third value, and nums[6] is out of range. Off-by-one here is the single most common tracing error.

FOR EACH

FOR EACH visits every element once, in order, without you managing an index — useful when you need the values but not their positions.

"},"D684/trace_drill/t8":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO TRACE THIS

When a line contains a call, work out the call first, write its returned value above the line, then finish the expression.

RETURN hands a value back

doubleIt(5) + 3 is 10 + 3 = 13. The argument is not added first — the call completes, then the rest of the expression runs.

Scope

A variable created inside a function is local: it exists only during that call and disappears afterwards. Assigning to a local of the same name does not change the outer variable.

Loops with a condition inside

Every pass reaches the IF, but only the passes that satisfy it perform the action. Trace which values pass the test first, then apply the action only to those.

◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

The question gives you a goal in English and four candidate lines. Ask one thing first: does the option store its result? If it does not, it cannot be the answer.

A statement assigns; an expression does not

f - d works out a value and immediately loses it. set b = f - d keeps it. Options written as bare expressions are there to catch you.

Order matters for - and /

"Subtract d from f" is f - d, not d - f. Read which value is being taken FROM which. Addition and multiplication survive being reversed; subtraction and division do not.

Two other decoy shapes

Plain English ("subtract d from f") is not pseudocode, and function-call forms like sub(f, d) are not how this course writes arithmetic.

"},"D684/write_drill/p2":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Conversions are named after the type you WANT, and input/output questions are decided by direction.

Conversion is a function named for the target

float(a) turns the integer a into a floating-point number. int(num) goes the other way. Decoys invent methods (a.to_float()) or bolt on a decimal (a.0) — neither is how this course writes it.

int() truncates, it does not round

int(8.9) is 8. The decimal part is chopped off. This is a favourite one-mark question.

Direction decides input vs output

INPUT/read brings a value IN from the user. OUTPUT/print/DISPLAY sends one OUT to the screen. Decide which way the value is travelling before you read the options.

"},"D684/write_drill/p3":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

A handful of routines come up again and again. Learn their SHAPE and you can recognise the right option instantly — and name what each wrong option actually does.

The four shapes

Average: add the values, then divide by how many. Max: compare with > and keep the winner. Swap: three lines using a temp. Accumulator: set the total to 0 before the loop, add inside it.

Name the decoys

Wrong options in these items are usually a DIFFERENT valid routine — a swap offered for an average, or a min offered for a max. Ask what the option really does rather than whether it looks plausible.

The precedence trap

val_1 + val_2 / 2 is not an average: division runs first, so only val_2 is halved. The average needs the sum computed first, or brackets around it.

"},"D684/write_drill/p4":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

These are vocabulary questions: the exam gives the definition and wants the name, or gives the name and wants the shape. Precision matters more than intuition.

The two ifs

Single-alternative: if (condition) then — acts when true, does nothing when false (that empty path is the null case). Dual-alternative: if (condition) then … else — two paths.

Stacking vs nesting

Stacked structures run one AFTER another. Nested structures sit one INSIDE another, so the inner test is only reached when the outer one passed — that is how you express combined conditions without repeating tests.

The loop words

Loop control variable — tested in the condition and changed in the body. Counter — goes up by a fixed 1. Accumulator — adds a varying amount. Sentinel — a value that means STOP, never real data. Priming read — the input before the loop that gives the first test something to look at.

"},"D684/write_drill/p5":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Almost every question here is answered by knowing the order and being able to translate between two vocabularies.

The order

Understand the problem → Plan the logic → Code the program → Translate the code → Test the program → Put into production → Maintain. It always starts with understanding the problem, no matter how urgent the project sounds.

The same work, two vocabularies

"Plan the logic" = design (flowcharts and pseudocode live here). "Code the program" = implementation. "Translate the code" = the compiler or interpreter. Questions often switch vocabulary mid-sentence.

Which error, which step

A misspelled keyword is a syntax error and is caught at translation. A program that runs but gives wrong answers has a logic error and is caught by testing.

Maintenance is the long tail

Software spends far longer being maintained than being written, which is why changes to a live program belong to maintenance and why documentation pays off.

"},"D684/write_drill/p6":{"body":"
◆ HOW TO ANSWER THESE

Scenario questions give four situations and ask which breaches the codes. Read each one and ask: who could be harmed, was anyone deceived, and was anything taken that was not theirs?

What both codes demand

Put the public's safety and welfare first; be honest in claims and estimates; respect privacy and access only what you are authorised to; credit others' work; work only within your competence (or disclose the gap); accept and give honest review, and correct errors; treat people fairly; reject bribery and disclose conflicts of interest; and support colleagues' professional development.

The trap in these items

Options that sound corporate are often perfectly ethical — signing the code annually, halting production when harm is found, paying for training. The violation is usually the one that removes a protection, hides something, or takes credit.

Responsibility does not transfer

"My manager told me to" is not a defence in either code, and neither is handing the task to a colleague.

SDLC as an ordered process (WGU steps)

\n
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of building software like building a house. You don't start nailing boards before you know what the owner wants, and you don't move people in before you inspect it. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is just that ordered checklist — and WGU loves to ask “you just finished step X, what's next?” So the order matters more than the vibe.

\n
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

A common WGU ordering runs: 1) Analyze/define the problem (gather requirements — what must it do?), 2) Plan the logic/design (flowcharts and pseudocode describe the steps), 3) Code/translate (write it, then translate the code so the machine can run it), 4) Test/debug (find and fix errors), 5) Put the program into production (deploy it for real use), 6) Maintain the program (fix, patch, and enhance over its life).

The biggest cost over a program's life is usually maintenance, not the original coding.

\n
📝 HOW WGU WORDS IT
★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Know the WGU SDLC steps in order and what each produces — requirements gather needs, design plans the solution, implementation codes it, testing verifies, deployment releases, maintenance sustains.

▸ QUICK CHECK

Given a scenario ('the team is writing test cases'), name the phase: that's testing, which comes after implementation.

Pseudocode the WGU way

\n
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Pseudocode is fake code — plain steps that read like English but follow programming logic, without any real language's punctuation. WGU tests whether you can read its specific style: how it converts types, adds to a variable, and chooses between paths.

\n
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Three control structures cover everything: sequence (do actions one after another, in order), selection (choose a path based on a condition — an if), and loop/iteration (repeat while a condition holds). A dual-alternative if means if…else (two possible paths). A single-alternative if runs a block or skips it.

Type conversion: turning a number into a decimal or vice-versa is done with a conversion operation named after the target type.

\n
📝 HOW WGU WORDS IT

WGU's exact operations: float(age) converts the integer age to a floating-point number. int(num) converts a float to an integer (truncating). To add 10 to a variable, the expression is value + 10. Integer division of 7 by 2 is 3 (the fractional part is dropped). “Sequence structure” = executing actions one after another in order. “Selection structure” = choosing different paths based on conditions. A “dual-alternative if” has both an if and an else branch.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Pseudocode expresses an algorithm in plain, language-neutral terms using INPUT/OUTPUT, IF/ELSE, WHILE/FOR — no strict syntax, focus on logic.

IF score ≥ 60 THEN OUTPUT "pass" ELSE OUTPUT "fail" — readable logic, not tied to any language.

CPU scheduling algorithms by name

\n
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When many programs want the one CPU, the operating system plays traffic cop, deciding who goes next. Each strategy has a name, and WGU asks you to match the name to its one-line behavior. Learn them as a set of contrasts.

\n
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): runs jobs in arrival order (simple, but a long job blocks everyone behind it). Shortest Job Next (SJN), also called shortest-job-first: picks the job with the smallest total execution time next. Shortest Remaining Time: picks the job with the smallest execution time remaining (the preemptive cousin of SJN). Priority scheduling: highest-priority job runs next. Round-Robin (RR): each job gets a fixed time slice in turn, cycling around — this is what gives fairness and responsiveness.

\n
📝 HOW WGU WORDS IT

WGU's phrasings to memorize: “selects the process with the smallest execution time remaining” → Shortest Job Next / Shortest Remaining Time. “Each process gets a fixed time slice in rotation” → Round-Robin. For memory: “allocating fixed-sized blocks of memory” describes paging (not swapping whole processes). A process that “has completed its execution” is in the terminated state.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

CPU scheduling by name: FCFS (first-come first-served), SJF (shortest job first), Round Robin (fixed time slice per process), Priority.

▸ QUICK CHECK

Round Robin gives each process a time quantum in turn — good for responsiveness/fairness; SJF minimizes average wait but can starve long jobs.

ACM & IEEE Codes of Ethics

\n
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two professional bodies — the ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) and the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) — publish ethics codes that working computer professionals promise to follow. WGU asks which actions honor or violate them, so you need the gist of what each commits you to.

\n
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Shared themes across both codes: protect the public (safety, health, welfare come first), be honest and avoid conflicts of interest, respect privacy and confidentiality, credit others' work (no plagiarism or IP theft), and maintain and improve technical competence (keep your skills current). A violation is anything that harms the public, deceives, steals credit, or breaches privacy.

\n
📝 HOW WGU WORDS IT

WGU wording: adopting the IEEE Code of Ethics means a company commits to “maintain and improve technical competence.” A situation that violates both the ACM and IEEE codes is typically one that harms the public or breaches honesty/privacy — e.g., knowingly shipping unsafe software or concealing a data breach. Read each option for who is harmed and whether honesty or public welfare is broken.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

The ACM code covers computing broadly; the IEEE code centers on hardware/electrical engineering. Both stress public good, honesty, and avoiding harm.

▸ QUICK CHECK

A question about a code focused on hardware/electronics → IEEE; a general computing-professional code → ACM.

Programming paradigms & their subsets

\n
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A “paradigm” is just a style of organizing a program — a philosophy for how you tell the computer what to do. WGU asks you to identify the style from a description, and to know which styles are subsets of which.

\n
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Imperative styles say how step by step: procedural (organize into procedures/functions that run in sequence) and object-oriented (OOP) (organize into objects that bundle data fields and methods together). Declarative styles say what you want, not how: functional programming (build programs from pure functions, avoid changing state) is a subset of declarative, and so is logic programming and query languages like SQL.

\n
📝 HOW WGU WORDS IT

WGU wording: the object-oriented paradigm “organizes a program into smaller components that bundle together fields and methods.” The paradigm that is a subset of the declarative paradigm is functional programming. “Imperative/procedural” describes code as an explicit sequence of steps; “declarative” describes the desired result and lets the system figure out the steps.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Imperative (how): procedural + object-oriented. Declarative (what): functional + logic. Knowing which family a paradigm belongs to is a common OA item.

▸ QUICK CHECK

OOP is a subset of imperative; SQL and Prolog are declarative. Functional programming avoids mutable state and side effects.

Memory management, fair use & software types

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three quick but testable ideas your notes call out by name. First, how an operating system slices up memory to share it among programs. Second, the one big exception to copyright — fair use. Third, the difference between the software that runs the machine and the software you actually use.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Memory-management techniques — how the OS divides RAM among programs: Single contiguous = one program plus the OS occupy all of memory at once (the simplest, oldest scheme). Fixed partitioning = memory is split into a set number of fixed-size blocks decided in advance; simple, but wastes space when a program is smaller than its block (internal fragmentation). Dynamic partitioning = partitions are created to fit each program's exact size; less waste inside, but leaves scattered gaps between programs over time (external fragmentation). Paged memory = memory is divided into equal-size frames and programs into equal-size pages that can be placed in any free frame, non-contiguously — which eliminates external fragmentation.

Fair use = a legal doctrine allowing limited use of copyrighted material without permission — for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching, or research. It's the main exception to copyright: quoting a short passage in a review is fair use; copying a whole book is not.

System software vs application software: system software runs and manages the computer itself and provides a platform for other programs — the operating system, device drivers, utilities. Application software is what you use to get tasks done — a browser, a word processor, a game. System software serves the machine; application software serves the user.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Single contiguous = one program + OS fill memory. Fixed partitioning = preset equal blocks (→ internal fragmentation). Dynamic partitioning = sized to each program (→ external fragmentation). Paged memory = equal pages in equal frames, non-contiguous (removes external fragmentation). Fair use = limited use of copyrighted work without permission (criticism, teaching, news). System software = runs the machine / platform for other software (OS, drivers); application software = user tasks (browser, word processor).

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Fragmentation trap: fixed partitions waste space inside a block (internal); dynamic partitions leave gaps between blocks (external); paging is the fix for external fragmentation. And don't blur the software types — the operating system is system software, not application software.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

System software (OS, drivers) manages the machine; application software does user tasks. The OS handles memory management (allocation, virtual memory, paging).

▸ QUICK CHECK

An OS is system software; a spreadsheet is application software. Virtual memory gives each program its own large address space.

📖 Edge Computing (and where it fits next to the cloud)

Edge computing processes data close to where it’s generated (on or near the device) instead of shipping everything to a distant cloud data center first.

WHY PUSH WORK TO THE EDGE?
• Lower latency: decisions in milliseconds, no round-trip to the cloud (a self-driving car can’t wait).
• Less bandwidth: send summaries, not raw video/sensor floods.
• Works offline: keeps functioning when the connection drops.
Trade-off: edge devices have limited compute/storage — heavy analysis and long-term storage still live in the cloud. Edge and cloud are partners, not rivals.
WORKED EXAMPLE — sort the scenario
• A factory camera flags defective parts on the assembly line in real time → edge (latency-critical, high-volume video).
• The same factory runs monthly analytics over all plants’ data → cloud (big compute, not time-critical).
• A smart doorbell detects motion locally but stores clips online → both: edge detection + cloud storage.
⚠️ EDGE ≠ “NO CLOUD”
Edge computing doesn’t replace the cloud — it filters and pre-processes near the source, then hands the important results to the cloud. If a question stresses “real-time,” “low latency,” or “reduce data sent,” the answer is edge.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Processing sensor data on the device itself to avoid network delay is called:
  1. Edge computing
  2. SaaS
  3. Batch processing
Show answer
A — edge computing. Compute happens at/near the data source for speed and bandwidth savings.

Cloud computing: SaaS, PaaS & IaaS

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Cloud computing means renting computing over the internet instead of owning the hardware. The three service models are just about how much someone else manages for you. Think of getting dinner: cook it yourself from raw ingredients (most control, most work), use a meal kit (some done for you), or order delivery (you just eat). SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS are the same trade-off for software.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent the raw building blocks — virtual machines, storage, networking — and manage the operating system and everything above it yourself. Most control, most responsibility. (Think: renting an empty kitchen.) Examples: AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine.

PaaS (Platform as a Service): you rent a ready-made platform to run your own code — the provider handles the servers, OS, and scaling; you just deploy your app. (The meal kit: ingredients prepped, you assemble.) Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine.

SaaS (Software as a Service): you use finished software in a browser and manage nothing but your own data and settings. (Delivery: you just eat.) Examples: Gmail, Google Docs, Netflix, Salesforce.

The rule of thumb: as you move IaaS → PaaS → SaaS, you manage less and the provider manages more.

Deployment models are a separate question — where the cloud lives: public cloud (shared, rented from a provider like AWS), private cloud (dedicated to one organization), and hybrid cloud (a mix of both).

📝 EXAM WORDING

IaaS = rent infrastructure (VMs/storage), you manage the OS & up. PaaS = rent a platform to run your own code, provider manages servers/OS. SaaS = use finished software in a browser (Gmail, Docs). Moving IaaS→PaaS→SaaS, you manage less. Deployment: public (shared), private (one org), hybrid (both). Cloud benefits: scalability, on-demand access, pay-for-what-you-use.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The tell-tale clues: “finished app in a browser” = SaaS; “run MY code without managing servers” = PaaS; “rent VMs / full control of the OS” = IaaS. Don't confuse the service model (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS = how much is managed) with the deployment model (public/private/hybrid = where it runs) — the exam mixes these.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Cloud service models: SaaS (ready software), PaaS (platform to build/deploy on), IaaS (raw compute/storage you manage).

▸ QUICK CHECK

Gmail = SaaS; a managed app platform = PaaS; renting virtual machines = IaaS. More control = lower up the stack (IaaS).

Software licenses & the public domain

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Copyright automatically protects whatever someone creates — but a license is the creator saying “here's what YOU are allowed to do with it.” Software licenses run on a spectrum from totally locked-down (proprietary) to totally free (public domain), with open-source licenses in the middle setting the rules for reuse.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Proprietary: the owner keeps all rights; you buy a license to USE it but can't see or change the source (most commercial software).

Open-source licenses grant rights to use, modify, and share the source, with conditions. MIT license is very permissive — do almost anything, just keep the copyright notice. GNU GPL is “copyleft” — you can reuse it, but anything you build on it must ALSO be open-source under the GPL.

Creative Commons (CC) licenses are for creative works (images, text, media), letting creators pick conditions like attribution or non-commercial use. Public domain means no copyright applies at all — anyone can use it freely for anything (either the creator waived rights, or the copyright expired).

📝 EXAM WORDING

Proprietary = closed, all rights reserved. MIT license = permissive open-source (keep the notice, do what you like). GNU GPL = copyleft (derivatives must stay open-source). Creative Commons = flexible licenses for creative works. Public domain = no copyright, free for all use.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The GPL's “copyleft” is the classic trap: it's open-source, but it FORCES your derivative work to also be GPL open-source — unlike the permissive MIT license, which lets you do nearly anything, even in closed products. Public domain is not a “license” so much as the absence of copyright.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Proprietary (closed), open-source — split into copyleft (GPL: derivatives must stay open) and permissive (MIT/Apache: few restrictions) — and public domain (no rights reserved).

▸ QUICK CHECK

Ship a product built on GPL code and you must release your source under the GPL; MIT would not require that.

📖 Encryption Basics — Ciphers, Symmetric vs Asymmetric Keys

Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption reverses it with a key. The exam wants the vocabulary and the symmetric/asymmetric distinction.

CLASSIC CIPHERS (the historical warm-up)
• Caesar cipher: shift every letter a fixed number of places (shift 3: A→D, B→E). Easy to break — only 25 shifts to try.
• Substitution cipher: replace each letter using a scrambled alphabet mapping. Broken by frequency analysis (E is the most common English letter, etc.).
These show WHY modern crypto uses math and long keys instead of letter tricks.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Caesar shift of 3
Encrypt “CAB” with shift 3: C→F, A→D, B→E → ciphertext “FDE”. Decrypt by shifting back 3. The “key” is just the number 3.
SYMMETRIC vs ASYMMETRIC (the big distinction)
SymmetricAsymmetric (public-key)
KeysONE shared secret key — same key encrypts and decryptsTWO related keys — public key encrypts, private key decrypts
SpeedFastSlower
Hard partSharing the secret key safely with the other sideNone — the public key can be posted openly
ExamplesAESRSA
Real systems combine them: asymmetric to exchange a key, then fast symmetric for the data (this is how HTTPS works).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — who can read the message?
Amara publishes her public key. Ben encrypts a message with it and sends it. Only Amara’s private key can decrypt — so even if the message is intercepted, only Amara reads it. Notice Ben and Amara never had to meet to share a secret — that’s the point of asymmetric encryption.
⚠️ PUBLIC ENCRYPTS, PRIVATE DECRYPTS
In public-key crypto, the key that scrambles a message TO you is the one everybody can see (public); the one that unscrambles is the one only you hold (private). If a question says “one shared key,” it’s symmetric; “key pair” means asymmetric.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Encryption that uses the SAME key to encrypt and decrypt is called:
  1. Symmetric
  2. Asymmetric
  3. Hashing
Show answer
A — symmetric. One shared secret key both ways. Asymmetric uses a public/private key pair.

Digital forensics, surveillance & decryption

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When something goes wrong — a breach, a crime, misuse — someone has to reconstruct what happened from the digital traces. That's digital forensics. Surveillance is the ongoing monitoring of activity, and encryption/decryption is the lock-and-key that keeps data private in between.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Digital forensics is the recovery, preservation, and analysis of digital evidence (files, logs, deleted data, metadata) — done carefully so it holds up in an investigation or court.

Surveillance is the monitoring of behavior or communications — from network logging to camera systems. It raises real privacy and ethics questions about consent and proportionality (a core ACM Code of Ethics concern).

Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption is the reverse — using the key to turn ciphertext back into readable plaintext. Only someone with the correct key should be able to decrypt.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Digital forensics = recovering and analyzing digital evidence. Surveillance = monitoring activity/communications (a privacy & ethics issue). Encryption converts plaintext → ciphertext; Decryption converts ciphertext → plaintext with the key. Confidentiality depends on keeping the decryption key secret.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Encryption and decryption are opposite halves of the same system — encryption locks, decryption unlocks, and both need the right key. Surveillance is ethically sensitive: the ACM Code stresses respecting privacy, so “because we can” is never sufficient justification.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Digital forensics preserves evidence with a documented chain of custody. Encryption protects data; a warrant/authority is typically required to decrypt or surveil lawfully.

▸ QUICK CHECK

Altering original evidence breaks the chain of custody — investigators work on verified copies (hashes match).

📖 Octal & Hex — the other two bases you must convert

Besides binary (base 2) and decimal (base 10), the exam uses octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16). Same place-value idea, different base.

THE FOUR BASES AT A GLANCE
BaseDigitsPlace values
Binary (2)0–1…8, 4, 2, 1
Octal (8)0–7…512, 64, 8, 1
Decimal (10)0–9…1000, 100, 10, 1
Hex (16)0–9, A–F (A=10…F=15)…4096, 256, 16, 1
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — octal to decimal
Octal 127 = 1·64 + 2·8 + 7·1 = 64 + 16 + 7 = 87. (Careful: the digit 8 never appears in octal — “128” is not a valid octal number.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — the 3-bit / 4-bit grouping trick
Binary groups convert instantly:
• Octal = groups of 3 bits. 110101₂ → 110|101 → 6 and 5 → octal 65.
• Hex = groups of 4 bits. 11010110₂ → 1101|0110 → D and 6 → hex D6.
That’s why programmers like octal/hex: they’re shorthand for binary.
⚠️ GROUP FROM THE RIGHT
When splitting binary into 3-bit (octal) or 4-bit (hex) groups, start from the right end and pad the leftmost group with leading zeros if needed. Grouping from the left gives wrong digits.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Octal 34 in decimal is:
  1. 28
  2. 34
  3. 26
Show answer
A — 28. 3·8 + 4·1 = 24 + 4 = 28.

Why binary? Place value in any base

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A computer is millions of tiny switches, and a switch has exactly two states: on or off. So the machine can only “count” with two symbols, 0 and 1 — that's binary. Everything else (numbers, letters, images, sound) is ultimately a pattern of those on/off switches.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Decimal (base 10) uses place values that are powers of ten: 1, 10, 100, 1000… The number 305 means 3×100 + 0×10 + 5×1. Binary works the same way, but the places are powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32…

So binary 101101 = 1×32 + 0×16 + 1×8 + 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 45. To go the other way (decimal → binary), keep subtracting the largest power of two that fits, or repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders bottom-to-top.

Hexadecimal (base 16) is just shorthand for binary: one hex digit = exactly four binary digits, because 2⁴ = 16. That's why programmers use it — compact and clean to convert.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Bit = one binary digit (0 or 1). Byte = 8 bits. A question may ask you to “convert 0x2F to decimal” (hex 2F = 2×16 + 15 = 47) or the “number of distinct values n bits can represent” — that's always 2ⁿ. Know that 2¹⁰ = 1024.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Hex digits go 0–9 then A–F, where A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. Also: n bits give 2ⁿ values, but the largest value is 2ⁿ − 1 (because one value is zero).

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Place value works in any base: base-2 (binary) uses powers of 2, base-16 (hex) powers of 16. Convert binary→decimal by adding the place values of the 1 bits.

▸ QUICK CHECK

1011₂ = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11₁₀. And 13₁₀ = 1101₂ (8+4+1).

➖ Two's Complement: Storing Negatives

THE RECIPE
Computers have no minus sign. To negate a number: flip every bit, then add 1. The leftmost bit becomes the sign bit: 0 = positive, 1 = negative.
WORKED EXAMPLE — build −5 in 8 bits
StepBits
+500000101
Flip11111010
Add 111111011 = −5
Why bother? 5 + (−5) with plain binary addition = 00000000 (the carry falls off the end) — zero, exactly right. The hardware never needs a separate subtract circuit.
FactValue
8-bit signed range−128 to +127
n-bit signed range−2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1
⚠️ TWO TRAPS
The negative range goes ONE further than the positive (−128 but only +127) because zero eats a positive slot. And don't confuse two's complement (flip + add 1) with one's complement (just flip).
🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
How are signed integers represented in nearly every computer?
  1. Two's complement
  2. One's complement
  3. Sign-and-magnitude only
  4. BCD
Show answer + steps
A. "Invert the bits and add one" — subtraction becomes addition, one representation of zero.
📖 Full lesson — every definition & detail (tap to collapse)

Two's complement: storing negatives

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Computers have no minus sign — only 0s and 1s. So how do you store −5? The trick: give up the top bit to mean “negative,” and store negatives so that subtraction just works as addition. That scheme is two's complement, and nearly every computer uses it.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

To get the negative of a number: flip every bit, then add 1. In 8 bits: +5 is 00000101. Flip → 11111010. Add 1 → 11111011. That's −5.

Why bother? Because 5 + (−5) done with plain binary addition gives 00000000 (the carry falls off the end) — zero, exactly right. The hardware never needs a separate “subtract” circuit; it just adds the two's-complement form.

The leftmost bit is the sign bit: 0 means positive, 1 means negative.

📝 EXAM WORDING

“Two's complement” is the standard answer for how signed integers are represented. The recipe “invert the bits and add one” is common phrasing. An 8-bit signed range is −128 to +127; n bits signed is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹−1.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The negative range goes one further than the positive (−128 but only +127) because zero eats a positive slot. Don't confuse two's complement (flip + add 1) with one's complement (just flip).

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Two's complement stores negatives so one circuit adds both signs. To negate: flip all bits, then add 1. The leftmost bit is the sign (1 = negative).

▸ QUICK CHECK

In 8-bit two's complement, −1 = 11111111 and 0 = 00000000. The value −1 is always 'all ones'.

📖 More Gates (NAND, NOR, XOR) & Short-Circuit Evaluation

Two add-ons the test asks about beyond AND/OR/NOT: the combined gates, and how programming languages short-circuit Boolean expressions.

THE COMBINED GATES
• NAND = NOT-AND: output 0 only when both inputs are 1 (otherwise 1).
• NOR = NOT-OR: output 1 only when both inputs are 0.
• XOR (exclusive OR): output 1 when the inputs differ (exactly one is 1). 1⊕1 = 0!
NAND and NOR are universal gates — either one alone can build every other gate, which is why chips are full of them.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — XOR by table
aba XOR b
000
011
101
110
“One or the other but NOT both.” XOR is used for parity checks and simple encryption (x ⊕ key ⊕ key = x).
SHORT-CIRCUIT EVALUATION
Languages evaluate Boolean expressions left to right and stop as soon as the answer is decided:
• In A AND B: if A is false, the whole thing is false — B is never evaluated.
• In A OR B: if A is true, the whole thing is true — B is skipped.
Programmers exploit this for safety: if (x != 0 AND 10/x > 2) never divides by zero, because when x is 0 the division is skipped.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — what gets evaluated?
With count = 0:  if (count > 0 AND total/count > 5).
count > 0 is false → AND short-circuits → total/count never runs → no crash. Reverse the order and it divides by zero. Order matters!
⚠️ XOR OF TWO TRUES IS FALSE
The most-missed row: 1 XOR 1 = 0. XOR means exclusively one. And in short-circuit questions, ask “can the left side alone decide?” — if yes, the right side is skipped.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
In the expression (FALSE AND X), what happens to X under short-circuit evaluation?
  1. X is never evaluated — the result is already FALSE
  2. X is evaluated anyway
  3. The program crashes
Show answer
A. FALSE AND anything = FALSE, so evaluation stops at the left operand.

Boolean logic & truth tables

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Underneath every program is true/false logic. Boolean logic is just the rules for combining true/false values with three basic operations: AND, OR, and NOT. If you can read a truth table, you can predict what any combination does.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

AND is true only when BOTH inputs are true. OR is true when AT LEAST ONE is true. NOT flips the value. XOR (exclusive or) is true when the inputs DIFFER.

These map directly to physical logic gates in the CPU — an AND gate outputs 1 only when both wires carry 1. Complex circuits (adders, memory) are built from thousands of these.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Know the truth tables cold. A AND B = A∧B; A OR B = A∨B; NOT A = ¬A. De Morgan's laws appear constantly: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B).

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The classic trap: OR in logic is inclusive — “A or B” is still true when BOTH are true. Everyday English often means “one or the other but not both” — that “exactly one” meaning is XOR.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Boolean logic: AND (true only if both), OR (true if at least one), NOT (invert). A truth table with n inputs has 2ⁿ rows.

▸ QUICK CHECK

3 inputs → 2³ = 8 rows. NAND = NOT(AND); its output is 0 only when both inputs are 1.

These map directly to physical logic gates — an AND gate outputs 1 only when both wires carry 1. Complex circuits (adders, memory) are built from thousands of gates.
⚠️ OR IS INCLUSIVE
"A or B" in logic is STILL TRUE when both are true. Everyday English's "one or the other but not both" — that "exactly one" meaning — is XOR.

How the CPU runs your program

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A program is just a list of tiny instructions in memory. The CPU does one boringly simple loop, billions of times a second: get the next instruction, figure out what it means, do it, repeat. That loop is the whole show.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

The loop is fetch–decode–execute. Fetch: copy the next instruction from memory (RAM) into the CPU. Decode: the control unit works out what it is. Execute: the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does the math/logic and stores the result.

Registers are tiny, ultra-fast storage slots inside the CPU for the values in use right now. RAM is larger but slower. This is the memory hierarchy: registers → cache → RAM → disk, getting bigger and slower each step.

📝 EXAM WORDING

The “fetch-decode-execute cycle” is how a CPU processes instructions. The ALU does arithmetic/logic; the control unit directs traffic; registers hold operands. CPU speed is the clock rate (GHz).

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Don't mix up memory (RAM) — temporary, clears on power-off (volatile) — with storage (disk/SSD), which persists. Registers are inside the CPU; they are not RAM.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

The CPU runs the fetch–decode–execute cycle. The program counter (PC) holds the address of the NEXT instruction; the control unit directs, the ALU computes.

▸ QUICK CHECK

Each cycle: fetch the instruction at the PC → decode it → execute it → advance the PC.

Compiled vs. interpreted

A compiler translates the whole program to machine code BEFORE it runs (fast execution, errors surface up front); an interpreter translates and runs line by line (slower, more flexible). Java does both: source compiles to bytecode, and the JVM runs that.

Abstraction: hiding complexity

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Nobody could build an app if they had to think about individual transistors. Computing is built in layers, where each layer hides the messy details of the one below and offers a simpler interface. Big-O: how algorithms scale

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two programs can both be “correct” but one takes a second and the other a week on the same data. Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows as the input gets bigger — not the exact time, just the shape of the growth. It answers: “if I double the data, does the work double, quadruple, or barely change?”

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

O(1) constant: same work regardless of size. O(log n) logarithmic: halves the problem each step (binary search); barely grows. O(n) linear: work grows in step with data.

O(n log n): good sorting. O(n²) quadratic: nested loops; doubling input quadruples work. O(2ⁿ) exponential: explodes, usually impractical.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Big-O describes worst-case time (or space) complexity as n grows. Order best→worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ). Binary search is O(log n); a simple nested loop is O(n²).

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Big-O ignores constants and small terms — O(2n + 100) is just O(n). It's the growth trend for large inputs, not stopwatch time on small ones. Bigger-O = “scales worse,” not “slower right now.”

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Big-O describes how work grows with input size. Ranking best→worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ). Drop constants and lower-order terms.

▸ QUICK CHECK

A loop inside a loop, each over n, is O(n²). Halving the input each step (binary search) is O(log n).
