📖 Compression Techniques — Run-Length, Keyword & Huffman

Compression shrinks files. Lossless methods let you rebuild the original exactly (text, code, spreadsheets); lossy methods throw away detail people barely notice (JPEG photos, MP3 audio). Know the three named lossless techniques:

THE THREE LOSSLESS TECHNIQUES
• Run-length encoding (RLE): replace a repeated run of the same character with one copy + a count. Best when data has long runs.
• Keyword encoding: replace frequent whole words with short symbols (“the” → ~, “and” → +). A lookup table maps symbols back.
• Huffman coding: give frequent characters short bit codes and rare characters longer codes. Frequency-based, provably efficient.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — run-length encoding
AAAAABBBCC → 5A3B2C: 10 characters stored as 6. But on text with no runs (ABCABC), RLE saves nothing — technique must match the data.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Huffman by hand
Codes: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111 (A is most frequent, so shortest).
Encode “ABAD”: 0·10·0·111 → 0100111 = 7 bits, vs 32 bits in 8-bit ASCII.
Decode 010110: 0=A, 10=B, 110=C → “ABC.” No code is a prefix of another, so decoding is never ambiguous.
COMPRESSION RATIO
Ratio = compressed size ÷ original size. A 500 KB file compressed to 100 KB has ratio 100/500 = 0.2 (or “5:1”). Smaller ratio = better squeeze. Lossless ratios are limited by the data’s redundancy; lossy can go much smaller because it discards information permanently.
⚠️ MATCH TECHNIQUE TO CLUE WORDS
“Long runs of repeated characters” → RLE. “Common words replaced by symbols” → keyword encoding. “Most frequent characters get the shortest codes” → Huffman. “Opens identical to the original” → lossless; “some quality lost forever” → lossy.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Which technique assigns the SHORTEST bit patterns to the MOST frequent characters?
  1. Huffman coding
  2. Run-length encoding
  3. Lossy compression
Show answer
A — Huffman coding. It builds codes from character frequencies: common = short, rare = long.

Data representation: text, floats & media

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Binary integers are the easy case. But how does a computer store the letter 'A', the number 3.14, or a photo? The answer is always the same trick: agree on a code that maps the thing to a pattern of bits. Text uses a character-code table; decimals use a scientific-notation-in-binary scheme; images/sound are just huge grids of numbers.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Text: each character maps to a number via a table. ASCII uses 7–8 bits (128–256 characters, English + symbols); Unicode/UTF-8 extends this to every language and emoji. 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97, '0' the character is 48.

Floating point: decimals are stored like binary scientific notation — a sign, a mantissa (the digits), and an exponent (where the point goes). This is why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 — some decimals can't be represented exactly in binary.

Images/sound: an image is a grid of pixels, each a number for its color (RGB); sound is a stream of numbers sampling the wave. More bits = more detail = bigger files.

📝 EXAM WORDING

ASCII encodes characters in 7–8 bits; Unicode (often UTF-8) covers all languages. Floating-point numbers have a sign, mantissa, and exponent. Know that floats are approximate — rounding error is expected. Digital media is discrete samples of continuous signals.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

The character '5' is not the number 5 — '5' is ASCII 53. And floating-point numbers can't represent every decimal exactly, so never test floats with ==; compare within a small tolerance.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Everything is bits: text via ASCII/Unicode code points, numbers via integer/floating-point (IEEE 754), images as pixels, sound as samples.

▸ QUICK CHECK

If 'A' = 65 in ASCII, then 'C' = 67. More bits per sample/pixel = higher fidelity and larger files.

📖 Hash Tables & Recursion — two algorithm ideas that appear on the OA

HASH TABLES — jump straight to the data
A hash table stores key→value pairs. A hash function converts the key into an array index, so lookup is (on average) O(1) — no searching at all.
• Collision = two keys hash to the same index. It’s normal, and handled by chaining (keep a list at that slot) or probing (try the next open slot).
• A good hash function spreads keys evenly; a terrible one sends everything to one slot and lookups degrade toward O(n).
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — a tiny hash table
Table size 10; hash(key) = key mod 10. Insert 27 → slot 7. Insert 42 → slot 2. Insert 37 → slot 7 — collision with 27! With chaining, slot 7 holds a small list [27, 37]. Lookup of 37: hash to 7, scan the 2-item list. Still nearly instant.
RECURSION — a function that calls itself
Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of itself. Every correct recursive function needs:
1. A base case — the smallest input, answered directly (no call). This stops the recursion.
2. A recursive case — do a step, then call yourself on a smaller input.
Miss the base case (or never shrink the input) and you recurse forever → stack overflow.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — factorial, traced
factorial(n): if n ≤ 1 return 1 (base); else return n × factorial(n − 1).
factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) = 4 × 3 × factorial(2) = 4 × 3 × 2 × factorial(1) = 4×3×2×1 = 24.
Each call waits on the smaller one; the base case ends the chain and the answers multiply on the way back up.
⚠️ THE BASE CASE IS NOT OPTIONAL
“What is wrong with this recursive function?” — the answer is nearly always missing/unreachable base case (infinite recursion → stack overflow). And any recursion can be rewritten as a loop (iteration); recursion trades memory (the call stack) for elegance.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Two different keys hashing to the same table index is called:
  1. A collision
  2. An overflow
  3. A deadlock
Show answer
A — a collision. Handled by chaining (a list per slot) or probing (next free slot).

Searching & sorting algorithms

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two everyday jobs: find something in a list, and put a list in order. There are simple, slow ways and clever, fast ways. The exam wants you to know which is which and roughly how fast each is — this is where Big-O becomes concrete.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Linear search checks each item one by one — works on any list, O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves a SORTED list — O(log n), much faster, but only works if the data is already sorted.

Simple sorts (bubble, selection, insertion) are easy but O(n²) — fine for small lists. Efficient sorts (merge sort, quicksort) are O(n log n) — the go-to for large data. Merge sort splits, sorts halves, and merges; quicksort partitions around a pivot.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Linear search = O(n), works unsorted; binary search = O(log n), requires a sorted list. Bubble/selection/insertion sort = O(n²); merge sort and quicksort = O(n log n). “Which sort is fastest for large data?” → the O(n log n) ones.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Binary search ONLY works on sorted data — that's the #1 trap. And a sort being “simple” (bubble sort) does not make it efficient; simple usually means O(n²).

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Linear search O(n) works on any list; binary search O(log n) requires a SORTED list. Sorts: bubble/selection/insertion O(n²); merge sort O(n log n).

▸ QUICK CHECK

Binary search on 1000 sorted items needs ≈ 10 comparisons (log₂ 1000 ≈ 10), vs up to 1000 for linear search.

📖 The Network MODELS — OSI (7 layers) & TCP/IP (4 layers)

Exams love these. A network model is a layered blueprint of how data travels: each layer does ONE job and hands the data to the next layer. Two models to know: the 7-layer OSI model (the theory) and the 4-layer TCP/IP model (what the real Internet uses).

THE OSI MODEL — 7 layers, top to bottom
#LayerJob (plain words)Examples
7ApplicationWhat the user’s program seesHTTP, email
6PresentationFormat/translate data (encryption, compression)SSL, JPEG
5SessionOpen/manage/close conversationslogins, sessions
4TransportDeliver reliably end-to-end, in orderTCP, UDP
3NetworkRoute packets between networks (addresses)IP, routers
2Data LinkMove frames on one local linkEthernet, MAC, switches
1PhysicalRaw bits on the wire/aircables, radio, hubs
Memory hook (bottom-up): Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
THE TCP/IP MODEL — 4 layers (the practical one)
TCP/IP layerCovers OSI layersKey players
Application7, 6, 5HTTP, DNS, email (SMTP)
Transport4TCP (reliable), UDP (fast)
Internet3IP addresses, routing
Network Interface (Link)2, 1Ethernet, Wi-Fi, MAC
Same ideas, fewer boxes. When a question says “the TCP/IP suite,” think this 4-layer stack.
WORKED EXAMPLE — follow one web request down the stack
You load a page: the browser makes an HTTP request (Application) → TCP breaks it into ordered, tracked segments (Transport) → IP addresses each packet to the server and routers pick the path (Internet/Network) → Ethernet/Wi-Fi turns packets into frames and bits on your local link (Link/Physical). At the server, the layers unwrap in reverse.
TCP vs UDP (the transport-layer choice)
• TCP: connection-based, reliable — every packet acknowledged, lost ones resent, order guaranteed. Use for web pages, email, files.
• UDP: connectionless, fast but best-effort — no resends, no ordering. Use for live video, gaming, voice calls, where a late packet is worse than a lost one.
MAC ADDRESS vs IP ADDRESS
• MAC address = the hardware ID burned into a network card (like a serial number). Works at the Data Link layer, only on the local network. Format: six hex pairs, e.g. 3C:2A:F4:1B:9E:07.
• IP address = the logical, changeable address used to route between networks (Network/Internet layer), e.g. 192.168.1.10.
Analogy: MAC = your fingerprint (permanent, identifies the device); IP = your mailing address (changes when you move networks).
⚠️ MATCH THE JOB TO THE LAYER
Routing/IP → Network (Internet) layer. Reliability/ordering → Transport (TCP). MAC/frames/switches → Data Link. Cables and radio → Physical. If a question asks “which layer…,” find the job word (route, deliver reliably, frame, transmit bits) and map it.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Which layer of the TCP/IP model is responsible for reliable, in-order delivery?
  1. Transport (TCP)
  2. Internet (IP)
  3. Network Interface
Show answer
A — Transport. TCP acknowledges, resends, and orders packets. IP just routes; the link layer just moves frames locally.

Networking & the internet

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The internet is just an enormous number of computers passing messages. To make that work, every machine needs an address, messages get broken into labeled chunks, and everyone agrees on rules (protocols) for how to talk. Most of it follows a “client asks, server answers” pattern.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

IP address = a computer's numeric address. DNS is the phonebook that turns a name (google.com) into an IP. Data travels in packets — small labeled chunks reassembled at the destination.

Protocols are agreed rules: HTTP/HTTPS for web pages, TCP/IP for reliable delivery, DNS for name lookup. The client–server model: your browser (client) requests, a server responds.

📝 EXAM WORDING

IP address identifies a device; DNS maps names → IP addresses; data moves in packets. HTTP/HTTPS = web, TCP = reliable transport. The client–server model = requester and responder. HTTPS adds encryption.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

DNS resolves names to addresses — it is not where the webpage lives. And a URL, a domain name, and an IP address are three different things that point at the same destination.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Data travels the Internet in packets, routed by shared protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP). An IP address identifies a device; DNS maps names to IPs.

▸ QUICK CHECK

Typing a URL: DNS translates the domain name → IP address, then packets route to that address and reassemble.

📖 The SDLC Process MODELS — Waterfall, Agile, Iterative, Spiral, Prototyping

Knowing the SDLC steps isn’t enough — exams also ask about the models: different strategies for moving through those steps. Each model answers “how do we organize the work?” differently.

THE FIVE MODELS TO KNOW
ModelHow it worksBest whenWeakness
WaterfallFinish each phase completely, then flow down to the next — no going backRequirements are fixed & well understoodRigid; errors found late are costly
AgileShort cycles (sprints, ~2 weeks) each delivering working software; constant customer feedbackRequirements change oftenLess predictable schedule/docs
Iterative/IncrementalBuild a small working version, then repeatedly improve and add piecesYou want usable software earlyArchitecture may need rework
SpiralLoops of plan → assess risk → build → evaluate; each loop grows the productLarge, high-risk projectsComplex and costly to manage
PrototypingBuild a quick throwaway mock-up to nail down requirements before real developmentUsers aren’t sure what they wantPrototype may get mistaken for the product
WORKED EXAMPLE — pick the model from the scenario
• “A government contract with fully specified, unchanging requirements and formal sign-offs at each phase” → Waterfall.
• “A startup wants to ship features every two weeks and adjust to user feedback” → Agile (sprints, stand-ups, Scrum).
• “A huge banking system where failure is catastrophic; managers demand explicit risk analysis every cycle” → Spiral (its signature = risk assessment each loop).
• “Users can’t articulate what they need, so the team mocks up screens to explore” → Prototyping.
AGILE VOCABULARY (Scrum terms)
• Sprint: a short fixed-length work cycle (usually 1–4 weeks) ending in working software.
• Scrum: the most popular Agile framework — daily stand-up meetings, a product backlog of features, a Scrum Master who clears blockers.
• User story: a requirement written from the user’s view (“As a student, I want…”).
TESTING TYPES (the other exam favorite)
• Unit testing — test one small piece (a single function/module) in isolation. First and lowest level.
• Integration testing — test that modules work together (interfaces between units).
• System testing — test the complete assembled system against requirements.
• Acceptance testing — the customer/user verifies the software meets their needs (last gate before release).
• Black-box testing — tester sees only inputs and outputs, not the code (tests behavior/spec).
• White-box testing — tester sees the code and exercises specific paths/branches inside it.
• Regression testing — re-run old tests after a change to be sure nothing that used to work broke.
⚠️ THE TWO MOST-MISSED DISTINCTIONS
1) Waterfall vs Agile: waterfall = one pass, no revisiting; agile = many short cycles with feedback. If the scenario mentions changing requirements or sprints, it’s Agile.
2) Black vs white box: the color says what the tester can SEE. Black = can’t see inside (spec-based); white = can see the code (path-based). Unit tests are usually white-box; acceptance tests are black-box.
🎯 QUICK CHECK
Which SDLC model is defined by explicit risk analysis on every loop?
  1. Spiral
  2. Waterfall
  3. Prototyping
Show answer
A — Spiral. Its four repeating quadrants are plan, analyze risk, build, evaluate. Risk analysis every cycle is its fingerprint.

The software development lifecycle

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Software isn't just “sit down and code.” Teams follow a lifecycle so they build the right thing without chaos: figure out what's needed, design it, build it, test it, ship it, and maintain it. Different methodologies (Waterfall, Agile) sequence these stages differently.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Typical SDLC phases: requirements (what to build) → design (plan the logic) → implementation (code it) → testing (verify) → deployment (release) → maintenance (fix & improve).

📝 EXAM WORDING

The SDLC phases: requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance. Waterfall is sequential; Agile is iterative/incremental (sprints, adapting to change). “Plan the logic” = design; “code the program” = implementation.

The SDLC runs in order: requirements/analysis → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance. Each phase feeds the next.

Programming paradigms

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

There's more than one philosophy for structuring code. Some styles give step-by-step commands; some organize around objects; some describe WHAT you want rather than HOW. Knowing the paradigms helps you recognize why languages feel different.

⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Procedural (imperative): step-by-step instructions and procedures/functions (C). Object-oriented: organize around objects bundling data + behavior (Java). Functional: build programs from pure functions, avoiding shared state (Scheme, Haskell).

Declarative: describe the desired result, not the steps (SQL, HTML). The same problem can be solved in multiple paradigms; many modern languages mix them.

📝 EXAM WORDING

Procedural/imperative = step-by-step commands; object-oriented = objects with data + methods; functional = pure functions, no side effects; declarative = describe WHAT, not HOW (SQL is the classic example). Scheme is a common example of a declarative/functional language.

⚠️ WATCH OUT

Declarative (SQL: “give me these rows”) vs imperative (“loop and check each row”) is the key contrast the exam draws. Java is object-oriented but also imperative under the hood.

★ ON THE OA — WATCH FOR

Major paradigms: procedural (steps/functions), object-oriented (objects + classes), functional (pure functions, no side effects), declarative (describe the what, e.g., SQL).

▸ QUICK CHECK

Java/C++ lean object-oriented; SQL is declarative; Haskell is functional. Many languages are multi-paradigm.

Encapsulation — an object bundles its data with the methods that use it and hides the internals behind a public interface — is a defining trait of the object-oriented paradigm.

LAN vs WANLocal (one site) vs wide (spans cities/the internet)
Router vs switchRouter connects NETWORKS; switch connects devices WITHIN one
DNSResolves names → IP addresses (it doesn't host pages)
HTTPS= HTTP + encryption
⚠️ THE ROUTER/SWITCH DISTINCTION
It's the most-missed device question: switches work inside one network; routers join different networks together. The full reference follows, nothing removed.

Section 5 Cheat Sheet — Computer Architecture & Networking

Lessons 1.1–3.1: CPU/motherboard, disk geometry, device types, and the big networking glossary.

① CPU & computing components

TermMeaning
CPUThe "brain" — executes instructions and processes data.
ALUArithmetic Logic Unit — does arithmetic + logic operations.
Control unitDirects operations and coordinates components.
RegisterSmall, very fast CPU storage for temporary data.
Instruction registerHolds the current instruction being executed.
Program counterHolds the address of the next instruction.
Cache memorySmall, fast, volatile memory for frequently used data.
Bus widthBits transferred at once — wider = more data per cycle.
PipeliningOverlaps instruction phases to boost performance.
AddressabilityNumber of bits stored at each addressable location in memory.
MotherboardMain board housing CPU, memory, and core components.
⚠ CLASSIC TRAP
Instruction register = the instruction running now. Program counter = the address of the next instruction. Don't mix them up.

② Disk geometry & timing

TermMeaning
TrackA circular path on a platter where data is stored.
SectorThe smallest unit of disk storage.
BlockA fixed-size unit of data stored/transferred.
CylinderThe same-position tracks stacked across all platters.
LatencyThe delay before data transfer starts.
Access timeTime to retrieve data from memory/storage.
Transfer rateSpeed at which data moves (bps).
⚠ TRAP
Latency = the wait before transfer begins. Transfer rate = how fast data then moves. They are not the same.

③ Device types

DeviceBest for
ServerProvides resources/services to clients over a network.
Desktop / laptopStationary personal PC / portable personal PC.
Tablet / smartphoneLarger touchscreen for media/reading / phone + apps + internet.
MainframeLarge-scale transaction processing (banks, government).
SupercomputerMassive scientific calculations & simulations.
Server farmMany servers together for huge scale (Google, AWS).
Multicore processor2+ cores → run multiple tasks at once.
GPUGraphics + parallel processing (3D, machine learning).
Embedded computerBuilt into a device to control it (car, microwave).
IoTEveryday devices connected to the internet to share data (smart thermostat).

④ Networking — reach, models & topologies

TermMeaning
Computer networkDevices linked to communicate and share resources.
BandwidthMax capacity of a path — like lanes on a highway.
Data transfer rateHow fast data actually moves (bps).
ProtocolRules for how data is formatted/transmitted (HTTP, TCP/IP).
Client/server vs P2PCentral server serves clients vs peers act as both client and server.
LAN / MAN / WANBuilding/campus → city → country+ (the internet is the biggest WAN).
TopologyLayoutWeak point
StarAll connect to a central hub/switchHub failure
RingCircular chainOne link break stops the loop
BusAll on one cableCable break disrupts all

⑤ Network devices & connections

TermMeaning
GatewayConnects two different networks and translates protocols.
RouterDirects packets between networks along the best path.
RepeaterAmplifies a signal to extend distance.
BluetoothShort-range wireless for peripherals.
Internet backbone / ISPHigh-speed core carrying long-distance traffic / your internet provider.
Phone modemConverts digital ⇄ analog for phone lines (dial-up).
DSLHigh-speed internet over phone lines — voice + data at the same time.
Cable modem / broadbandInternet over cable-TV lines / high-speed, always-on connection.
Download vs uploadReceive from a server vs send to a server.

⑥ Packets & protocols

TermMeaning
Packet / packet switchingSmall data unit with routing info / packets take multiple paths, reassembled at the end.
Proprietary vs open systemVendor-controlled (Apple iOS) vs public standards (Linux).
InteroperabilityDifferent systems working together seamlessly.
OSI reference modelOrganizes networking into 7 layers; aids troubleshooting.
Ethernet / protocol stackWired LAN standard / layered set of protocols working together (TCP/IP).
TCPReliable, ordered, error-checked delivery.
IP / TCP/IPAddressing + routing of packets / the suite powering the internet.
UDPFast, connectionless, less reliable — gaming, streaming.
Ping / tracerouteTests reachability + round-trip time / shows each hop along the path.
Port / MIME typeVirtual endpoint for a service (HTTP = 80) / file format label (text/html).
Firewall / access control policyFilters traffic by security rules / rules for who can access what.

High-level protocols: SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer), HTTP (web), Telnet.

⚠ TCP vs UDP TRAP
TCP = reliable + ordered (files, web). UDP = fast + connectionless, may drop packets (live video, gaming). Pick UDP when speed beats reliability.

⑦ Naming & DNS

TermMeaning
HostnameHuman-readable device name. It's the part before the first dot — in jenkins.develocorp.org the hostname is jenkins.
IP addressNumeric device label for routing (192.168.1.10).
Domain nameHuman-readable web address (www.example.com).
Top-Level Domain (TLD)The last segment: .com, .org, .edu.
ICANNGlobally manages domain names + IP allocation.
Domain squattingRegistering domains (often trademarks) to resell for profit.
DNS / domain name serverTranslates a domain → IP / the server that answers DNS queries.
Network neutralityISPs must treat all traffic equally (no throttling/favoring).
✓ SECTION 5 MUST-KNOWS
  • Instruction register = current instruction; program counter = next address.
  • Latency = delay before transfer; transfer rate = speed of transfer. Sector = smallest disk unit.
  • Topology weak points: star → hub, ring → one link, bus → the cable.
  • Gateway translates between networks; router picks the best path; repeater amplifies.
  • TCP = reliable/ordered; UDP = fast/connectionless (gaming, streaming). HTTP = port 80.
  • Hostname = before the first dot. DNS converts domain → IP; ICANN governs domains + IPs.

⑧ Input / output devices & touch screens

Input = data in (keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic, camera). Output = results out (monitor, printer, speakers). Both = touch screen, storage, network card.

Touch screenDetects byGloves?
Resistivepressure — two layers touchYes
Capacitivechange in electrical charge (needs conductive skin)No
SAW (surface acoustic wave)interruption of high-frequency sound wavesYes
Infraredbreaking a grid of light beamsYes

Only capacitive fails with an ordinary glove — it is the one that needs the touch to conduct electricity. Capacitive also gives multi-touch, which is why phones use it.

THE TWO-WEEK PLAN

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Intro to Computer Science (D684) OA is a multiple-choice objective assessment, and you only need to reach "Competent" to pass — roughly 70% of the questions. It is pass/fail (no letter grade), you can retake it if needed, and you can flag questions and come back. Knowing how the exam works, and studying the way memory actually works, removes most of the fear.

How the objective assessment works

  • Format: a set of multiple-choice questions in a proctored, locked-down browser. Each has one best answer (a few may say "select all that apply" — read carefully).
  • To pass: reach the "Competent" cut (about 70%+). Aim higher in practice so test-day nerves still leave you a cushion.
  • No guessing penalty: a blank and a wrong answer score the same — so never leave a question blank. Always lock in your best guess.
  • You can flag & return: if a question is eating time, mark it, move on, and circle back with a fresh head.
  • Retakes exist: if you don’t pass, you get feedback on weak areas and can retake after a short waiting period. One exam is not your only shot.

The five study techniques that actually work

Decades of learning research keep pointing to the same handful of methods. They feel harder than rereading — and that "desirable difficulty" is exactly why they work.

TechniqueWhat to do
Active recallClose the notes and retrieve the answer from memory. Use this app’s quizzes and flashcards instead of rereading — testing yourself is the single most powerful technique there is.
Spaced repetitionReview a topic today, in two days, then in a week. Short sessions spread over time beat one long cram by a wide margin.
InterleavingMix topics in a session rather than drilling one to death. The mixed/interleaved quiz mode forces you to pick the right approach — which is what the exam demands.
Practice testingTake the full exam simulator under timed, no-notes conditions. Each attempt is both practice and a diagnostic of what to fix next.
Teach it back (Feynman)Explain a concept out loud in plain words, as if teaching a friend. Where you get stuck is exactly what you don’t truly understand yet.
▲ A SIMPLE 2-WEEK PLAN

Week 1 — Learn & recall: read each lesson once, then immediately quiz that section. End each day with a short mixed quiz over everything so far.
Week 2 — Simulate & patch: take the full exam simulator, note the topics you miss, and spend your time only on those. Re-simulate every couple of days until you’re comfortably above the pass line.

Exam-day tactics for multiple choice

  • Read every word. Watch for NOT, EXCEPT, ALWAYS, NEVER — they flip the meaning of a question.
  • Eliminate first. Cross out the obviously wrong options; even cutting two turns a hard question into a coin flip in your favor.
  • Predict before you peek. Try to answer in your head before reading the choices, so a tempting-but-wrong option can’t anchor you.
  • Trust your first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to change it — second-guessing flips more right answers to wrong than the reverse.
  • Watch the clock. Budget about a minute per question; flag anything slower and return to it.
  • Answer everything. With no penalty for wrong answers, an educated guess always beats a blank.

Calm nerves, clear head

Some adrenaline is normal and even helpful. If it tips into panic, slow your breathing — in for four counts, hold four, out for four — for a few cycles to reset your body. Reframe the moment: this is a checkpoint, not a verdict on you, and you can retake it. Sleep the night before matters more than one more hour of cramming; a rested brain recalls far better than a tired one. Eat something, arrive early, and remember how much you’ve already prepared.

✓ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • You need ~70% ("Competent") to pass; it’s pass/fail and retakeable.
  • Never leave a blank — there’s no penalty for guessing.
  • Quiz yourself (active recall) and space it out; don’t just reread.
  • Take the exam simulator until you’re comfortably above the pass line.
  • On test day: read carefully, eliminate, answer everything, breathe.

What is the flaw?","options":["The function runs twice","The computed result is discarded when the function ends","The program will not compile under any circumstance","The total becomes global automatically"],"correct":1,"explain":"Locals die when the call ends, so a result must be returned (or stored somewhere shared) to survive. This is the practical consequence of variable lifetime."},{"id":"dp_22_4","topic":"Recursion","text":"A recursive function is missing a base case. What is the MOST likely outcome?","options":["The compiler rejects it before the program runs","It recurses until the call stack overflows and crashes","It returns the default value for its return type","It executes its body once and then returns"],"correct":1,"explain":"Every call adds a stack frame. With no terminating condition the frames pile up until memory runs out. \"Stack overflow from recursion\" means \"check the base case.\""},{"id":"dp_22_5","topic":"Recursion vs iteration","text":"When is an ITERATIVE solution generally preferred over a recursive one?","options":["When the language supports functions","When the depth could be large","Whenever the problem involves numbers","Recursion is always better"],"correct":1,"explain":"Recursion is elegant for naturally nested problems (trees, divide-and-conquer), but deep recursion risks stack overflow and adds call overhead. Loops keep memory flat. Each recursive call consumes stack memory."},{"id":"dp_22_6","topic":"Side effects","text":"Why is a function that only uses its parameters and returns a value easier to test than one that modifies global state?","options":["Globals cannot be tested at all","Its output depends solely on its inputs","It executes faster","It needs no parameters"],"correct":1,"explain":"Hidden dependencies on global state make results depend on execution order. Self-contained functions can be tested in any order with predictable results. A test is fully repeatable."},{"id":"dp_31_1","topic":"Class vs object","text":"A program defines Car once and creates 200 Car values. What is Car, and what are the 200?","options":["Car is an object; the 200 are classes","Both are classes","Both are objects","Car is the class (blueprint); the 200 are objects (instances)"],"correct":3,"explain":"The class defines structure and behavior once; each object is a separate instance with its own data. One blueprint, many houses."},{"id":"dp_31_2","topic":"Encapsulation","text":"A class stores temperature internally in Celsius but exposes only getFahrenheit(). Later the team switches internal storage to Kelvin. What happens to calling code?","options":["It must all be rewritten","It breaks at compile time","The class can no longer be used","Nothing"],"correct":3,"explain":"That protection IS encapsulation: the public interface is a contract, the internals are free to change. This is the practical reason for private fields and public methods. The internal change is hidden behind the public method."},{"id":"dp_31_3","topic":"Inheritance vs composition","text":"A Car needs an Engine. Which relationship is correct?","options":["Inheritance — a Car IS-A Engine","Either is equally correct","Neither; use a global","Composition — a Car HAS-A Engine"],"correct":3,"explain":"Inheritance models IS-A (a Car is a Vehicle); composition models HAS-A (a Car has an Engine). Choosing inheritance for a HAS-A relationship produces nonsense hierarchies — a favorite exam trap."},{"id":"dp_31_4","topic":"Polymorphism","text":"Shape defines draw(), and Circle and Square each override it. Code loops over a list of Shapes calling draw(). What happens?","options":["Only Shape's version runs","A type error occurs","Only the first object is drawn","Each object runs its own version of draw()"],"correct":3,"explain":"That is polymorphism: one call site, behavior chosen by the object's actual type. It lets you add a new shape without touching the loop."},{"id":"dp_31_5","topic":"Encapsulation","text":"Why expose a private field through a setter instead of making the field public?","options":["Public fields are not allowed in any language","It halves memory usage","The setter can validate input before storing it","Setters run faster"],"correct":2,"explain":"A public field accepts anything, including an age of −5. A setter is a gate where you enforce the rules that keep an object in a valid state."},{"id":"dp_31_6","topic":"Abstraction","text":"A driver operates a car without knowing how fuel injection works. Which OOP principle does this illustrate?","options":["Polymorphism","Recursion","Abstraction","Inheritance"],"correct":2,"explain":"Abstraction is the modeling decision about WHAT to expose; encapsulation is the enforcement that keeps the internals private. The steering wheel is the abstraction. The interface exposes what matters and hides the mechanism."}],"D684/depth_drill/g2":[{"id":"dp_ct_1","topic":"Decomposition","text":"A team must build an online store and starts by splitting it into catalog, cart, payment and shipping modules. Which computational-thinking pillar is this?","options":["Algorithm design","Decomposition","Pattern recognition","Abstraction"],"correct":1,"explain":"Decomposition breaks one overwhelming problem into parts that can be understood, assigned and tested separately. It is normally the FIRST move on a large problem."},{"id":"dp_ct_2","topic":"Pattern recognition","text":"An analyst notices that catalog, cart and shipping all need \"look up a record by ID, then format it for display.\" Recognizing this repetition is:","options":["Decomposition","Abstraction","Debugging","Pattern recognition"],"correct":3,"explain":"Spotting repeated structure is what lets you write one reusable routine instead of three near-identical ones — it is the step that turns decomposition into economical design."},{"id":"dp_ct_3","topic":"Abstraction","text":"A subway map shows station order and connections but not real distances or street layout. This is an example of:","options":["A syntax error","Abstraction","Decomposition","An algorithm"],"correct":1,"explain":"Abstraction keeps what matters for the task (which stops connect) and discards what does not (geography). The classic exam illustration of the idea. Irrelevant detail is deliberately removed."},{"id":"dp_ct_4","topic":"Algorithm design","text":"After decomposing and spotting patterns, the team writes exact ordered steps for checkout. Which pillar is this?","options":["Abstraction","Pattern recognition","Decomposition","Algorithm design"],"correct":3,"explain":"Algorithm design produces the unambiguous, ordered, finite steps that solve the problem — the stage where a plan becomes implementable."},{"id":"dp_ct_5","topic":"Applying the pillars","text":"What distinguishes ABSTRACTION from DECOMPOSITION?","options":["Decomposition applies only to hardware","Decomposition splits a problem into parts; abstraction removes detail that does not matter","They are two names for the same activity","Abstraction splits code into functions; decomposition hides data"],"correct":1,"explain":"Decomposition is about STRUCTURE (dividing), abstraction is about DETAIL (simplifying). Exam questions distinguish them by asking which activity is described."},{"id":"dp_ct_6","topic":"Problem solving","text":"A requirement reads \"the system should be fast.\" Why is this unusable as written?","options":["It is too technical for stakeholders","Speed cannot be improved in software","Requirements never mention performance","It is not measurable"],"correct":3,"explain":"Good requirements are specific and testable — \"search returns within 2 seconds for 10,000 records.\" Vague requirements are the root of disputes at delivery time. No one can verify whether it was met."},{"id":"dp_sd_1","topic":"Cost of change","text":"A misunderstood requirement is discovered AFTER deployment rather than during requirements gathering. What is the impact?","options":["Cost is the same at any phase","It is cheaper because the system already exists","It affects only documentation","Cost to fix is dramatically higher"],"correct":3,"explain":"Fix cost rises sharply the later a defect is caught, because everything built on the wrong assumption must also change. This is the standard argument for investing in requirements and reviews. The error is baked into design, code and tests."},{"id":"dp_sd_2","topic":"Choosing a model","text":"A client expects requirements to evolve and wants working software every few weeks. Which approach fits BEST?","options":["Waterfall with a longer requirements phase","Agile — short iterations that welcome changing requirements","Waterfall — full requirements locked before design","No methodology at all"],"correct":1,"explain":"Waterfall suits stable, well-understood requirements (often regulated work). Agile suits uncertainty and frequent feedback. The exam gives you a scenario and expects you to match it."},{"id":"dp_sd_3","topic":"Phase order","text":"Which sequence reflects the standard SDLC?","options":["Design → planning → coding → analysis → testing","Implementation → testing → planning → design","Analysis → testing → design → implementation","Planning → analysis → design → implementation → testing → maintenance"],"correct":3,"explain":"You decide WHETHER to build (planning), WHAT to build (analysis), HOW (design), build it, verify it, then support it. Order questions are common — learn the chain."},{"id":"dp_sd_4","topic":"Maintenance","text":"Across a typical system's full lifetime, which phase usually consumes the MOST total effort?","options":["Planning","Maintenance","Implementation","Requirements analysis"],"correct":1,"explain":"Systems live for years and accumulate fixes, enhancements and adaptations. Maintenance commonly dominates lifetime cost — which is why readable, well-structured code pays off."},{"id":"dp_sd_5","topic":"Testing","text":"A team writes code first and only then decides how it will be verified. What is the main risk?","options":["The code will not compile","Nothing — this is standard practice","Requirements may be untestable, and defects surface late when they cost most","Testing is unnecessary if code is written carefully"],"correct":2,"explain":"Deriving test criteria from requirements EARLY exposes vague requirements before code exists and shortens the feedback loop."},{"id":"dp_sd_6","topic":"Analysis vs design","text":"What separates the ANALYSIS phase from the DESIGN phase?","options":["They are the same phase","Design happens before analysis","Analysis defines WHAT the system must do; design defines HOW it will do it","Analysis writes code; design tests it"],"correct":2,"explain":"Analysis produces requirements (the problem); design produces architecture, data models and interfaces (the solution shape). Mixing them leads to solutions in search of a problem."},{"id":"dp_et_1","topic":"Public welfare","text":"An engineer finds a defect that could injure users, but the manager wants to ship on schedule. What does the ACM/IEEE code direct?","options":["Ship it and document the risk privately","Resign immediately without reporting","Prioritize public safety","Defer to the manager because they hold authority"],"correct":2,"explain":"\"Hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public\" is the first principle in professional computing codes — it outranks schedule and employer preference. Escalate the concern rather than stay silent."},{"id":"dp_et_2","topic":"Privacy","text":"Customer data was collected for order fulfillment. Marketing wants to sell it to a third party. What is the ethical issue?","options":["It is acceptable if it is profitable","It is fine as long as it is legal in one state","Using data beyond the purpose the user consented to violates privacy principles","No issue — the company owns all data it stores"],"correct":2,"explain":"Consent is purpose-bound. Repurposing data without informed consent breaches privacy obligations regardless of who stores it — and legality is a floor, not the ethical standard."},{"id":"dp_et_3","topic":"Competence","text":"A developer is offered a safety-critical medical project far outside their expertise. The professional response is to:","options":["Accept and outsource it secretly","Always refuse any unfamiliar work","Accept only with appropriate training, supervision, or disclosure of the limitation","Accept quietly and learn as they go"],"correct":2,"explain":"Codes of ethics require accepting work only within your competence — honest disclosure and getting proper support is the professional path, not bluffing."},{"id":"dp_et_4","topic":"Conflict of interest","text":"An engineer evaluating vendor bids holds a financial stake in one bidder. What must they do?","options":["Sell the stake after awarding the contract","Award to a different vendor to look neutral","Disclose the interest and step back from the decision","Say nothing if they believe they can stay objective"],"correct":2,"explain":"The obligation is disclosure and recusal. Perceived conflicts damage trust even when the judgment happens to be sound."},{"id":"dp_et_5","topic":"Intellectual property","text":"A developer copies a large block of GPL-licensed code into proprietary closed-source software. What is the problem?","options":["Open-source code has no conditions attached","It is fine if the comments are removed","The license terms are legally binding and this likely violates them","Anything on the internet is public domain"],"correct":2,"explain":"Open source is licensed, not unowned. Copyleft licenses like the GPL attach obligations to redistribution — respecting them is both a legal and an ethical duty."},{"id":"dp_et_6","topic":"Honesty","text":"A status report is due and a module is 40% done. The lead reports it as \"nearly complete\" to avoid a difficult conversation. This primarily violates:","options":["Only company policy, not ethics","The duty to maintain competence","The duty to be honest and realistic in stating claims about work","Nothing — estimates are always approximate"],"correct":2,"explain":"Professional codes require honest, realistic reporting. Optimistic status hides risk until it is too late to manage — a well-documented cause of project failure."}],"D684/depth_drill/g3":[{"id":"dp_al_1","topic":"Binary search","text":"A developer runs binary search on an UNSORTED array. What is the result?","options":["It works but more slowly","It sorts the array first automatically","It always returns the first element","Results are unreliable"],"correct":3,"explain":"Binary search discards half the data based on a comparison, which is only valid if the data is ordered. The precondition is the whole point of the algorithm. Binary search requires sorted data."},{"id":"dp_al_2","topic":"Complexity","text":"Binary search on 1,000,000 sorted items needs roughly how many comparisons in the worst case?","options":["About 1,000,000","About 20","About 1,000","About 500,000"],"correct":1,"explain":"Each comparison halves the search space, so the count is log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20. Contrast with linear search's 1,000,000 — this gap is why sorted data matters."},{"id":"dp_al_3","topic":"Choosing an algorithm","text":"A list of 12 items is searched once, and the data is unsorted. Which approach is most sensible?","options":["Sort it, then binary search","Build a hash table first","Merge sort, then linear search","Linear search"],"correct":3,"explain":"Algorithm choice depends on size and how often you search. Sorting is an investment that pays off across MANY searches; for one pass over 12 items, just scan. Sorting first would cost more than it saves."},{"id":"dp_al_4","topic":"Complexity","text":"Bubble sort on n items is O(n²). What does that mean practically when n grows from 100 to 1,000?","options":["Work grows roughly 20-fold, as 2n","Work grows roughly 100-fold, not 10-fold","Work grows roughly 10-fold, in step with n","Work grows roughly 1,000-fold, as n cubed"],"correct":1,"explain":"Squaring the growth factor: (1000/100)² = 100. Big-O describes how cost SCALES, which is why O(n²) algorithms collapse on large inputs."},{"id":"dp_al_5","topic":"Trade-offs","text":"Merge sort runs in O(n log n) but needs extra memory proportional to n. What does this illustrate?","options":["That merge sort is always the wrong choice","That memory use never matters","That O(n log n) is slower than O(n²)","A space"],"correct":3,"explain":"Space–time trade-offs recur across computing (caching, indexes, lookup tables). Exams describe a constraint — limited memory, huge data — and ask you to pick accordingly. Time trade-off — buying speed with memory."},{"id":"dp_al_6","topic":"Algorithm properties","text":"Which property must EVERY algorithm have?","options":["It runs in under one second","It terminates after a finite number of well-defined steps","It is written in a specific language","It uses recursion"],"correct":1,"explain":"An algorithm is finite, unambiguous, and produces output from its input. Language and speed are implementation concerns, not part of the definition."},{"id":"dp_ps_1","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET x TO 10 / SET y TO x MOD 3 / OUTPUT y — what is printed?","options":["0","1","3","3.33"],"correct":1,"explain":"10 = 3·3 + 1, so the remainder is 1. Trace pseudocode line by line, writing each variable's value down — do not try to hold it in your head."},{"id":"dp_ps_2","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET total TO 0 / FOR i FROM 1 TO 5 / SET total TO total + i / END FOR / OUTPUT total — what is printed?","options":["5","10","120","15"],"correct":3,"explain":"The accumulator adds 1+2+3+4+5 = 15. Note the pattern: total must be initialized OUTSIDE the loop, or it resets every pass."},{"id":"dp_ps_3","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET a TO 4 / SET b TO 9 / SET temp TO a / SET a TO b / SET b TO temp / OUTPUT a, b — what is printed?","options":["4, 4","9, 4","4, 9","9, 9"],"correct":1,"explain":"The classic three-step swap. Without temp, the first assignment would overwrite a and both variables would end up 9 — a favorite trace question."},{"id":"dp_ps_4","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET count TO 0 / FOR i FROM 1 TO 3 / FOR j FROM 1 TO 2 / SET count TO count + 1 / END FOR / END FOR / OUTPUT count","options":["5","3","2","6"],"correct":3,"explain":"Nested loops multiply: 3 × 2 = 6 executions of the increment. Same reasoning as the O(n²) growth of two nested loops."},{"id":"dp_ps_5","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET score TO 85 / IF score >= 90 THEN OUTPUT \"A\" ELSE IF score >= 80 THEN OUTPUT \"B\" ELSE OUTPUT \"C\" — what is printed?","options":["B","A","C","Nothing"],"correct":0,"explain":"Conditions are tested top to bottom and the FIRST true branch wins. 85 fails >= 90, satisfies >= 80, so \"B\" prints and the rest is skipped."},{"id":"dp_ps_6","topic":"Tracing","text":"SET n TO 7 / SET half TO n / 2 (integer division) / OUTPUT half — what is printed?","options":["3","3.5","4","7"],"correct":0,"explain":"Integer division truncates toward zero, so 7 / 2 is 3. Pseudocode on the OA usually assumes integer arithmetic unless it says otherwise."},{"id":"dp_pr_1","topic":"Error types","text":"A program compiles and runs but computes the wrong average. What KIND of error is this?","options":["A syntax error","A compile-time error","A hardware failure","A logic error"],"correct":3,"explain":"Syntax errors stop compilation; runtime errors crash execution; LOGIC errors run fine and produce wrong output. Logic errors are hardest because nothing announces them."},{"id":"dp_pr_2","topic":"Error types","text":"A program crashes partway through with \"divide by zero.\" This is a:","options":["Syntax error","Logic error only","Linker error","Runtime error"],"correct":3,"explain":"The code was valid enough to run; the failure depended on the DATA encountered. Guarding with a condition before dividing prevents it."},{"id":"dp_pr_3","topic":"Compiler vs interpreter","text":"Which statement correctly contrasts a compiler with an interpreter?","options":["A compiler runs code line by line","An interpreter produces a standalone executable","They are identical","A compiler translates the whole program before execution; an interpreter translates and runs statement by statement"],"correct":3,"explain":"Compiled programs generally run faster and surface many errors up front; interpreted ones start immediately and are easier to test interactively. Java does both: source → bytecode → JVM."},{"id":"dp_pr_4","topic":"Debugging","text":"What is the most reliable FIRST step when debugging a reported defect?","options":["Rewrite the module from scratch","Add try/catch blocks everywhere","Ask users to avoid that feature","Reproduce the failure consistently"],"correct":3,"explain":"If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot confirm a fix. Reproduce, narrow down the smallest failing case, then correct the cause — not the symptom."},{"id":"dp_pr_5","topic":"Tools","text":"What does an IDE primarily provide over a plain text editor?","options":["A runtime that executes bytecode on any platform","A guarantee that the compiled code contains no defects","A repository that tracks the history of every change","Integrated editing, building, running and debugging in one environment"],"correct":3,"explain":"IDEs shorten the write–build–test loop with syntax checking, breakpoints and step-through debugging. They assist the programmer; they do not replace judgment."},{"id":"dp_pr_6","topic":"Documentation","text":"What is the best use of comments in source code?","options":["Restate each line in English","Store the programmer's name on every line","Replace meaningful variable names","Explain WHY the code does something when it is not obvious"],"correct":3,"explain":"Good code shows WHAT it does; comments should capture intent, constraints and reasons a reader cannot infer. \"i = i + 1 // add one to i\" adds nothing."}],"D684/depth_drill/g4":[{"id":"dp_os_1","topic":"Processes vs threads","text":"What is the key difference between a process and a thread?","options":["Each process has its own memory space; threads within a process share memory","Threads are always slower than processes","A process cannot contain threads","They are the same thing"],"correct":0,"explain":"Shared memory makes threads cheap to create and communicate but introduces race conditions. Process isolation is safer but costlier — the core trade-off."},{"id":"dp_os_2","topic":"Virtual memory","text":"A system runs a program larger than its physical RAM. Virtual memory makes this possible by:","options":["Compressing the program's code so that it fits in RAM","Splitting the program across several physical machines","Using disk space to hold pages not currently needed in RAM","Holding recently used data in a small fast memory"],"correct":2,"explain":"The OS moves pages between RAM and disk on demand. It works because programs exhibit locality — only part of the code and data is active at any moment."},{"id":"dp_os_3","topic":"Thrashing","text":"A machine slows to a crawl and the disk runs constantly while several large programs are open. The MOST likely cause is:","options":["Thrashing","A CPU that is too fast","A corrupted file system","A network outage"],"correct":0,"explain":"When active memory demand exceeds RAM, pages are evicted then immediately needed again. The fix is more RAM or fewer concurrent programs — not a faster CPU. The OS is spending its time swapping pages instead of doing work."},{"id":"dp_os_4","topic":"Scheduling","text":"Round-robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time slice in turn. Its main advantage is:","options":["Zero context-switch overhead","It guarantees the shortest job finishes first","Fair responsiveness","The best possible average completion time"],"correct":2,"explain":"Round robin optimizes fairness and interactivity; shortest-job-first optimizes average wait but can starve long jobs. Match the algorithm to the goal in the scenario. No process waits indefinitely."},{"id":"dp_os_5","topic":"Deadlock","text":"Process A holds resource 1 and waits for 2; process B holds 2 and waits for 1. This situation is:","options":["A deadlock","A race condition","Thrashing","Normal multitasking"],"correct":0,"explain":"Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait simultaneously. Breaking any one condition — such as always acquiring resources in a fixed order — prevents it. Neither can proceed."},{"id":"dp_os_6","topic":"OS role","text":"Which is NOT a core responsibility of an operating system?","options":["Scheduling the CPU","Controlling access to devices and files","Writing the application's business logic","Managing memory"],"correct":2,"explain":"The OS manages resources and provides services to programs; the application supplies its own logic. Exams like this \"which is not\" framing."},{"id":"dp_fs_1","topic":"Paths","text":"What distinguishes an ABSOLUTE path from a RELATIVE path?","options":["A relative path is always shorter","Absolute paths work only on Windows","They are interchangeable in every situation","An absolute path starts at the root; a relative path starts from the current working directory"],"correct":3,"explain":"Absolute paths resolve identically no matter where the program runs; relative paths depend on the current directory — a frequent source of \"file not found\" in deployed code."},{"id":"dp_fs_2","topic":"Permissions","text":"A file is set so the owner may read and write, while others may only read. A non-owner tries to save changes. What happens?","options":["Permissions apply only to folders","The write is denied by the permission system","It succeeds and overwrites the file","The file is deleted"],"correct":1,"explain":"Read/write/execute permissions are enforced per user class (owner, group, others). Least privilege — granting only what is needed — is the underlying security principle."},{"id":"dp_fs_3","topic":"Fragmentation","text":"Over time, files on a magnetic hard drive become scattered in non-contiguous blocks. The main effect is:","options":["Permanent data loss","Files become unreadable","Storage capacity doubles","Slower reads"],"correct":3,"explain":"Fragmentation costs seek time on spinning disks. SSDs have no moving heads, so defragmenting them provides little benefit and consumes write cycles. The drive head must seek to multiple locations."},{"id":"dp_fs_4","topic":"Journaling","text":"What problem does a journaling file system address?","options":["Unauthorized access to another user's files","Corruption from an interrupted write","Fragmentation of a file across the disk","Running out of space in the root directory"],"correct":1,"explain":"The journal records intended changes before applying them, so after a power loss the system can replay or roll back rather than leaving a half-written structure. The journal allows recovery to a consistent state."},{"id":"dp_fs_5","topic":"File organization","text":"Why do operating systems use a hierarchical directory structure instead of one flat list?","options":["Hierarchies use less disk space","It is required for encryption","It groups related files and keeps names unique only within a directory","Flat lists are impossible to implement"],"correct":2,"explain":"Hierarchy scales: two files may share a name if they live in different directories, and related items stay grouped. The same principle organizes packages and namespaces in code."},{"id":"dp_fs_6","topic":"File types","text":"A user renames report.docx to report.txt. What actually changed?","options":["The file was compressed","Nothing at all","Only the name","The file was converted to plain text"],"correct":2,"explain":"The extension is a hint for choosing an application, not a conversion. Understanding that content and label are independent explains many \"this file won't open\" scenarios. The bytes inside are unchanged, so the file may not open correctly."}],"D684/depth_drill/g5":[{"id":"dp_ar_1","topic":"CPU components","text":"Within the CPU, which component performs arithmetic and logic operations, and which directs the sequence of operations?","options":["Both are done by cache","The ALU computes; the control unit directs","The control unit computes; the ALU directs","Both are done by registers"],"correct":1,"explain":"ALU = arithmetic/logic; control unit = fetch, decode and orchestrate; registers = tiny fast storage for operands. Naming the parts and their jobs is standard exam material."},{"id":"dp_ar_2","topic":"Memory hierarchy","text":"Order these from FASTEST to slowest access: RAM, CPU register, SSD, cache.","options":["Cache → register → RAM → SSD","RAM → cache → register → SSD","Register → RAM → cache → SSD","Register → cache → RAM → SSD"],"correct":3,"explain":"Each level down is larger and cheaper per byte but slower. The hierarchy exists because we cannot afford register-speed storage at disk capacity."},{"id":"dp_ar_3","topic":"Cache","text":"Why does a small cache measurably speed up a program that accesses far more data than the cache can hold?","options":["It replaces virtual memory","Locality","It permanently stores the whole program","It increases the clock speed"],"correct":1,"explain":"Temporal locality (reusing the same item) and spatial locality (using nearby items) mean a small fast cache serves most requests. A \"cache miss\" is when the item is not there and slower memory must be read. Programs reuse the same data and nearby addresses repeatedly."},{"id":"dp_ar_4","topic":"Volatility","text":"Which best describes the difference between RAM and an SSD?","options":["RAM keeps data permanently; SSDs do not","Both lose data at power-off","Both retain data at power-off","RAM is volatile and loses contents at power-off; SSD storage persists"],"correct":3,"explain":"Volatility is why unsaved work disappears in a power cut: it lived only in RAM. This distinction shows up constantly on intro exams."},{"id":"dp_ar_5","topic":"Performance","text":"A workload runs many independent tasks at once. Which upgrade helps MORE: a higher clock speed on one core, or more cores at the same speed?","options":["More cores help only single-threaded work","More cores","Higher clock speed always wins","Neither affects performance"],"correct":1,"explain":"Parallel workloads scale with cores; a single long sequential task benefits more from clock speed. The exam gives the workload and expects you to match the hardware. Independent tasks can genuinely run in parallel."},{"id":"dp_ar_6","topic":"Buses","text":"What is the role of a bus in a computer?","options":["It stores data permanently","It performs arithmetic","It converts analog signals to digital","It carries data, addresses and control signals between components"],"correct":3,"explain":"A bus is the shared pathway connecting CPU, memory and I/O. Its width and speed can bottleneck the whole system no matter how fast the CPU is."},{"id":"dp_nw_1","topic":"Addressing","text":"How do an IP address and a MAC address differ in purpose?","options":["They are two names for the same identifier","MAC addresses route across the internet","IP addresses are burned into the network card","IP addresses route across networks and can change; MAC addresses identify hardware locally and are fixed"],"correct":3,"explain":"IP is logical (assignable, routable, changes with network); MAC is physical (assigned to the adapter, used on the local segment). Scenarios about a laptop moving networks hinge on this."},{"id":"dp_nw_2","topic":"TCP vs UDP","text":"A live video call tolerates an occasional lost frame but not delay. Which protocol suits it BEST?","options":["Neither; use HTTP","UDP — lower overhead, no retransmission delays","TCP — guaranteed delivery and ordering","Either performs identically"],"correct":1,"explain":"TCP retransmits lost packets, which costs time — great for files, bad for live media where a late frame is useless. Match protocol to whether reliability or timeliness matters more."},{"id":"dp_nw_3","topic":"DNS","text":"A user types a website name and the browser must find the server. Which service performs that translation?","options":["DHCP","FTP","SMTP","DNS"],"correct":3,"explain":"DNS is the internet's phone book. A \"site loads by IP but not by name\" symptom points straight at DNS. It resolves domain names to IP addresses."},{"id":"dp_nw_4","topic":"Devices","text":"What is the essential difference between a switch and a router?","options":["They are interchangeable","A switch forwards traffic within a network; a router forwards traffic between different networks","A router works only with wireless","A switch connects to the internet directly"],"correct":1,"explain":"Switches operate inside a LAN using MAC addresses; routers connect distinct networks using IP addresses. That is why your home router is the boundary to the internet."},{"id":"dp_nw_5","topic":"Latency vs bandwidth","text":"A connection advertises very high bandwidth, yet a video call is choppy.
